=== Canvas 8 (Prelim. 1v) ===
[Full Page]
When Easter Term does begin:
Be it known that Easter Term always begins the 18th day after Easter
and [counts] that same day for one, and ends the Monday next after Ascension Day.
Trinity Term does begin:
Always the Friday next after Corpus Christi Day; and ends
the Wednesday fortnight after.
Michaelmas Term does begin:
Always on the ninth or tenth day of October; and ends
the twenty-eighth or twenty-ninth day of November.
Hilary Term does begin:
The twenty-third or twenty-fourth of January, and ends
the twelfth or thirteenth day of the month of February.
Note this: that in Easter Term on Ascension Day; in Trinity Term
on the Nativity of Saint John the Baptist; in Michaelmas Term on
the Feast of All Saints and on All Souls' Day; in Hilary Term on Candlemas
Day; nor upon any Sunday: the King's Judges do not use to sit
in judgment.
For the carp, either in pool or in the river.
Take a bait that is called a cod-bait [caddis-fly larva], and first put your hook through the middle
of him, or any of them; then put one on the point of your hook lengthwise,
and so angle with this, and the carp will bite at it. — H.
To make a bait for [carp / to make a paste?]
Take the shavings of horn, and good strong wort, and boil your horn and your wort together
until it be as thick as tile [or jelly], and then strain it through a linen cloth that shall be
newly washed, and then dry it well, and then put it into your tub and so make it up.
[Trial pen-strokes / faint note: for sinew ache ...]

Henry Dingley

[Right Column (Feb End, Spring Regimen, March)]
Days 25-28 Feb (Invention of Paul, St. Alexander, St. Julian, St. Oswald)
Ver or spring-time begins when the sun enters
into the sign of Aries: and it endures 93 days, that is from the
11th day of March unto the 12th of June. In this time the
day and night are equal in this region; the time grows
pleasant and sweet; the air is purified; the springs
boil out of the earth; the moisture that in winter abode
in roots ascends up into the crops [tops] of every plant;
beasts and fowls renew their kinds, and fishes go to their spawning,
and trees themselves, and bring forth their fruits in their
kinds. The earth is beautified with flowers of fresh colours
and the trees with flowers and fruit, and everything that bears life is
refreshed. The world is then likened unto a maid
of 17 years of age that is beautiful both of face, body,
and all kind of gorgeous apparel. Ver [Spring] is hot and
moist, and it is temperate like unto the air; the blood
of man is quickened and stirred abroad into all parts
and members of the body; and it settles in that which is equal
in complexion, that is to say temperate. And in the time
of Spring thou shouldst eat hen, chickens, capons,
and such like, and new-laid eggs soft-dressed among them
— that is to say seldom — and eat wild lettuce, i.e. raisins; drink
eat goat's milk, for it restores natural breath. There
is no time of the year more better or more profitable
to bleed in; and in that time labour and moving of the
body is good; to bathe, to provoke sweat, to drink
and eat syrup made of spice and of herbs that are semi-
purative, and to take purgations is good. H.
March has 31 days.
Days 1-18 March (St. David, St. Chad, Sun in Aries 11 Mar, St. Gregory 12 Mar, St. Edward 18 Mar)

Note: Easter Day is never lower than the 22nd of March nor higher than the 25th of April.
Days 15-30 Apr (St. Alphege 19 Apr, St. George 23 Apr, St. Mark 25 Apr)
Night has 10 hours, day 14. | May has 31 days.

[Right Column (May-Jun Calendar & Summer Regimen)]
Days 9-31 May (Sun in Gemini 12 May, St. Dunstan 19 May, St. Bernard 20 May, St. Augustine 26 May, St. Bede 27 May, St. Petronilla 31 May)
Night has 8 hours, day 16.
Aestas or Summer begins when the sun enters into
the first degree of the Crab [Cancer]: and it endures 92 days, that
is to say from the 12th of June unto the 13th of September.
And in this time the days are lengthened, and the nights
shortened, and in all regions heat increases; the
winds are inflamed by heat and dryness; the sea is pass-
able; streams are gathered [low]; venom is destroyed; the fruits
lie well in their strength, and leaping are flies and venomous
at their food whereof they have plenty. The air is
clear, corn grows ripe, and then the world is like
a spouse complete of body and of ripe age inflamed with heat.
The time of Summer is hot and dry, in which red choler
is raised, exercised, and abounding in bodies disposed. And it be-
hoves thee to beware of every meat that is hot and dry of
complexion, for that excites red choler. Abstain that time
from repletion both of meat and drink, lest natural heat
be quenched; but eat those and such things that are moist and
cold of nature, as veal with vinegar, fat chickens, capons,
cucumbers, and such other. Your pottage should be made with the
bran of barley. In that time those which are of sour taste
and sour-apples do less hurt to the body. And in this time
of Summer forbear the loss of women [venery], letting of blood, and
baths, and from overmuch moving of the body; for all
those things are counselled not to be overmuch used in this
time of Summer: therefore beware, and again I say to thee, beware! H.
June has 30 days.
Days 1-7 June (St. Nicomedes 1 June, St. Boniface Pope 5 June)

[Right Column (Aug Calendar, Autumn Regimen, Sep Calendar)]
Days 10-31 August (St. Lawrence 10 Aug, Sun in Virgo 14 Aug, Assumption 15 Aug, St. Bartholomew 24 Aug, St. Cuthburga 31 Aug)
Night has 10 hours, day 14.
Harvest [Autumn] begins when the sun enters into the first
degree of Libra: and it endures 89 days, that is from the 14th
day of September unto the 13th day of December. In that time the day
and the night are equal, and the night begins to grow and takes part
of the day; the air grows cold; the winds blow; waters grow [low];
the green things of the earth fade; fruit and leaves fall; and the
beauty of the earth, trees, and herbs are gone; fowls fly into hot regions;
wild beasts seek their dens and repair their burrows where they gather food
to sustain them in winter; the fishes draw towards the deep places
of the rivers and waters. Then the world is likened unto a woman of
58 years of age that has need of clothes, for youth is gone from
her. Harvest is a time cold and dry, in which black choler [melancholy]
sleeps [abounds]. Therefore it behoves thee to eat meats that are hot and moist,
as chicken's flesh, chickens, young doves, pork with powder of ginger,
and drink old wine of deep colour, sweet wine, and eat sweet grapes
pies, and abstain from all meat that engenders melancholy, as beef,
goose, old pigeons, pork, sour grapes, shellfish, cheese, and such
other. Then put in exercise the moving of the body more rather
than in summer; use baths in this time if need be, and use laxatives, and
if a man need to open a vein, let it be but a little, and that in the
hottest hour of the day, for in such hours of the day superfluities
are gathered in a man. Also the purging of the womb/belly is to be used
in that time with pills called diasena, and with electuario rosato,
lapis lazuli, and vinegar, and such other as purge or drive
out black choler, and also repress humours. H.
September has 30 days.
Days 1-20 September (St. Giles 1 Sep, Nativity of Mary 8 Sep, Sun in Libra 13 Sep, Exaltation of the Cross 14 Sep, St. Edith 16 Sep, St. Lambert 17 Sep)
The summer is day by day / Go good husband by and by...

[Right Column (Nov End, Winter Regimen, Dec Calendar)]
Days 28-30 November (Vigil & St. Andrew Apostle)
Night has 16 hours, day 8.
Hiems or Winter begins when the sun enters into the
first degree of the Goat [Capricorn]: and it endures 89 days, that is to say from the 13th day
of December unto the 11th of March. In that time the days are shortened
and the nights are lengthened; cold grows mighty; the winds grow
sharp; the leaves of trees are fallen, and all green things for the
most part die; the most part of beasts that are wild do draw into
caves and deep places of the earth to keep them from the bitterness of the
time, and air with hoar-frost dark; beasts both wild and tame do crouch in
dens, and the strength of their bodies is weakened; the fishes of fresh
waters do draw into the deeps and lurk in hollow banks, and into great
shoals, and all for fear of the winter's cold. Then the world is likened
unto an old woman nearly naked going to death. The time of winter
is cold and moist; in which time it behoves to change thy diet,
and to return to hot meat and hot substance, as chickens, hens, capons,
partridge, pheasant, birds of the bush both wild and small, goat's flesh roasted,
hog's flesh, and lambs; all hot spices, and red wine, figs and nuts; also
hot electuaries and syrups. Abstain from loosing of the belly
with medicines, and from letting of blood, unless great need require
it. Then change the air, that is to say draw thee into warm and
close places from the coldness of the air; anoint your body with hot and precious
ointments, and tepid baths. Much moving of the body, nor the deeds of venery,
nor sudden or much eating hurts not, so that digestion be not enfeebled;
for in that time of great cold the natural heat is gathered into the
inner part of the body, and therefore in winter is the digestion best; and in
Ver [Spring] and in Summer the weather is hot, and in those times the pores are
opened, and the natural heat dispersed into all parts of the body; and
for scantness of heat the digestion of the stomach is enfeebled and hindered.
And humours are moved to the extremities. Give God thanks for preservation. H.
December has 31 days.
Days 1-31 December (St. Eligius, St. Nicholas, Conception of Mary, Sun in Capricorn, St. Lucy, St. Thomas Apostle, Christmas, St. Stephen, St. John, Holy Innocents, St. Thomas Becket, St. Sylvester)
Night has 18 hours, day 6.

=== Canvas 13 (Prelim. 4r) ===
[Full Page]
4 [Folio number]
The weights which are most in use at this day do follow written:
The 10th day of August in the year of Christ 1564, and in the 6th year of Queen Elizabeth.
A pound is written thus: li. j, li. ij, etc. Half a pound is written thus: li. s., or thus: li. d., or li. s.
An ounce is written thus: ℥ j, etc. Half an ounce is written thus: ℥ s., or ℥ d., or ℥ s.
A dram is written thus: ʒ j, ʒ ij, etc. Half a dram is written thus: ʒ s., or ʒ d., or ʒ s.
A dram and a half is written thus: ʒ j s., or thus: aureos, or thus: aure.
A scruple is written thus: ℈ j, ℈ ij, etc. Half a scruple is written thus: ℈ s., or ℈ d., or ℈ s.
A handful is written thus: M. j, M. ij, etc. Half a handful is written thus: M. s., or M. d., or M. s.
A little handful is written thus: p. x. or pugillus. A great handful is written thus: Manipulus.
A quarter of a pound is written thus: qrt. or q. Half a quarter is written thus: qrt. s., or q. d., or s.
A corn-weight or a grain is written thus: grana, or gra., or gr., or g.
And when you must take of each one alike much, or of each a like quantity, it is written thus: āā or ana.
And this figure following signifies ginger: ℥ʒ, or thus ℥ʒ, or else thus ℥ʒ j ginger.
The least of all weights commonly used among physicians is a barley-corn weight; and 20 good corns
make a scruple (℈), and 3 scruples make a dram (ʒ), and 8 drams make an ounce (℥), and 3 ounces a quarter, and 12 ounces make a pound (li.).
Wheresoever you see this character H.D. stand in the margin of this my book against any medicine, oil,
ointment, salve, plaster, water, powder, syrup, electuary, unguent, water, or any other thing contained
within this book, that same I, Henry Dineley, proved; no other doubt, and no other have I myself proved. Finis.

Poultices come to my hands
Lastment toward the this
on the other side
[1] Take of mallow leaves 2 handfuls, bugloss,
groundsel 1 handful; bind them in a linen
cloth and boil them in the broth of
veal until they be tender; then
stamp them very small and add
to them cream of sweet milk, 1
half-pound, crumbs of white bread as much as suffices, beat them
over... mixed with half a pound of oil of roses,
3 oz. Boil all together and in the...
adding thereto of yolks of eggs
2 in number, and make a cataplasm. This
assuages pain and suppurates
tumors.
To cleanse and heal filthy ulcers
[2] Take of best coriander and herb Robert 3 lb,
leaves of ground ivy, marigold, wormwood
and mallow of each 1 handful, leaves of honeysuckle
and celandine of each 2 handfuls, tops of rosemary
and leaves of cabbage of each 1 handful, roots
of bryony mixed 3 oz.; shred that which is to be cut
very small, then boil them until they
be tender, then add bean flour, linseed
and fenugreek of each 3 oz.; boil and stir
them until it comes to the form of
a cataplasm; apply it hot and...
morning and evening; it cleanses
and heals rotten and filthy ulcers.
This another poultice 47 B
[3] Take of best coriander 1 lb, yolks of eggs
3 in number, fine wheat flour q.s.; mix them well
and gently boil them to a cataplasm;
then add thereto powdered verdigris 1 oz.; mix
them thoroughly, and after due washing
apply it to any old rotten, stinking, and
filthy ulcers morning and evening warm.
For Inflammation
[4] Take leaves of henbane, boil them in milk
and after stamp them with a little saffron
in powder and make thereof a cataplasm;
apply it warm. 54 B.
For dropsical tumors
[5] Take cow dung 1 lb, goat dung
3 oz., aniseed, fennel, caraway of each ½ oz.
Make a cataplasm. 55 f.

[6] Take white dog dung and honey of each q.s., make a

For pain in a hot cause in the joint
[7] Take crumb of a loaf 1 lb, fresh milk

=== Canvas 19 (Prelim. 7r) ===
[Left Column]
Poultices
To dissolve a hard impostume
[16] Take mallows, violets, and hollyhocks
of each 2 handfuls; boil them in a pottle of
spring water until they be tender;
then take them out and cut them and pound
them small; then put them on the fire
again in the same water, and put to
linseeds bruised 4 oz., barrow's grease and
fresh butter of each 3 oz., and boil it until
it be thick, and apply it hot and it will
dissolve or break the impostume.
For an uncome ache, and for many other evils
[17] Take brooklime, wormwood, smallage,

Out of Leonardo Fioravanti
Petra Philosophale of Fioravanti, against all diseases
Take saltpetre, rock alum, Roman vitriol of each
1 lb: first dry the vitriol in an earthen pan,
then beat it to powder and mix it with the other
things, then put to sal gemmae 4 oz.; then put all
in a gourd with head and receiver well luted, and in a
wind furnace distill it with wood fire; little at
first and increase it according to art; and when
wet closes upon the head and receiver, because
the spirits shall not fly away, the receiver
will wax red like blood, and after turn white,
and when you give it strong fire it will turn
red again, and lastly it will turn white again,
and then it is ended; keep this close stopped in glass
to make the Petra Philosophale.
Take mercury 1 lb, quicklime 6 oz., common
ashes 4 oz.; mix them together in a mortar of
stone; put them in a retort, and distill it with
strong fire until all the mercury be run into
the receiver; then take it again, then wash
it clean; then take it forth and keep it in a glass to make the composition.
Take the water that was first made and
put it in a gourd of glass well luted, then put
in the mercury that was distilled; then take gold
in thin plates 1 dram, silver in thin plates 2 drams, gold leaves
1 dram; put them all together in the glass, and shake
it, put on the head and receiver, and set the glass into the
furnace; give it fire until all the water be run
forth in the fume; let it cool and keep it close.
Break the glass and in the bottom is the Petra Philosophalis.
Grind it small, searce it, then wash it
with distilled wine, and when it is dried again wash
it with rose water, and dry it very well, still
over the fire; then keep it in a glass.
The water that was distilled from
the stone will serve for the same purpose
again, but you must take but half the quantity
of the aforesaid matters.
When the water is again distilled,
keep it close for infinite purposes.
It cleanses the stomach.

Alchemy of Anselmus Boëtius [de Boodt]
Preparation of Lapis Lazuli
Let the stone be reduced into pieces the size of a hazelnut,
which with tepid water and lye...
so that they may be cleansed, and...
quench them in best white vinegar, or
distilled and filtered; and repeat this several times, the
oftener the better; some repeat six times. The calcined
pieces are pounded in a covered brass mortar,
then pass through a fine sieve; keep the powder
diligently. And it is washed thus:
Take spring water ½ lb; to this add as much honey as
a hen's egg can hold, and boil these in a new pot
so long until you have removed all the scum, then
take from the fire and keep. Afterwards take dragon's
blood (best) 3 drams, grind on marble with a small
quantity of the aforesaid water, then put in a glass, and
add so much of the aforesaid water until it acquires
a violet colour; keep this well washed for use.
Washing of the powdered stone
Take a barber's basin, or similar turned vessel
wide, put in this the powder of lazuli, and pour
over sweet lye so that it stands 3 fingers above, and
wash well with the hand...
while it settles, afterwards pour the water into its vessel,
and let the powder dry a little in the shade, until
spread upon a porphyry stone until it be wholly dried.
Preparation of sweet and strong lye
Take ashes of vine-twigs passed through a sieve
10 lb, put in a vessel having a hole at the bottom, so
that it be stopped and pressed down firmly; pour on
hot water 20 lb little by little; then open the lower
orifice so that it can only flow out drop by drop. When
it flows no longer, stop the orifice and the lye
which flowed out distill twice through a filter, and
keep in glass; this is prepared strong.
Upon the ashes again pour 20 lb of hot water
and do as before, and you have medium lye.
Repeat with other water a third time, and it becomes sweet lye.
You shall prepare the stone this way for a plaster
When you have broken it into pieces, put in a vessel and reverberate,
then wash with vinegar; thus it becomes the best part, which resists.
Of Lapis Armenus
To induce vomiting, of the unwashed stone are given 2 scruples to
3 drams, more or less according to the disease and patient, to move the belly.
Take the stone washed fifty times and until taste and odour
vanish, ½ dram or 6 drams in tepid water etc.;
in no way does it trouble nor provoke any vomiting,
and with less trouble black humours are expelled
with great relief. Wherefore, even if
another patient should shrink from its use, we may
boldly use it; for this medicine has no
bitter, nauseous, or malignant quality.
More concerning Lapis Armenus is profitable.
Pills of Lapis Armenus
Take hiera picra ½ oz., epithymum ½ oz., agaric 3 drams,
scammony 1 scruple, cloves 1 dram; pound all together
and incorporate with honey of roses q.s.; dose from
2 scruples to 3 drams. These pills purge all humours, but chiefly
black humours without trouble.
Take the washed stone as before ½ oz., hiera picra
2 drams, mace, cloves, saffron of each 1 scruple, honey
of roses a little; make a pill mass; dose from 1 to 2 drams according to disease and patient.

epilepsy, nightmare, insanity, mania, folly,

black humours...

Tincture of Coral
Dissolve coarsely bruised coral in distilled vinegar;
when it dissolves no more, pour off and pour on fresh as often
until all are dissolved. Then evaporate
the vinegar so that the corals become dry,
to which pour on pure water, and make sweet
the calx by a third washing until no taste
appears, and the corals appear white. Put the calx
upon marble in a cellar, so that it turns into
water; to have the tincture pour onto the calx
spirit of wine so that it stands 5 fingers above, and digest
for some days; thus the spirit turns yellow, which being poured off,
pour on more as often until it is tinged no more.
Put all this spirit in a glass, and set to
separate in ashes. Then afterwards
draw off the spirit until the corals grow white.
Upon the dregs pour again spirit of wine, and
cohobate 7 times, distilling until no taste
remains, but only the tincture or oil
remains; if rightly worked, it will have the colour
of conserve of roses.
Virtue of the Tincture
It brings the body into temper by a certain celestial power,
and therefore removes all internal affections
by the roots, because of a certain analogy
it has with the vital spirits and innate heat, which
it increases and strengthens so that it may easily
overcome contrary diseases.
It is reported to cure epilepsy completely in a few weeks,
especially if prepared with spirit of vitriol,
even if one has laboured under it from fatal causes.
Therefore the tincture is commended for
white and red fluxes, which it stops so that no other
medicine better...; it also restrains all
flux of the belly and of blood from whatever part it flows.
It also heals chronic gonorrhoea,
far more efficaciously and with less danger than powder of prepared coral.
In the French pox or plague, in...
if fever is present it gives wonderful succour.
Pestilent diarrhoeas or dysenteries are no less cured by the same dose.
For melancholy and tympanites
Take coral 3 oz., oriental saffron 4, St John's wort of each 3 oz.,
storax calamita, labdanum of each ½ oz., white spirit of wine
2 lb; boil together in a glass cucurbit 24
hours, then let the fumes exhale and pour off;
thus the corals become hard and red; pound them in a mortar
and grind on porphyry...
Liquor of corals for all aforesaid effects
Take coarsely bruised corals, dissolve in strong
vinegar and digest the dissolved [corals] for a month; thus the
vinegar is tinged, which pour off and pour on more until
it is coloured no more. Then filter what was poured off, and with gentle
fire evaporate all, wash the residue, dry,
and rectify in spirit of wine, then distill, and
lastly dissolve upon marble; thus you shall have
the true liquor, of which give 6 or 8
drops in a convenient liquor for all said evils.

Tincture of Corals with Spirit of Oak
When the moon is waning, in the first three days before
sunrise, while the moon travels in an earthly sign,
cut off some branches [of oak], which cut into small
pieces, distill gently through a retort, casting away
the phlegm that comes out first, or receive it separately;
you can separate the phlegm in a water-bath from
the spirit and oil. Reduce corals into the finest powder,
which calcine until they nearly glow white, then
put them in the spirit which follows the phlegm in
distillation; leave in digestion
for two days; thus the spirit extracts the red colour,
which being poured off, heat the corals again, and
cast them into fresh spirit until
it has all the colour; which obtained, draw off
the spirit by distillation and at the bottom you shall have the tincture.
Essence of Corals is thus prepared
Take corals reduced to fine powder 1 lb, white nitre
and sal gemmae of each 1 oz., grind all upon
marble, put in a vessel and pour on chicory water
1 lb; stop the vessel and place in sand or ashes,
and give fire of the second degree, digest for a month,
and pour off the water, and coagulate, or
if you will draw off the moisture by alembic, so that
a red liquor remains in the bottom. If the redness
does not please, repeat the work. Of which essence
are given 10 or 12 drops in an appropriate
water or wine for all aforesaid things for which
tincture of corals is offered. With an appropriate water
it eases pain of the eyes, stops tears, and
cleanses and disperses spots growing in the eyes.
Of the Tincture of Corals, Anselmus Boëtius [p.] 157
I can certainly testify that I, lying in the extremity of a pestilent
fever, and having fainting fits every
moment, and for four days and nights without any sleep,
with all bystanders despairing of my recovery,
having drunk six drops of the tincture in a cordial
draught, was immediately and as if miraculously
delivered. For as soon as I had taken two
cordials of the tincture, the spirits of the heart
were so refreshed, and...
I felt it pass through all parts, so that forthwith,
as if the darkness of the disease were driven away by light,
without danger it moved sweats and
cough (though no matter had preceded),
and drove out very many purple spots
to the skin; by which continuous sweat
I shortly recovered my former health.
Virtues of Coral against perils

[Right Column]
Of Amber or Balsam
By descent with a vehement fire from amber, no
powder being reserved, is made...
almost of asphalt, burnt
fluid, of the colour of liquid bitumen, in consistency
like oil...
Put this into a retort, and of a most clear gold colour
an oil of sweet odour...
finer it brings forth. This afterwards distilled through
a water-bath yields a most subtle oil
and to be referred to all the aforesaid...
most fit for curing and preventing epilepsy, apoplexy, palsy,

Oil of Amber otherwise
Take powdered amber, let it be poured with strongest lye
then put into a glass cucurbit
and roasted with a fit fire;
above is placed an alembic...
a tall glass canal is added so that the oil
may have a longer way, for thus it is better distilled.
Being distilled it is rectified again. Moreover,
a third time it is distilled by some so that it may be purer,
with salt or oil of salt added.
Others first dissolve it pure in spirit of wine,
macerate the amber and then distill the oil.
Others in strong or distilled vinegar.
Others distill by slow fire and afterwards rectify by repeated distillation in a water-bath.
This method is celebrated by many
Take fragments of amber not finely powdered
1 lb, add powder of calcined flints or clean
sand 3 lb; put in a luted retort and place
it in the furnace with a glass receiver
with water; proceed with slow fire and there will come forth
white oil descending into the water. When it begins
to grow yellow, change the receiver, and collect it
separately in another receiver; in this way
you have the oils: white oil from 1 lb, 2 oz.; yellow ½ oz.;
red 1 oz. The fire ought not to be stronger than
is required to melt wax. If it becomes greater
it will boil over. You can rectify them
and they will come out limpid like water.
Magistery from Amber thus
It is pounded most finely, onto which is poured spirit
of wine so that it may dissolve, and digested for a month.
Afterwards all the tincture...
so that in the bottom remains the oil/magistery of amber,
by which vertigoes are driven away
and it avails for all things for which the oil does, and
a single drop of the oil does more than six of the magistery.

To prevent contagions of the air, plague, and catarrhs,

Of Crabs' Eyes
Crabs' eyes are celebrated for the dissolving
and expulsion of coagulated blood; wherefore
they are used in potions of great efficacy.
They also break stones, and expel gravel through urine:
reduced into powder and drunk with diuretic wine.
Essence of Crabs' Eyes
Crabs' eyes reduced into the finest powder, and
put into cucurbits; pour over thrice-distilled vinegar, stop,
close, and digest for a night upon warm ashes.
On the following day pour off the dissolved [liquor], and
pour on more, so often until you see them dissolved. Filter the
collected vinegar, evaporate in a bath; there will remain at
the bottom the salt of crabs' eyes. Repeat this on porphyry
marble and leave in a cellar until it dissolves into
a liquor, of which 8 or 10 drops may be given with radish
water for the stone, for urine, and for symptoms
to prevent and cure suppression of the powder.
For ulcers and powdered [preparations]
Let crabs' eyes be dissolved with part of essence and
spirit for the space of a month in a water bath: afterwards in a
gentle fire let them be distilled purely
by making a distillate. Lastly in
a water bath let essence of wine be extracted six times from the other
cohobating; then you shall have an arcanum of which a scruple
with 2 spoonfuls of fumitory water or some [other],
taken morning and evening, renews, purges, cleanses,
purifies all that is against nature and remains
excellent.

[Right Column (Preparatio Magnetis, Olei Martis, Callaminaris, Crocus)]
Preparation of the Magnet [Lodestone]
First let it be beaten into powder in a crucible
let it be heated red-hot, and quenched in oil of Mars [iron]
measured of the same weight, then at the fire the same
let it be dried; thus the magnet is prepared.
Magnetic Plaster: Cures all
wounds inflicted by thrust or cut immediately, and
symptoms which are wont to follow upon powders
it prevents. Whatever malignant thing is in the wound
or in the weapon it separates from the body, and generates
sound flesh.
Take of purified wax 2 lb, of common turpentine
turbid 1 lb, of olive oil 3 oz; melt all together,
adding juice of comfrey, juice of oak leaves,
juice of lady's mantle, juice of lion's foot, of each 1/2 oz;
boil all together until the juices are consumed;
afterwards add ammoniacum, galbanum, and opopanax
purified in vinegar, of each 2 oz, colophony 1/2 oz,
amber 1/2 oz, mastic, myrrh, frankincense, bdellium,
of each 2 oz; mix all into the plaster. When it
has cooled, mix in of bruised and prepared magnet
3 oz, crocus martis 1 oz, immediately then
1 oz, prepared tutty 2 oz, calamine stone
prepared 10 oz. Mix all these afterwards into the plaster
and when it has now almost cooled, add sweet earth
of vitriol so much that the plaster becomes reddish; well
mixing, afterwards take out and knead with hands
and reduce into the form of rolls, and upon a wooden
board anointed with oil of roses and into tablets
form of such thickness, keep for use: see page 43.
This ought to be so tempered that when it warms it softens well
and when it cools, it does not crumble, but like glass
breaks. See page 43: earth of vitriol.
Preparation of Oil of Mars [Iron]
Take alum 1 lb, common salt 3 oz, from which distil
water, with which water moisten iron filings several times
a day, so shortly you will have rust,
which wash with water, and evaporate it thence to the
consistency of oil. Again by one distillation
you shall sweeten it, namely pour water on each and
evaporate, as before; thus the oil will be prepared.
Preparation of Calamine and Tutty
Reduce into the finest powder, and let it be heated red-hot;
being red-hot throw into a pot filled with the strongest vinegar
and immediately cover the pot until the powder is extinguished;
afterwards pour off the vinegar quietly. Heat the powder
red-hot again, and extinguish in the same vinegar; lastly
again let the powder be heated and, cooled, be kept.
Tutty is prepared like calamine,
except that instead of vinegar one should use fennel water or
celandine [water].
Crocus and Prepared Salt
Take thin plates of copper, put them in a pot, let the plates
be buried with common salt, and the pot placed on the fire
let them grow white-hot; afterwards pour out the plates with
the salt into cold water and put in the plates, so that the
blackness is removed; again add salt and put in the pot, grow white-hot
in the fire again and throw into cold [water] and wash, extinguish the
plates as long as you please; pour off the water in which they are
extinguished, afterwards gradually pour off warm water,
so at the bottom you will have crocus of Venus [copper].
Red like blood, which wash and cleanse
very well until it has no saltiness, dry it
grind very well, [put] cleanly and keep for use.

Bleaching of Wax is thus done:
Let wax be melted in a thin vessel, then
let it be dipped in cold water: and thus draw out
the wax subtle and thin like leaves of a tree,
and upon a clean board expose it to the sun, and
let it be sprinkled with water for some days, and
it will be whitened like cloth; in every ointment
for the face to be used.
To make white wax to rub silk to hang hooks:
Take resin 1 oz, wax 2 oz, hog's grease 2 oz; melt
them, pour it into cold water, then draw
it and mix it well, etc.
To make musty vessels sweet:
Dip linen clout in melted brimstone and
strew upon the clout powder of cumin
and of cloves; set fire on the brimstone and
put it in the vessel and stop the bung close
and so let it burn to ashes.

=== Canvas 35 (Prelim. 15r) ===
[Left Column (Rod Bands & Soldering)]
I delighted in angling and made my rods myself.
For white tin bands:
Buy double [tin]plate and cut it fit for
your cane, and let it be a little too big;
then wrap the sides over on an
other and make them round, and
bind them about with a wire, and
make them fit and close to the cane.
Then you must cut your solder
in small thin pieces no bigger than
little straws — and lay it in the
inner side close upon the joint,
and put a little fine powder of
resin upon the pieces of solder.
Then hold the plate in the
flame of a candle and the tin
will melt and the solder run;
when it is run, it is fast.
Then wash the smoke of the
candle off the outside and put
it upon the cane; or scour
it with a clout and some sand.
If you make boxes to put in hooks or other things:
First solder the band: then
cut a square piece of plate a little
too big for the end: and in the
four corners strike in holes: then
take four little pieces of wire and
make a hook at one end: put
that hook upon the out-end of
the box and the other end through
the holes: and so thrust them all
abroad to hold the bottom fast;
then lay on your pieces of solder
and resin, then hold it over the
candle and so make it run in one
place first, then in another, until
all be done; then with a pair of
shears cut off the plate round,
and so you may make the top.
For yellow [brass] bands:
Buy double latten for pointing;
cut them, then bind the edges to-
-gether with wire: then have silver
solder cut as small as hair — or else
smaller — and wet the brass with spittle
in the joint; then put on your solder
in little pieces; then put on borax
in powder a little all along; then
lay it in burning coals and blow it
and you shall see it run together;
take it out of the fire and cool it;
then scour it clean: upon a lathe
is best with a felt: you may do the like
with latten brass: and it must be made
bright with a file in a little lathe.

[Right Column (Solder Recipes & Bait Paste)]
Old pins of solid latten
very thin will solder well, or you
may buy silver solder at the
goldsmith's weight for weight:
it is 3 parts silver, 1 copper.
White solder is 3 or 6
parts lead and 1 or less of
tin: a piece of an old glass
lead melted with a pewter dish
is excellent good solder.
Good for other means to make
white tin bands, but here's
easy and fine enough.
Both these sorts of bands must
be as close in the joint as may be,
but the white may be the wider
of the lead.
A pair of old tailor's shears
will cut both.
A Paste to fish with:
Take crumbs of white bread, put
them to water coloured yellow
with saffron; put it in a dish,
beat it with a pestle until it be
paste; put to [it] a little sugar in powder
and beat it again (it must be
very soft); then put it in a lead
box and hang it at your girdle.
If the water be clear, then
straw-coloured paste is best;
if foul water, then somewhat
yellow your paste.
Note: if your paste be too stiff, then
it is not good; for unless the fish
when he pulls take some of the paste
away, he will not bite it.
Therefore make it so soft and
tender that you must take it out of
your box with your finger and thumb
and put it betwixt your lips and
so roll it, and then gently put it
upon the point of the hook: the
loss of the bait makes the fish
bite the better.
Have crumbs of white
bread and honey in a box in your
hand when you fish: you
must be liberal, and feed well:
and then they will bite and spring
paste as a hen's egg is enough
at once if you feed...
A tinker told me that solder will run and solder yellow bands with borax.

=== Canvas 36 (Prelim. 15v) ===
[Left Column (Perch Invention 1632, Pastes, Rods & Floats)]
A new invention to take Perch, 1632:
Take young green peas, boil them so
tender as you would butter them:
cast in some to bait withal, and
put on upon your hook: when the
peas be greater, pikes etc. will
not bite at them, but only whilst
they be young and tender.
If you colour your paste with saunders or
bole, or red lead, in some places the
fish will bite the better.
Wheat flour, water, the white of
an egg, and pound, make fine
white paste, but it will dry too
fast in the sun.
Wheat flour, water, salt, and a
little butter, is good paste.
A plumb without a quill | A plumb with a quill | Pruned wood is best for trout
The best rods be of hazel or 11
yards of cane or bigger...
alder, and carried it in a case; the
rod may be 12 foot long.
Fish with a small line with paste in
places; at the hook a quill and
blackthorn cropped are better
than hazel wands, but they must
be gathered in winter and hung to
dry: they will stand crooked or
else hazel [with] a whalebone.
Two swan's quills thrust one into
the other: that which is downward
and the little hole cut off, put on the
quill; to hold the line let your quill be
of a reasonable length and bigness.
Hang your lead on your line and not upon
the hook; when the hook is hanged
8 inches from the hook is enough.

[Right Column (Ground-Baiting, Avon, Of Wormes & Silk Lines)]
In a still water you may bait with
ground malt wet in the water in
your hand and thrown in: but in the
hinder [deep] of Severn you cannot do
so. And here when the water
is high, fish near the shore, and
when the water is low, far off
the shore.
In Avon and the bank-sides is best
fishing at all times.
Fish with lead kneaded and the thumb
in Severn, and therefore plumb
the depth.
And so fish at passage in Severn:
it is best that is to stand and cast in
your hook up the stream and let
it run down as far as you can
reach: and then strike in: the
fish enough if it may sink.
Of Worms:
Your worms must lie upon the ground
a foot or two about and lie still,
and then you must have a great
quill or a cork: the cork must
be long and cut biggest in the
middle and round; stick upon
a pin a quill thrust through,
and upon it sprung, and not too
long above the cork the quill
downwards...
to run through.
The best water trick is but upon 2
pins: that is one inch of either line and
betwixt put stone and a plumb
hard and then drawn together.
Cast plummet in a coffin of paper and
put upon a small green stick and
bore a hole in the top and thrust in
a quill or a forked stalk.
Boil...
or milk and then with your quills and
be rendered...
for you may cast plummet in clay...
into the clay and make a green
stick enough in the middle to make a hole
for the back...
When you fish with great worms make your
lines of silk and hair at the hook,
and have silk twisted green or
the hair and in silk, and at the hook
2 hairs of silk at the most.
Water-coloured lines:
the white hair is on black, and the
flingers twist to black in the middle.

[Left Column (Toad & Adder Toothache Remedies, 1618)]
Toothache ☾☾
Take the greatest toad you can get,
thrust him through with a sharp
stick and pin him fast to the ground;
then with a woollen cloth take him by
the hinder foot, and with a sharp
knife cut off his head and gristles
left on; the... and the left bones...

Put a dead toad in a [ant?] hill full
of holes and set the box into an
ant-hill and the ants will eat
away the flesh and leave the bones.
Put either of these bones upon
the aching tooth — the...
and the tooth, and...
contrary way upon one side and
the pain will run forthwith always,
and the ache will stop presently.
I have proved it 100 times ☾☾.
The... of the gristles and the bones look brown and rusted.
I was told ☾ 1618:
Anoint the cheek against the sore
tooth with the grease of an adder, and
it helps presently. I had this
here in August 1618: but I will, if God
please God, and want...
For the toothache ☾☾:
Take alum 1 oz, long pepper 1/2 oz;
in finest powder mix them well.
Get a cup upon coals
with a draught of ale (the cup
must have a wide mouth: a
black goddard); put in half
your powder and so much honey
as a great bean or more;
stir them well together and let
them boil.
Then have ready 2 little linen
clouts as long as a finger; put
them into the ale: and standing
hot, with a knife take out one and
put it into the cheek that aches
hanging down your head on one side;
and when that clout is cold,
put in the other; let it do half
an hour, keeping one clout in
the ale, the other in the mouth
as warm [as you can bear], and so
it is most...
and I have very often proved
it and never failed ☾☾.
I called the bones of a Cinophia, an Indian bird.
Backwards is...

[Right Column (Latin & English Toothache Remedies, Tobacco Pipe Smoke)]
Pain [Toothache]
Take vitriol and dissolve in strong vinegar in
a pan, add mercury as much as you will and
let it be boiled, and you will find when it comes out
an amalgam: of that amalgam
put into the hollow of the tooth and it hardens
like a stone and avails in every hollow.
For the same:
Take olive oil 1/2 measure, pellitory 3 drachms,
and 1 oz roses... all finely
powdered infuse in the oil in a well-luted glass;
set in the sun 14 days, then strain
and press out strongly: then put in
of white vitriol very fine powder 1/2 drachm and
again expose to the sun, until applying
apply a drop with cotton
to the aching tooth; it assuages the pain.
For the same ☾☾:
Take a toad, kill him and put him in
a pot and burn him to ashes, or
dry him and make him into powder;
put as much of that powder as a
pea in a clout, knit it with a
thread close, and put it to the tooth
hollowed or not; it will stop
the ache quickly ☾☾.
Otherwise ☾☾:
Bruise the herb brooklime and
put it into the ear upon the
same side the tooth aches, or drop
2 or 3 drops of the juice into
the ear: lie down on the other
side and it will stop the ache.
I have proved this often ☾☾.
To take out a tooth without pain:
Fill an earthen pot with emmets [ants] and their eggs;
let them melt upon the coals and then
burn to powder or ashes: make this
into powder and touch the tooth therewith.
It is written that the powder of
a black toad will do the like;
the gums must be wrapped with the
juice of plantain presently after
the tooth is out — which I do not believe.
Toothache ☾ ||| Margaret:
Take distilled water of plantain 1 lb,
of rosemary leaves 1 handful; let them be boiled
to half; hold it in your mouth and wash the
tooth therewith.
For the Toothache:
Cover a drinking glass with parchment
and bind it fast that no air go out;
cut a little hole in the parchment; put in the
little end of a tobacco pipe: blow the glass
full of smoke; stop the hole with your finger
and the smoke will turn to oil: do so until
you have 2 or 3 drops of oil: put it on a
to the hollow tooth: the hole must be cut and
the paper left on in this sort and thrust
down with your forefinger.

[Left Column (Weights & Measures, Crescent Marks, Bone in Throat, Barber Balls)]
Weights and Measures
Granum, a grain, marked gr.
A scruple or 20 [10] grains, ℈ j
A drachm is 3 scruples, marked ʒ j
One ounce (℥) is 8 drachms (ʒ).
A pound, lb 1 or 16 oz
Half: semis, ß, or di., or s.
A handful: M. j, manipulus
Pugillus [a pinch] between the finger and thumb is marked p.
A spoonful: coc. [cochleare]
Number: no. 1, 2, 3.
As much as suffices: q.s.
According to art: s.a.
Of each: ana, or an., or aa.
Apothecaries' / Avoirdupois at 16 oz to the lb:
A pound contains 6912 grains;
An ounce contains 432 grains;
A drachm contains 54 grains;
A scruple contains 18 grains;
Obolus contains 9 grains.
At 12 oz the pound [Troy]:
A pound contains 6912 grains;
An ounce contains 576 grains;
A drachm contains 72 grains;
A scruple contains 24 grains or 2 oboli;
A halfpennyweight contains 12 grains.
So that in 16 oz the pound:
Obolus is less by 3 grains;
A scruple, 6 grains;
A drachm by 18 grains; than at 12 oz the pound.
An ounce by 144 grains.
Which is great odds in the
giving of physic.
And in making ointments and plasters,
therefore weigh the things all 12 oz the pound.
These two marks ☾ ☾ show those that
be medicine[s] marked by me; and
one mark by some other ☾.
For a bone in the throat (empirical):
Hold your mouth close together, and
sniff cold water at the nose, until it
come out at the mouth.

A Pipe to heal thrusts [stab wounds], page 71, of my own invention; and in boxwood it will not be much bigger, in length 6 inches.
Twist and wind the pipe with your finger
and thumb as far into the wound as
you can: then put a sponge into the
pipe and thrust out the blood that stops [it].
Then put in your balm, thrust with a wand
gently so the balm sinks; or else it
is stopped: then stop it with your probe; wind
the pipe out gently, tent the wound,
cover the mouth with a plaster, as page 71.
An Excellent Probe:
Take the sinew in the back of an ox
newly killed, cut it in long slices: lay it
in the sun, or by the fire, and nail it
straight on a board: when they be dry,
shave them to what bigness you will.
Or buy probes, page 27.
Nail it at both ends or tie it fast.

=== Canvas 39 (p. 1 (2)) ===
[Page Header]
In the name of God

[Left Column (Repercussives)]
Repercussives
I have often found by experience that
by repercussion and driving back of a
humour that has been gathering unto a
place, there has ensued no sore
at all in that place, to the great ease
of the patient.
When I did use repercussion, I used
to purge the patient with purgation first;
I chose to let blood very seldom, be-
cause I delighted not in it.
The matter either well purged
or drawn away, then I used
some of these simple or compound
medicines following:
Simple Repercussives with-
out stopping are:
Oil of Roses
Petite morel [black nightshade].
Something stopping are:
Umbilicus veneris [navelwort]
Stonecrop
Endive, Succory.
Labrum veneris [teasel].
Some stop and dull the sense:
Juice of lettuce, Poppy,
Mandragora, Henbane,
Dwale, i.e. Solanum [deadly nightshade], opium.
These are used in great need and
extremity, or not.
Repercussives full
stopping are:
Garden purslane,
Orpine, Smyxebue [houseleek],
Brooklime.
Good repercussions are made
of:
All the sanders [sandalwoods], dried roses,
Spodium, Bole Armeniac, Red
lead, Terra Sigillata, White
lead, etc.
If you use the first of the
powders:
Take of the first 2 oz., oil of roses
3 oz., vinegar ½ oz.; make an ointment.
Otherwise:

[Right Column (Refrigeratives)]
Refrigeratives.
Take oil of roses 2 oz., bole ½ oz., of
vinegar ½ oz.; make an ointment. If you add
terra sigillata 2 oz., you need not
fear corrupting the member.
Repercussivum
Take psyllium seed; let it be tied in a linen cloth
and boiled in vinegar; press out
the mucilage, and apply the mu-
cilage to the painful place, and often re-
new it: for it drives back excellently, soothes,
and mitigates the pain.
Repercussive and Refrigerative
Take white of egg, and bread soaked in
cold water and vinegar together;
mixed with juice of sempervivum, i.e. houseleek
[barba Jovis]; mix well, apply cold,
and change frequently. Excellent.
Unguentum Morell [ointment of nightshade] for
heats.
Take petite morel [black nightshade], green plantain,
smyxebue, violets?, lettuce, beet,
brooklime, of each 4 oz.; stamp them
and mix them with fresh butter 2 lb.,
and so let them stand 9 days
infused, then boil them and
strain them.
Refrigerative Defensive
Take red lead or white lead, oil
of roses or rosatum Mesue; pound
them to an ointment in hot cause.
Refrigerativum
Take spume of silver [litharge], juice
of coriander, vinegar and oil; mix
in a mortar; make an ointment.
Ointment of Egg Whites, Refrigerative
Take whites of 2 eggs, beat them well
together, then with wheat flour
like pap; then add bole in powder,
½ ob. [scruple?], oil of roses and vinegar of each,
and make thereof an ointment.
Note: if the place be broken
or apostumed [abscessed] ready to break, then
use no repercussive, but a defensive.
Note also that a cold matter
may not be repercussed, but defended
in the beginning.
Refrigerative
Gather May dew after a fair day
in a dry night, and wash heat in
arms or leg therewith.

Refrigeratives
An excellent cooler, and
Repercussive.
Take adris pares [?] and white dog's
turd; make it into powder very
fine. Temper it with scum of
white bread vinegar a little and
the juice of smyxebue q.s.; pound
all together to a thick poultice, and

dried, put to more vinegar and the

be wanting, take spring water
or verjuice, and some fair water.
Unguentum album [white ointment] made to dry,
abate heat and swelling.
Take white lead in powder sifted

over the fire in a pan and

stir them well until they do
begin to wax hot. Then take it
from the fire and stir it still,
then put in ½ oz. or 3 drams of
fine powder of camphor and
stir it until it be cold.

it cools and heals.

Scabies [The Itch / Scabs]
Scabies from blood are known
by redness in the limbs and softness,
then indeed also a sweetish itching is
frequent and...
From choler, by dryness and
aridity in the limbs, by pricking
and biting burnings and sharp
itchings, by fissures of the limbs,
and by which sanies is generated.
From salt phlegm, the places grow
yellowish and from the scabby place scales
fall, and the itching is moderate, and
moderately generates sanies.
Note: if scabies abounds from
above the diaphragm, the cephalic vein
is opened:
If below the diaphragm, the
hepatic vein is opened.
For itch and scabs:
Take turpentine, oil, and a little salt together;
let them be ground until they turn white and
be laid up in a vessel; then add
soap... a little, and let them be well ground;
make a plaster and anoint the body with the ointment
Also...
anoint the scabs and it will be healed.

extinguished 1 dram; let them be mixed.

or strong vinegar 1 dram; let them be mixed.

This is black ointment.

For Scabs and Itch (Black Ointment):
Take mercury sublimate ½ dram in fine pow-

... set it on the fire in a gallipot;

=== Canvas 49 (p. 11) ===
[Left Column (Maturation Discourse & Poultices)]
When neither repercussion, refrigeration,
nor purging will keep the humour back,
but that it must be ripened and broken,
then does it turn [to] an ulcer or foul
sore, and being not well looked unto, does
continue long before it be healed; and
many times turn into a fistula.
I have therefore thought good for
to follow my intended course for the
maturation and ripening of such of
these humours as will not be repercussed.
And first, for the things which the
country's so-called cunning women do
call 'taking': which white, black, or red
fauces [swellings] being indeed nothing but humour
settled in a place, and will not be stricken
back, nor cooled, because there came putting
thereto scabs or ointments to them,
and so suffered the humour to get a head
and then must be ripened, and broken
and healed: which may be done two
ways: by poultices of sundry sorts
which must be applied hot and break the
head and abate pain, or by ointments
that [are] maturatives or ripening medicines.
The first I did not love, but in
case of greater heat, because I see it to
be a torment to the patient and...
done; yet I did know many excellent
poultices as follows:
A Poultice to assuage swelling
and take away pain:
Take spring water 4 lb., smallage,
mallows of each 2 handfuls; chop them small
and boil them well. Then add oatmeal
and linseed beaten small 3 or 4 handfuls,
vinegar a little, red wine a pint, and
almost ½ oz. [pint?] milk from the cow,
sheep suet 1 lb.; boil them and stir
them until it be thick, and apply
it hot as may be.
Otherwise:
Take mallows 3 handfuls, violet leaves or flowers
½ handful; chop them small, then boil them
in the water wherein a pullet was boiled
and herbs with wine and barley flour;
then add 2 egg yolks, mix all well
and apply it hot.
To assuage heat, redness, etc.:
Take coltsfoot [?], red sage of each 1 [or] 2 handfuls;
chop them, then pound them small; then put to
sheep suet and pound all together: then have
oatmeal and milk ready boiled, put therein
the herbs and suet and let them seethe until
it be thick, and apply it hot, and over
12 hours change it and lay it on hot.
Mr. A. L.

[Right Column (Poultices)]
Poultices
Mr. Trew's Poultice in Baronetta:
Take the leaves of the great spurge 1 handful, the
leaves of white lilies ½ handful, oatmeal 1 handful
½ beaten small, ewe and sweet milk
of each q.s.; boil it into a poultice: and being
made, put to a little oil of roses. But if
it be an ulcer, add oil of St. John's wort
a little; apply it hot.
And wash it with this water:
Take pimpernel leaves, briar leaves, wax [?]
woad, woodbine, and plantain of each 1 handful;
boil them well in running water,
then strain it and boil it with white
honey and alum, and wash the sore warm.
These are excellent.
For Swelling or Bruise:
Take the grounds [dregs] of the strongest ale
a quart, of smallage, mallows, and
brooklime of each 1 handful; chop them small
as may be. Then boil them well and
strew therein by little and little oat-
meal or fine wheaten bran, and
being thick apply it hot.
Otherwise:
Take oatmeal groats, bruise them,

be thick like pap: then add sheep

together and apply it hot.
Otherwise:
Take the grounds of good ale...
crumbs of brown leavened bread;

spread it on a cloth and apply it hot.
Against Inflammation:
Take crumb of wheat bread as much as you will, put
in a pot, add beer: let them be boiled
until it become a paste, spread upon a cloth
of wool, and apply warm and well;
let it be bandaged; it drives back redness and inflammation.
For Impostumation [abscess]:
Take brooklime 1 lb., mutton suet 1 lb.; chop

the suet and boil them in part, and add
... then add salad oil and
aqua vitae of each 4 spoonfuls; stir them well
strain it: anoint the sore with the liquor
and bind the herbs hot to the place
as hot as you can, and leave all on hot.
For a King's Comb [carbuncle?] a Poultice:
Take linseed and wormwood of each by
weight; bruise the seeds in a mortar, chop
the wormwood, then boil it well in the

digestive, and mollificative that are for
loosing, ripening, softening must
be made both with care and soft;
etc. If it be too hard, they prick

and stick not to it.

hardened.

[Left Column (To Breake an ympostume / Apostume)]
To break an impostume:
Take Roman soap, 4 [oz] red lead in
powder, clean wax of each 3 oz, litharge
of silver powdered 3 oz. Boil all on a
soft fire until you may spread it;
test [with] your finger on a cold stone; then
take it from the fire and hold your
face away and pour on a little
vinegar, then make it up.
Make your plaster of this as big as
the wen or apostume is, and in the
top cut a little hole as big as a penny,
in which hole put of plaster of lapis
infernalis dissolved and cover it with
some of the plaster and let it lie so
24 hours; then change that little pla-
ster and warm/smoke the great one and
anoint under the great plaster
with hog's or hen's grease, and let
that little plaster lie 24 hours;
and so the sore will be hard in the midst
and soft round about, and will come
out in the whole core; then heal it.
Maturative:
Take mallows, violets, wormwood, of each
1 handful; mallow roots 4 oz, wheat
flour 1 handful; let them be bruised and boiled
with unsalted butter 3 oz and hog's
grease 2 oz, and apply. See 342 and 607, salt.
To break an apostume:
Take a lily root, roast it under the
embers in a wet paper. Dissolve
galbanum with badger's grease, mix
them and apply it.
To break an apostume:
Take vitriol, arsenic, of each 2 drams; sublimate
1 dram, bryony juice 6 drams, quicklime
powder 2 drams; let them be distilled for use in a re-
tort. One or two drops may be applied
to the place.
Otherwise:
Take one or two drops of oil of vitriol;
this does but burn the skin and
will assuage the swelling/poking but not
break it immediately.
An infallible medicine:
When it is gathered unto a head and
is almost ripe, open it with a knife,
for it is better than waiting when it
will break, especially in a bubo. But
safer with caustic medicines, and heal
it with basilicon; and you may touch the orifice with
oil of vitriol, one drop upon lint, after it is
open, and then apply dry lint with a drawing plaster
on the top, as diachylon cum gummis, de minio, and
melilot.

[Right Column (Bubo, Cataplasm, Plasters)]
I have known some lie 11 or 13
weeks with a bubo pent up and yet
not break it.
Bubo is an impostume in the
flank [groin] as big as a swan's egg,
and is gotten of corrupt women, and
many times is of diverse colours and
will stink when it is opened.
After a little time I found
it best to open them with a knife and
tent them, draw them, and heal
them as other sores with maturatives,
mundificatives, and sanatives.
It is more safe to open them with caustic medicines.
For where the skin is thick it
is far better to open the boil,
bubo, or impostume than fear its
weight: for hereby the pain is much
abated and eased.
Before you cut it, anoint it with
oil of roses 3 or 4 times, and after
it is cut you may anoint it also.
Beware you cut not felons or
cat's-hairs, for they must not be
touched with any sharp instrument;
yet one may rase the skin betwixt each
A cataplasm to ripen a bubo:
Take crumb of bread, raisins
stoned, of each 1 oz; fresh butter and
hog's grease of each 2 drams, cow's milk 6 oz,
saffron 1 dram, leaven 5 drams; make a cataplasm.
Wonderful from within.
A plaster for the same:
Take mallow leaves, violet leaves, of each 1 handful; roots
of althaea 1 lb, white lily bulbs 3 oz;
boil them very soft in fair water,
then pound them small, then add wheaten
meal or barley meal as suffices, oil and
fresh butter of each 3 oz, hog's grease
2 oz, 2 egg yolks; mix as a plaster.
I used to draw boils
with Emplastrum oxicroceum or
a plaster of Burgundy pitch, and
because they would stick: after
they were spread upon leather I
did rub them over with deer or
wether's suet, and then they would
come off gently. One plaster or 2
at the most will draw out the
root if it be ripe.
A good resolutive:
Take a thin cake of lead as broad as you will,
rub it over with quicksilver and apply
it; it resolves coldest humours / boils.

[Right Column (To prevent a ffelon & Alabuhar Absintij)]
To prevent a felon:
Boil groundsel in fair water until
it be tender; put away the water clean,
and add salad oil as suffices, and beat and work
them well together like a salve; apply
it warm. Do this in time and kill it.
For a felon:
Take smallage 1 handful, rosin, bacon as suffices,
the white of an egg, honey, and wheaten
flour; beat the smallage and bacon by
themselves, then add the white of the egg,
then the honey and flour. This will be
painful at the first laying on, etc., for
it must lie on till it grows easier;
change it, and lay on new; it is said
to be a most sure medicine.
For the same:
Take wormwood and smallage, of each 1 oz; of
hog's grease 2 oz; beat them all together in
a dish or a mortar and apply it; it
is a proved remedy.
Let the patient keep his own dung
as hot as it can be from his body, and
[it] will kill it when it first comes.
For the same:
Take salt, smallage, and oil stamped together
and applied; and in short time it
does kill it; or water bryony pounded
with hog's grease and applied.
Alabuhar Absinthii:
Take the juice of wormwood, plantain,
smallage, of each as suffices; put clean hog's
grease in a stone mortar; put to so much
of the juice as will cover it, beat it
with downright strokes 2 hours,
put in a clean thing, cover it close,
and let it stand nine days; pour
the water that is in it clean out,
put to more juice and pound it again;
this do thrice at 9 times or more,
then put it up and keep it close. This
keeps a wound open, abates the
swelling and burning of wounds,
applied with pledgets of flax.
The like may be made with scabious
for boils, felons, etc., or of half-
wood or saponaria [soapwort].
A better way is:
Take the juice of the herbs, put to it
swine's grease half as much, and
boil them until it will arise
no more, and then keep it.
Of the flowers all-heal scabious,
so etc., and keep them all the year.

until they be hard and may be powdered.
Take of that powder, of mastic, olibanum,
frankincense, myrrh masticated, and
verdigris, of each 3 oz, [rosin/resin] 1 lb,
all made in fine powder (along with mercury)
and sifted; of barrow's grease 1 lb.
Melt the grease, let it cool a little and
stir in the powders well; then the mercury,
stir it well that the mercury be not seen.
This heals old sore, pox,
or any fraudulent [malignant] sore, as I am told.
See page 30, Master Draper.
Perfume the leg with cinnabar, myrrh, and frankincense.
To break an impostume:
Take oil 1 lb, white lead or ceruse in
powder, clean wax of each 2 oz, litharge
of silver 1 oz. Boil and stir them
until you may spread it with your
finger upon a cold stone; then
take it from the fire, and hold your
face away, and pour in a little
vinegar; stir it well.
Make a plaster of this as big as will
cover the sore, and make a little
hole in the plaster as big as a penny
or a mite; upon the hole put some of
the lapis infernalis or other that
will mortify, and lay thereon
a plaster of the same salve; and
so let it lie 24 hours; then take
all off and wipe your great plaster
and lay it on again; then cover
the little hole with no lapis
infernalis on a new plaster, and
a plaster upon the top as you
did before, and let it lie 24 hours.
And when you take off the great
plaster, anoint the sore round
about with fresh hog's grease.
The sore will be hard
in the middle and soft round about,
and so the venom 2 or 3 [days] will
pour and come out, and then will be
a hole which you may heal up.
For hollow sores and ulcers:
Take oil of vitriol as suffices, put it into a glass with
as much oil of tartar and let it stand
four days; then take of that oil 1 dram and
good aquafortis 1 dram, mix them and therewith
wash hollow ulcers and it will heal in
short time, and it heals any rude kind
of scab or sore caused of the thick quality
of nature. This heals malign and cancrous
ulcers, fistulas, etc. S.G. is G.

[Right Column (1618 Case, Emplastrum Butirij, Diet Drink)]
There came to me in the year 1618 a woman
with a sore leg that had been sore
2 years, and it was a deep hollow
hole with thick edges. I applied the
first salve upon the next side and took
out the whole core, but it would
not heal nor incarnate by any
means. Then I distilled leaves of
all-heal, and in that water I put
white copperas, bole, and camphor
as on the next side the second
water, and washed it warm with it,
and applied the white sanative
as in p. 22, salve 2, and this did
begin to work well; then with this
water and Emplastrum Butyri p. 57
I brought it up in 40 days: the water
must be used warm twice a day or
the oftener the better.
Emplastrum Butyri (164. r. 2):
Take May butter clean strained,
colophony 1 dram, wax 1 dram; melt your
colophony and the wax, then take it
from the fire and stir in the butter,
but boil it no more, and it will be
a fine soft salve; apply in holes
with lint and lay a plaster thereof on
the top; dress it twice in 24 hours.
I dried up this sore with the powder
of the rinds of pomegranates.
See 164. r. 2, the best salve, 65.
An excellent drink for ulcers:
Take sarsaparilla 3 drams, guaiacum 1 dram,
roots of each 1 dram; macerate in purest water, boil
over a slow fire to the consumption of half, adding at
the end sanicle, bugloss, mouse-ear, pimper-
nel, ribwort, avens, comfrey
greater and lesser, and madder,
red wine 1 oz; make a decoction. Let him take it early
in the morning and sweat, and after dinner 4 oz without sweating,
and at other hours if he will. By Lowe, etc.
fol. 939, after dinner 4 oz without sweating.
In healing old sores:
Be sure to make them clean unto the
bottom and then begin your cure, etc.
After the proof of this I made butter of
herb-wort and therewith made the salve
called 74, to which butter in the one I put
alkanet and made it somewhat red; and the
salve did heal the better.
The herbs in the drink:
Sanicula is herba Walteri or diapensia;
pilosella is mouse-ear; pimpernel is anagallis;
quinquenervia is ribwort; caryophyllata is avens; consolida
major is comfrey; minor is daisies;
pimpinella is burnet; all these roots dried and boiled.

=== Canvas 57 (19) ===
[Left Column (Old Sores & Sublimate Water)]
Old sores
As I have said before, when small [sores]
will not be corrected but breed foul
and loathsome ulcers and sometimes they
grow to be fistulas, then I used this
course ensuing, which, finding them full
of dead flesh (as commonly they are),
I used this following:
To heal an old foul sore
out of [Adry]:
Take turpentine 1 oz; wash it three
times: 1st in common water, 2nd in plantain
water, 3rd in rose water (or any 2 of them);
put thereto half the yolk of an egg,
oil of roses 1 dram, sublimate in fine
powder 3 drams; mix them well and make
thereof a plaster and apply it.
This must be done in a morning,
for the pain is great for a time; let
the patient sit by the fire and keep warm,
for it causes a great deal of pain.
Let this lie on until it bring
out all the dead flesh; and that must
come out gently and not be forced out
nor caused to bleed if you can possibly,
and then will it heal of itself
alone, or its cleansers clean it;
and yet on the part put on fresh butter, etc.
as in fistulas I intend to describe, etc.
A defensive for the same:
Take oil of roses, vinegar, of each 1 oz,
bole as suffices; make an ointment. Anoint
with this round about the sore, or
with some other defensive, and it will
help much.
But if the sore happen to be broad and
deep, as oftentimes they are, then if
you mistrust the course, I have set
down in fistulas the incarnatives
and sanatives, and so heal them.
Besides this aforesaid I used one
other (at the first not knowing it):
Take spring water or rose water 1 lb,
sublimate in powder 2 drams; mix them and
let them stand that the sublimate may
dissolve; wet lint in this water and
wash the sore and lay on the lint all
wet. This water, if it be too strong,
will take away the flesh to the bone;
therefore when good clear red flesh
appears, put on no more water, but
heal it with incarnatives, sanatives,
and such like.
Or make the water weaker:
Take rose water 3 oz, mercury sublimate
powdered to the quantity of a grain; let them be dissolved
and make a lotion.
But you shall find aqua vitae
or the rectified spirit of wine to be
excellent in this case. And p. 43 for
pulvis secretus: for old sores, to make them
clean, etc.

[Right Column (vlceres, fistula, Pox-derived cure)]
Ulcers, fistula
But the savour and smell of aqua vitae is so
well known to all men that it did
make me refrain it and use this
water when I had not spirits, from
which I healed many that had been
very long time sore and had passed
many hands before they came to me.
Thanks be to God.
But if you will use aqua vitae, colour it
with red alkanet, by putting the root
in the nose of the alembic or mouth of
the receiver;
or make it yellow with saffron, thereby
not to have it known.
Look in the waters for waters that do
heal old sores.
And amongst mundificatives which follow,
there to know how to make them clean.
Then use sanatives to heal them,
or incarnatives first to fill them up
with flesh, and so heal them.
The second means to heal old
sores in women or men,
taken from healing the pox, yet
not known to many:
Take ointment [as set down] 1 dram, quick-
silver extinguished in good vinegar 1 dram, and
let them be mixed. See p. 111, r. 2.
Use it thus:
Anoint the leg about the sore very well
with this ointment; when the ointment is drunk
in, roll it with a linen cloth, and thereon
lay more cloth; the patient being in a bed,
you must apply hot bricks (and you may quench
them in salt water if you will) and
wrap them in cloths and apply them
on both sides the leg; and so change
them when they be cold, keeping the
leg 12 hours together or somewhat
less, according to will.
Or four bottles filled with scalding
water and close stopped, and apply them as
the bricks 12 hours; but bricks are of
less danger if the bottle unstop, and
of more heat for the purpose.
This done, let the leg cool and
then go about the healing.
This must be done so often (having
some convenient space betwixt) till
the patient's throat be sore, and then
forbear it.
The body of the patient must be first purged
before this be done, and purged in time
of healing, and some diet drink, etc.
Look in the title Pox, where also look
how to heal the throat being sore, etc.

20 Old Sores
And you must think this to be of some
force, that the pox are healed in this sort
by stroking [anointing] the whole body; but this
stroking the single member is
a new device taken from thence
and not public or common as yet in
Anno 1612.
Now ensue things fit for healing
of old sores, and first:
Three waters alike in this case:
Take white copperas in powder 3 oz, camphor
2 oz, bole 3 oz, all in fine powder. First
melt the copperas, then stir in your
camphor in a little iron pot, and stir it
with a little stick until you feel it begin
to stiffen; then let it cool, then beat
them to powder and sift them; then beat
them with the bole all together and mix them.
Take spring water a gallon, set it on
a quick fire until it be ready to boil;
then take it from the fire and put therein
two spoonfuls of the said powder, and
stir them well together, and keep it
close stopped and let it settle (see p. 28).
Wash the sore with the clear water
as hot as the patient can suffer it,
and lay linen cloth wet fourfold in the
same water.
The 2nd water:
Take white copperas 2 drams, camphor and
bole of each 1 dram, all in most fine powder
mixed together.
Set a pottle of spring water upon the
fire; let it boil well, then take it from
the fire and let it cool until it be
blood-warm; then put in the powders and
stir them well, and wash the sore with
it (see p. 46, 2 excellent waters).
The 3rd water:
Take bole 2 drams, white copperas and alum of each
3 drams, camphor 1 dram; melt the alum and
copperas together, then powder them.
Take spring water 4 lb and put therein of
bole and camphor and let it boil to
a quart; then take it from the fire
and put in the alum and copperas
in fine powder, etc.
These waters heal, dry, abate
heat and swelling.
For ulcers of the legs:
Take lye as suffices, in which put salt, other
boiled, of each 2 drams, sage 1 handful; let them be boiled
very well. Apply hot morning and evening for 8 [days]; then
let them be dried with linen cloths and put upon it
red lead, mastic, aqua vitae, camphor, of each
all mixed very well and moistened on linen
and laid on for 8 days.
A cleanser for foul ulcers so that they may heal:
Take extinguished quicksilver, [sarcocolla], and honey,
in form of an ointment, and apply.

Fistula, etc.

be powdered and stand in infusion, then
let it be boiled twice; then put
in a tub; put the feet up to the knees for an hour
or more, then let the man go to bed and afterwards
anoint with white ointment and bind well.
A wonderful white ointment for ulcers:
Take camphorated white ointment 3 drams, prepared
litharge 2 drams, powder of olibanum, sarcocolla, of each

hog's lard 6 drams, burnt alum 1 dram,
pine rosin 1 dram, 3 egg yolks, salt
1 dram, turpentine 1 dram; mix, make an ointment.
Which no one can cure:
Take ointment Basilicon described by Mesue,
nard oil 1 dram, oil of mastic and wormwood
of each 1 dram, capon and calf fat of each 1 dram,
wax as suffices; make a soft ointment.
For foul old sores:
Take a toad, put him into an earthen pot,
dry him well, make him into powder; cast
of that powder upon the sore and it
will eat off the crust and the good flesh
will appear; then heal it as others.
It incarnates or heals, etc.
Lest humours flow to ulcers of the shins:
Take oil of roses 1 lb, white wax 3 oz, roses 1 oz,
litharge 1 oz, prepared tutty 1 dram, red lead
1 dram, dragon's blood 1 dram; melt wax in
oil when ceruse is added, afterwards stirring;
at the end put dragon's blood, and let them not boil.
Lastly add tutty and stir until
cool, and add a little camphor at the end.
Fustian may be applied moderately
thin, so that the shin may be wrapped, etc.
Perhaps it is cooled in cold water;
knead and make a roll (magdalion). If
the sore break, let it be bathed over hot
water of plantain and roses;
it consolidates wonderfully.
Diachylon for ulcers of the shins:
Take simple diachylon 3 oz, let it melt, and
add washed ceruse 1 dram, mastic, olibanum, of each
1 dram, camphor 11 grains; knead together
well and make a roll.
A wash for ulcers of the shins:
Take white and green vitriol, alum, common salt,
verdigris, sulphur, of each 1 dram; let them be powdered
very finely; boil in water 2 measures
in which [herbs] were boiled to the consumption
of a fourth part, and strain and wash;
it avails also for fistula and bad, cor-
rosive ulcers difficult to cure.
Cancerous ulcers:
Take roche alum, calcine in a crucible,
reduce to powder, and of the said powder 1 dram, honey 2 oz; boil
until incorporated, always stirring; then
cooled and exposed to the air for a whole

Old Sores (p. 21)
Take oil of myrtles 4 lb 2 drams, very fine black powder

for half an hour; afterwards there is no

in the oil; afterwards lay the cloth upon a table
and pour cold water over it, and with a stone
lastly let the cloth be well smoothed on both sides
until it becomes bright and smooth. And such a plaster
lasts 12 days; it cures all ulcers.
