Take juice of smallage, common oil, of each 1 lb; new wax
1 dram, frankincense, birthwort, of each 1 oz;
mix. Instead of smallage juice, take ox gall.
For ulcers of the shins:
Take rainwater 4 [measures], tartar 2 drams, alum 2 drams;
powder and dissolve in a warm place.
If it please, boil a little and wash the place warm
with linen cloths moistened therein; it avails in
fistula, cancer, erysipelas, itching, etc.
Oil of camphor helps malignant
ulcers, and oil of wheat the same.
When it is written vermicularis qui
crescit super tectum, it is stonecrop.
See 159.

[Right Column (with underlying 'Ad ulcera antiqua' revealed)]
Old Sores (p. 21)
Take oil of myrtles 4 lb 2 drams, very fine black powder
together well and stir near a charcoal fire
for half an hour; afterwards there is no
need of stirring, and let it boil together 8
hours, and as long as a pill sticks between the fingers,
do not cease boiling, but when no pill appears,
then it suffices. Taking it from the fire, and
at the end when it is a little warm, put in
a strong fine linen cloth, and stir it
in the oil; afterwards lay the cloth upon a table
and pour cold water over it, and with a stone
lastly let the cloth be well smoothed on both sides
until it becomes bright and smooth. And such a plaster
lasts 12 days; it cures all ulcers.
A consolidating powder for ulcers:
Take yellow myrobalans powdered 1 dram, mastic, ceruse,
litharge, of each 1 dram; make a powder, mix.
Plaster for ulcers of the shins:
Take wax 10 drams, rosin 3 drams, hog's grease 1 oz;
melt over a slow fire, strain and strongly
express; afterwards add calamine stone quenched
5 times in rose water and very finely powdered,
ceruse powder, of each 1 oz; lastly add Roman
vitriol 3 drams; afterwards boil over a slow
fire to a convenient thickness;
make a plaster.
For old ulcers:
Take litharge 1 dram, alum 1 dram, mastic, myrrh, frankincense, of each 2 drams;
let all be powdered very finely, and of this powder
put a little into the ulcer, afterwards put upon it this
plaster: take olive oil 3 oz, wax 5 drams, rosin
2 drams; melt together and add the powder above;
let them be kneaded together; afterwards
let them boil a little and make a thick mass,
and in many other [ulcers].
Perfume: benzoin 4 drams.
My Aegyptiacum for foul sores:
Take burnt roche alum 1 oz, honey 3 oz,
or as in the next preceding page, red vitriol,
oil, verdigris, of each 1 oz, turpentine 1 dram;
boil to redness and make a good ointment.
I used this seldom because the other
cleanses and heals well. HD.
Ointment for cancerous ulcers:
Take very old hog's lard 3 oz, vitriol 3 oz;
melt the lard over the fire and strain; grind the vitriol
in a brazen mortar very long and
with a little oil, and afterwards mix with the lard
and make an ointment. If you add wax and
black pitch, you may make a plaster.
For purulent and moist ulcers:
Take gold litharge 1 lb, very fine powder; boil in
vinegar 1 measure; and dip a cloth in it and apply
to moist places; it heals.
Put frogs in a new earthen pot, stop it
close, dry them in the oven, powder them;
cast on the powder twice a day in summer,
once in winter; it heals Noli me tangere.

=== Canvas 62 (22) ===
[Left Column (Black Salue, Old Soore, Dogturd Plaster)]
22 Old
A Black Salve for ulcers,
very good for foul and stinking [ones]:
Take a gallon of strong ale and of leaves
of woodbine 1 handful, of red-seeded nettles 1 handful,
of redwort with the jagged leaf 1 handful, of
red onions peeled, of garlic peeled, of each
1 lb; of houseleek 1 lb, of bark-dust a little
dishful; stamp all these in a mortar
each by itself, and put them in-
to the ale with roche alum in powder 1 lb;
let them boil on a gentle fire until one
part be consumed, and so let all stand 3
or 4 days; then strain all through a clean
cloth into a fair vessel, and then put to
wax 1 lb, rosin 1 lb, salad oil green
and good 1 lb, of pure honey a quart;
then boil them on a soft fire until the
one half is consumed and that it be
but a pint and a half or thereabout;
then put it into a gallipot and keep
it very close, and use it with lint.
This has great praise. Sir John Chamberlain.
To heal an old sore:
Take white copperas in powder and make there-
of strong water, and wash the sore
therewith until it bleed; then
If it be too strong it will fester in nine [days].
Take white lead in powder 3 oz, chalk
in powder 2 drams, boar's grease as suffices, and
mix them well together in a mortar
unto as thick an ointment as may be;
spread it very thick upon a cloth
bigger than the sore, warm it
and lay it to the sore; then press
it hard and let it lie 6 or 8 days until it
be well hardened; and
when you open it let it take as
little air as you can possibly. Wash
it again with the water and lay thereon
a new plaster and press it hard as
you did before, and within three plasters
you shall see a great change.
See p. 79 & 80; a better p. 175.
For an old sore or pock:
Take the turd of a white [dog], dry it and
make it into powder, and strew of that
powder upon the sore, and apply
this plaster: take salad oil 1 lb, the
turd of a dog, white, hard, and
dry and made into fine powder 1 oz,
wax 1 dram, turpentine 1 dram; boil them
and strain them into an earthen pot
and keep it close.
Look amongst plasters for
unguentum, i.e. dog-turd plaster,
p. 60.
See p. 133, r. 2, Lucatellum.

[Right Column (1612-1617 Clinical Notes, Toad, Mercury)]
Sores
In the year 1612, rosemary well known
in request: they healed marvellous sore
legs by washing with the water and
applying the fat of bacon upon the
sores. And when the water did no good,
they were healed with smoked bacon.
A practice to heal an old sore:
Take claret wine and warm wash the
sore therewith, and apply this compound:
Take oil of roses 12 oz, white wax,
ceruse, burnt lead, tutty, calamine
stone, of each 2 drams; frankincense 1 dram, nightshade juice
6 oz. Boil all with the juice to the consumption of the juice,
afterwards add wax, and when they are cooled,
add the remaining powders and in the best mortar
mix. It dries, cools, cicatrizes,
fills up, and avails for ulcers of the shins and other
putrid and eating parts. This, when
all others failed, did it, 1613.
Diapompholigos, well
made, is the same, namely: take away the
calamine; so did I, and add unto
3 drams, 1 dram of diapompholigos, 2 drams of tutty, and it
did it freshly.
See p. 50, Master Draper's salve and water.
To heal an old sore:
Take a great toad, kill him, dry him in the
wind or sun, and wrap him in wax;
then lay the wax and toad upon the sore
and bind him fast; it represses humours and
makes clean the sore ready to heal.
p. 109, Pox: all the drinks are good to give
to them that have old sores.
A powder for the same:
Let one of a good complexion eat wheaten
bread, or let one eat his bread three
weeks or a month, and during that time
keep his stool and urine; put it into
an earthen pot, stop the pot close, set it
over a fire and dry the dung, then make
it into powder and use it; the pot must be stopped
with clay that no air go out.
For an old sore:
Take oil of bay 3 drams, quicksilver 1 dram, mix
them well; anoint about the sore, cover it
with a tent cloth; keep it still over the
sore until it be whole, because the quick-
silver stays in the cloth; but dress it with
salve and lay on the cloth over all.
After an old sore was cleansed
with sublimate, or with powder of a toad, I
found Emplastrum Butyricum excellent good.
12 Apr 1617: I saw an old sore, etc., was dressed
with wether's suet, wax, lard, oil of linseed
1 dram, verdigris as suffices to make it green,
put in with lint, and it wrought so very
strongly; note this. For oxygraeca.

=== Canvas 63 (25) ===
[Left Column (Fistula Remedies)]
Fistula
Take the barks of the root of the greater bramble, of the leaves
of female hemp or its seed, the top
of red colewort [cabbage], the tops of crowfoot with yellow
flower; let all be made into a powder without sun and wind,
and thereof let pills be made; and after supper give a small [pill]
tempered with wine, and immediately let him go to bed, and
upon the fistula put red colewort leaves.
And note: if the fistula should proceed
to putrefaction of the colour of the pill, it is incurable;
for certain; but if the infirmity casts forth white
colours, it shall be cured; and let this medicine
cure the malum mortuum [evil/dead sore].
If hellebore be powdered and this
powder be put in a little bag, and the bag be made pierced
for a natural day in wine; and with that wine
wash the fistula.
And the patient may sometimes [drink] of
that wine, unless it causes him vomiting, and
it cures the fistula.
For a fistula in an old book:
Take a sucking whelp under a month
old, a little dross honey; then dry him
that he may be made into powder, and here-
with dress the fistula.
For a fistula or hollow sore:
Take the juice of carduus benedictus [blessed thistle],
honey, alum, brimstone, of each a sufficient quantity; boil them
until it be thick and stiff; and when
it is cold, roll a tent thereof about, and make
suppositories [tents] according to the depth of the
sore. And melt alum and honey
in the juice of carduus benedictus, and
squirt into the sore, and then put in your
tent and bind it fast.
An ointment generating flesh,
killing a fistula, and cleansing bones:
Take juice of lemon, honeysuckle, and virgin wax, honey, and
white butter, white powder, 1 pound; let them be boiled and
a very good ointment.
For a fistula (Stooks):
Take rock salt, tartar, agaric, or powder, of each
and with honey let it be made in the form of an ointment, and
dip a tent and let it be put into the fistulas: broken
bones it draws out, evil flesh it corrodes,
and heals the fistula.
A plaster for a fistula:
Take strongest wine vinegar, oil or oil of roses, of each 2 ounces,
finely powdered litharge 3 ounces; let the litharge be ground
with vinegar in a mortar slowly until it dissolves;
then let it be put with the oil in a pot or pan;
let it be cooked together for a whole day until
they turn black and it be like black pitch
black, and in colour viscous, and put in
therein sal ammoniac, with a little honey; it cures
fistulas.
Fistula (Hall):
Hall's strong powder, grounded of strong
drink [ale], bean flour, [rye] flour, of each,
crumbs of leavened bread, bole [Armeniac], all to a paste;
this red ball is burnt in [ale?] and populeon.

[Right Column (Fistula Remedies & Hall's Powder)]
25 [Original page number]
Fistula
Against a fistula, it presupposes evacuation and
a good diet.
Take pine resin, oil of laurel, oil of [?], new
wax, gum elemi, frankincense, of each; mix, let them be made
into an ointment which is sent to the bottom of the fistula. Otherwise:
Take 6 pounds of the best white wine, put in rosemary
3 handfuls, boil a little, and let the whole infusion be put in
for two days; then according to art water [?], and
distill; of which water let it be put to
the fistula as far as the bottom, adding to 3 ounces
of such aqua vitae 1 dram of Saracen alum.
Otherwise:
Take clarified honey 2 ounces, let it be boiled gently to
some glutinosity, and when it begins to cool,
let a very fine powder of frankincense be put in,
aloes, of each 1 dram, and at the end put asafoetida 1½ drams;
then accordingly for a long time let it be ground in
a mortar, and let an ointment be made, much praised.
Otherwise:
Take tops of lesser centaury in the month of August,
3 handfuls, fresh roots of cinquefoil ½ handful, fresh roots
of greater hound's-tongue 1 part, herbs germander, scabious,
of each 1 handful, roasted wine or sapa 4½ pounds; boil
all in a new pot to half; afterwards the herbs
and roots strongly bruised, hard pressed
out; at length over a fire of coals gently
to the thickness of honey let it be boiled; it is an herb
of modern theory [practice].
To heal a fistula:
Take millet seed, hen's dung, of each a sufficient quantity,
burn in an unglazed pot well luted, and when
it is cold, grind it and add iron salt
Item, or more, and as much as you will of
root of earth-gall, i.e. centaury powder; mix
and then put it into the fistula.
Powder to mortify [kill] a fistula:
Take olibanum, sarcocolla, pomegranate flower, dragon's blood,
antimony, plumose alum, of each 1 dram, burnt brass 1 dram;
let a fine powder be made.
To heal fistulas:
Take the shreds of calf skins that the
glovers cut, put them in fair water, add
salt 1 handful, alum ½ ounce; then boil them unto
a stiff size. Roll your tent therein and
cast on the tent the powder of an old
shoe burnt; let your tent harden, then
put in your tent and cover the sore with
the powder of a burnt shoe. This does
dry and heal all fistulas in what
place soever they be.
For a fistula:
Take yolks of eggs, duck's grease, petroleum,
honey, of each; let them be boiled in a new pot until
a drop upon a cold stone hardens,
and therewith let the fistula or wound be filled.
25. Hall's powder: lay [?] the black side next

your finger you may rub the black coal off; then

hot irons make the powder in balls. Hall.

26. [Original page number]
An especial note:
Not long after I had written this before
of fistula, I put my hard tent into a
place on the top of the knee, and into
and a half deep, upon Tuesday, 1 of
December 1612, and it was Friday, 11 of the
same month, before the eschar came out:
I was never so served before, and there-
fore I note it: be not too hasty therefore
to pluck out the tent. [Diagram labels: a., B.]
a. is a piece of a plaster cut, ready to
make the tent of.
B. is the tent made, rolled between the
finger and the thumb, and 3 ends that
are turned off to stand at the mouth of
the hole to pluck it out by.
The tent may be made of
lint twisted hard, but I better
like this, and used none other.
Practice makes ready. Thanks be to God.
See page 30, recipe 2, in which [it treats] of sarcocolla, etc.
To heal a fistula:
Take the horn of an ox or bull for a man,
the horn of a cow for a woman; fill
the horn with soap and put it into an
earthen pot and burn it to powder; then
mingle the powder with hot soap and
thereof make an ointment; and make
a tent of the poor man's salve and roll
it in this ointment and dress it
twice in a day. See [p.] 59 at the end.
Afterwards in the year
1613, my tent deceiving me in the
ball/fleshy part of the hand being hollow, then
I used a quill, which quill I rounded
on with my plaster and placed it so
even upon the edges that it did lie
as close as might be; then did I
spread it with salve upon the top
and used it in all points as before.
Sometimes I found it good
to leave the little end of the quill open,
and then the plaster must be turned
into the quill at the lower end.
The mouth or great end of
the quill may be cut with a scissors or
a knife into 6 or more or fewer parts
to lie as close as the linen tent.
You may put on the plaster upon
the quill with glue if you will, and slit
the quill and turn it as small as you will.
26 [Original page number]
An excellent probe: take the sinew of a limb of beef newly killed; cut it in long slits, nail
both ends stretched out hard, set it in the sun or elsewhere to dry; then with a knife or a piece
of glass shave them as small as you will. They be like whalebone; I say it is a restoration, etc.

A tent for a fistula, be the

In hot summer keep the tents

=== Canvas 65 (27) ===
[Left Column (1616 Tent Case, Colubrina, Balsam of Sulphur, Probes & Sponge Tent)]
Fistula
In May 1616, I put in my tent, and it
was stirred by mishap so that it was
removed half an inch (the tent being
seven inches long), and when it
came out the point was bare, and
the tent left behind a gobbet as big
as a bean, which by reason of the depth
I did not see; but when I had laid on
my plaster (as aforesaid), the young
clear flesh rose up, and brought
out the dead flesh before it out at
the mouth of the hole, where it did
stick fast until I took it out,
and the sore healed. Thanks be to God.
Of snakeweed [dragon arum] for a fistula:
Root of colubrina, i.e., dragons, dried,
powdered, and mixed with black soap,
and applied to the fistula, heals, dries, cleanses it,
dilates and opens the orifice of the fistula, so that dead bones
corrupted may more freely come out and be extracted.
Balsam of sulphur from dia-
sulphur for ulcers:
Take oil of sulphur 3 ounces, wax 2½ ounces,
colophony 3 ounces, myrrh 1½ ounces, frankincense 3 drams;
let the wax, colophony, and oil melt together, and
be well mixed; let fine myrrh be sprinkled in
gradually; let it be boiled with a slow fire,
always stirring with a spatula, until
they are well incorporated; afterwards
after a quarter of an hour remove from the fire until
they be set down and gradually cool, and
it avails for moist ulcers, etc.
After I found the probe following, I did
never care for the other: I made needles
of least probes 12 of one inch long, etc.
A probe for a fistula or wound:
At the apothecaries' [and] chandlers' there is to be
sold a thing called a thumb [whalebone/baleen] to mend
pens [or stays] withal; some of them are bigger,
some lesser; cut off the great end as long
as you will, 5, 6, 7, or 10 inches or more, and
scrape [it] thin and very small; you may
buy of the best for a penny a yard long.
A tent of sponge to dilate the
orifice of a wound:
Take a sponge, wash it clean, cut off a
piece as big as a finger, as long as you
need; make it taper-grown, wet it in
the white of an egg; then bind it hard
with thread to what bigness you will, and
let it lie and dry; unroll the thread
and [cut] the tent with a sharp knife to the
bigness of the wound; anoint it with
what you will, and put it in the wound,
and it will swell and open the orifice, etc.
A water for a fistula:
Take strong water or good vinegar,
steep in vinegar powder of arsenic or
mercury, and distill into the fistula. See p. 23/27.
Strong water is aqua vitae.

[Right Column (Stockerus's Water, Diaflosma, Worm Water & Manicule Notes)]
27. [Original page number]
By strong water is meant
aqua vitae and such like.
Stockerus [Johannes Stocker] writes that oil
from human dung cures cancer and
mortifies fistulas; but to make oil
thereof I know not how.
But distill it and keep the water,
and squirt into the fistula; [it] is reported
by folk to be excellent of his own proof,
and I intend to try it if God will.
I distilled it 1619, etc. It is a good water, but...
For the fistula, stink like his father:
Take the juice of aloes 3 drams, and of
the powder of copperas 1 dram; mix them
well together and dip lint therein.
If the water from human dung
did not stink so much, it will dry and
heal well; but the smell is loathsome,
which I proved 1620.
For fleshy and incurable ulcers:
Take human dung burnt and into
ashes made, powder of black pepper
mixed, and apply.
Look for Diaflosma among
plasters: it [is] good for fistulas in making
of cerecloths made from turpentine:
first melt the oil and wax together;
take it from the fire and stir in the
turpentine; then put in your turpentine
and flour, and so you may have it as
hot and cold as you will. This is
much praised by Master Arderne, and proved.
A water for the fistula:
Take angletwitches [earthworms], i.e. great worms, and
distill thereof a water; also distill
water of radish root; take of the same
waters, of each by weight, and mix them
together, and therewith dress the fistula.
A knife quenched in this
water so mixed, being red hot 3 or 4
times, will cut iron as wood; which
I do not believe.
Note: the probe made of a thumb [whalebone] may
have an eye in the greater end to draw
lawn dipped in balsam through a
deep small wound: the eye must be
made with the point of a small knife and then
opened with a bodkin; put a thread through
the eye and fasten it to a piece of lawn;
wet it in the balm and draw through
the wound: heals with one dressing.
Which note.
I have observed that although the
sublimate be painful, yet when it
once is used, keep away these and dry
and it will heal itself and fill up
suddenly. Which note well.

A tent to heal withal (Dirouant?):
The sinews of an ox being dried and
made into tents to make a tent, is most excellent
and will work great effect.
An ointment to kill a fistula:
Take the juice of arsesmart [water pepper] and oil of roses,
and it will heal the fistula. If you put it
the juice of [the herb] it is good for any
sore fistulated and hard. See p. 126, and
121 of arsesmart: I cannot see how the oil
and the juice may be joined together
without boiling and some wax put [into] it.
But as in p. 126 it may be made an ointment.
Troches of red lead [minium]:
Take the crumb of bread not baked [or] fermented
4 ounces, sublimate 1 ounce, minium [red lead] ½ ounce, rose water as much as suffices;
it heals a fistula.
To heal an impostume that is broken:
Take oil of roses 3 ounces, litharge of gold in fine powder,
turpentine, of each 3 ounces, liquid storax 1 dram, white or
clean wax 2 ounces; boil them gently until it
be black; if it be too hard put more oil; and
on this lay Diapalma or Oxycroceum. [Fioravanti]
Impostume in the groin (Fioravanti):
Take marshmallows, common mallows, the [leaves]
of violets, colewort leaves, white flour,
oil of lilies; boil them, then stamp them
in form of an ointment; apply it until it
look red and is soft, then lance it.
When it is broken (Fioravanti):
Take wax, litharge of gold, oil of frankincense,
of each; boil them until it be black.
For the same (Fioravanti):
Take turpentine well washed, the yolk of one
egg, of each, and oil of roses, and mix them.
Fioravanti: Maturative for a hollow ulcer:
Take oil of vitriol and oil of tartar, of each 1 dram,
aqua vitae 2 drams; mix them and let them stand
10 days, and wash ulcers therewith. Fioravanti.
The oils must stand together before it be
put into the aqua vitae, etc.
To ripen and break a sore, to
heal it and allay the heat:
Take wormwood ½ handful, oatmeal groats 1 handful, milk
from the cow a pint; boil them until it
be thick; apply it as hot as may be
suffered, 2 or 3 [times] a day until it break, and
after the breaking lay on the same 2 days.
Then stamp houseleek [sengreen] and strain
out the juice, and therewith anoint about
the sore; then lay away the plaster.
Take the yolk of an egg, temper
it with 4 drops of oil and beat the
oil and the yolk very well together, and
wash the sore well with white wine, and
with lint dress the sore twice in 24 hours; and
if it be hot, wet a linen cloth in the
white of an egg and the juice of houseleek
well beaten together, and lay over
all the rest, and it will take [away] the heat.
In p. 20 the first water [is] better:
Take white copperas in powder 3 drams, camphor 1 dram,
in fine powder; put into a pot some rosewater and
then lay the camphor and break it all down,
then lay on the white copperas and press it
hard down, then milk as p. 20; then make
it into powder, then the bole as before.

Breast

when I laid on the black plaster

1620, April 29
The Lady Gerard had one of her

Oleum Theriacum [Oil of Theriac]
Take common mallows and not purslane,

of a thick ointment; add best theriac, onion

A poultice for sore breast
Take rue, featherfew, red sage, of each 1 handful; shred
them and pound them small, then pound them with
sheep's suet; have pounded oatmeal and milk
ready upon the fire and put therein the herbs
and suet, and let them boil until it be
thick; apply it hot and change it twice a
day and dress it. My sister A. Fermor.
Breast sore and not broken
Take hemlock, sage, of each 1 handful; take 2 clean

reddest honey 1 spoonful, vinegar or

the breast all saving the nipple hot; then
lay on the herbs hot upon the top and
dress the breast in 24 hours and keep them
warm, and they will not break.

on a plaster of the same.

☾ Perfect directions to heal
☾ the wounded head
First, mark well the cut or fracture in
the head, and cut it + equally crosswise;
if it be [so], begin from the cut or frac-
ture and cut every of your 4 cuts
towards the hurt, by sparing your
thumb stiff at the hurt; and be sure
you cut it wide enough and over it
be so great that it must be cut from
ear to ear; and let the point of
the knife run upon the skull.
Then with a spatula and your nail,
tear the flesh from the skull as
clean as you can and quickly.
Then have ready-made dozels
of lint in fashion like a [flesh/floss] [...]
wound up, big in the midst and
sharp at both the ends.
Begin below and place your
dozels one by one and by another
one above the other until it be all covered,
rowed and close and hard thrust together;
then bind it up and roll it
with 2 or 3 yards of roller [bandage].
In rolling it, have your roller
rolled up at both ends and meet
just in the middle.
That end of your roller that
comes first under must [go] in under the
other, else it will un[roll].
Then stitch your roller and let it
so remain 24 hours at least; if the
wound be dangerous, longer at the
first time.
Have in your hand a sponge
wet in warm water and wrung
out, to take up the blood that runs
out; and in the end the dozels will stop
the blood. This at the first dressing.
At the second [dressing] call the rest
Have dozels enough ready and
stupes the head with sack, or [confect/aqua]
wine, or sharp [tiffle/vinegar] wet.
Then look for broken bones and
splinters at the 3rd or 4th dressing, or
sooner if need be.
Keep the wound close under the
stupes from air and cold, and so
dress him still without salve.
The harder the stupes be, the
better the flesh will gather.
Keep the bare skull clean from
filth, and suffer none of the oil/lint
to stick on the skull.
If the flesh grow proud [proud flesh],
abate it with the powder of savin and
nothing else.
If the new flesh seem soft, it
will harden well enough.
If the quarters knit up at
the bottom, they will sink low enough
in the end, therefore fear them not.

Mundificative [Cleansing Medicine]
Old sores, fistulas, and sore breasts
have need of cleansing, therefore I do
follow in that order.
Some mundificatives do cleanse with
maturation or ripening of the matter
that was not fully ripened. And those
are best when one is forced to cut
an impostume before it be fully ripe,
and when the matter is in part gross
and not ready to be ripened; and in
the nose, and soon ripened as in the
scrofulas, squamy, kernels, and boils
that are hard.
Mundificative for a filthy
sore:
Take turpentine 1/2 lb, wash it in water
wherein barley has been sodden; add to [it]

3 drams, barley bran as much as suffices; make thereof an
ointment without fire and apply it
with lint.

all together and mixed a little

apply: it removes pain and perfectly cleanses.

Of vitriol and how to burn it
Take as much vitriol as you wish and put it in a pot
[of] 2, 3, or 6 drams, whose mouth is well stopped
with lute of wisdom or vinegar; allow it to
dry, and when it is dried, let it be buried in a pot
among coals, and let a slow fire be made, and for
2 hours blow with bellows; then let it be
left in peace until the fire dies out of itself; and
the pot being cooled, it shall be opened, and you shall find
vitriol of a red colour, which is reserved
in glass or in a very strong horn.
And such combustion, he says, [preserves] natural heat,
whitens, and staunching blood
in the nostrils stops it, and in wounds and elsewhere avails
also against herpes esthiomenus, canker,
and venomous and fraudulent apostemes.

Eschar
Look in page 188; take note
of the eschar.
When the corrosives have burnt
the flesh, there will remain dead flesh,
which is Escara, the eschar or crust; and
this scab must be taken away by
little and little, and it will loosen by the
sides, and that one may cut off with a
scissors; and in the end, when it is all off,
there will appear clean red flesh.
This eschar will come forth
by applying tanner's ooze [or: poultice] as
warm as may be suffered; the
scar must be taken ...
some other thing a little at once so
to let the warm oil go under it,
and it is good not to be too hasty in the
getting of it out.

Take honey, butter, yolk of egg, the juice
of marigold [?] mixed cold.
Mundificativum de Apio: p. 39

or such like applied warm; and

You may take them of the mundificative.
The virtues of the German doctor's
green balm, nothing worse:
1. Anoint the temples and forehead therewith
for pain in the head, rheum, pain in the
teeth, and deafness, and the smell taken into the
head; it strengthens memory, keeping the head
warm.
2. It helps sprains, sciatica, and all
pains in the back, joints, and side, by
anointing the place morning and evening.
3. It takes away the spasm, the cramp,
... the place well rubbed therewith.
4. All itches and scabs in old or young.
5. All tetters and scalled heads, the place
first washed with sharp lye.
6. Chapped hands and breast and chaps by the
washing with the same warm with a feather.
7. Wash wounds with your own water, or with some
wine and vinegar, and apply this with lint
and a plaster of the same.
8. All green wounds.
9. Burnings and scaldings, old ...
or fire.
10. It takes away warts on the hands and
corns on the feet, being pared nigh and
laid on plaster-wise.

root both kinds, of smixcenes [?], celandine
of each 1 handful, of alum 2 oz, white copperas 1 oz, of
ginger 1 dram, all in powder; boil them in a
pint of vinegar and a quart of water of a
spring, or in cauldrons, and strain it clean;
then put in mixture of sublimate [and honey?] one
spoonful; boil all a little, sublimate 1 dram.
Lead, but the sublimate [may] be put in
only vinegar; stop the pot with paste and
set it in the oven with bread; let it
cool; strain out the liquor and wash with it.
Then take the herbs and roots
and grind them and strain them; put to them as
much hog's or May butter; then beat
them with 2 oz of quicksilver until the
quicksilver seem not to be seen; put it
up close: for ringworm [?], wild scurf,
pimpled face, and other things.
Before this, strain it hard, and
to the strained wine put burnt copperas alto-
gether, unto the consumption of the wine,
still stirring it, and when it is cold beat
into it quicksilver as before.
A good water to the salve, 160. 2:
Get a pottle of spring water upon the
fire, and when it is hot put therein of
roche [alum] or green copperas 1 dram in powder, or
of good honey 2 oz, and boil them well and skim;
let it clean, and take them from the fire, and
put in it sage 1 handful, and when it is full
cold put the water in glasses, and wash the
sore therewith often, and lay on the plaster, etc.
A healing water:
Take good aqua vitae 10 lb, of myrrh 1 dram, of aloes
2 drams, saffron 1 dram, sarcocolla, frankincense of each 2 drams;
let them be mixed. Fill the wound with this water and
cast on this powder:
Take hepatic aloes 1 1/2 drams, myrrh 1 dram, sarcocolla,
mastic of each 1 dram; make a powder, mix. Or this powder:
Take hepatic aloes, myrrh, olibanum, dragon's blood of each 1 dram.
For cancer and wonderful [i.e. malignant] ulcers:
Take human dung, burn to ashes,
and of that ash and black pepper of each, mix;
it heals cancerous and almost incurable ulcers.
A green water, as on p. 45:
Take spring water 4 lb, alum 2 oz 2 drams, honey
1 lb; boil, skim it clean; add verdigris
in powder 1 oz; stir it until it be well coloured;
let it cool, strain it into a carafe.

[Bottom Spanning Entry (Aqua Caulium)]
See pp. 99, 112. Aqua caulium: Take the common colewort leaves 1 handful
(and small veins), but not the great stalks; chop them, bruise them
a little; boil them in a good quantity of spring water a long time, strain
it gently, wash the sore warm; then dry it with a cloth and lay on the plaster.
Bruise the same leaves and apply unto a sore, and it will make it clean and
heal it in time; dress it twice a day. Cleanses, heals.

[Left Column (Flos Unguentorum, Flos Dingley & Sweete Plaster)]
Plasters
Flos unguentorum, excellent:
Take perresin [rosin] 1/2 lb, virgin wax,
frankincense of each 4 oz, mastic 1/2 oz, deer
suet or sheep suet 3 oz, camphor 2 drams.
Melt that which is to be molten and powder
that which is to be powdered, and boil them and
strain them, and strain them into a
pottle of white wine; then boil them
all together in the wine, and let it
cool a little; then put in of turpentine
4 oz and stir all together until it
be thoroughly cold. This is good for
old or new sores; it heals and
cleanses, breeds good flesh, and does
suffer no corruption in a wound; it
helps the boiling of the ears, salt
phlegm face, thorn, splinter, wounds,
breasts, botches, boils, the spleen, the
reins [kidneys], burnt members, etc.
See p. 63. Emplastrum Henrici Dingley, or
Flos Dingley:
Take perresin 1/2 lb, clean wax,
pine resin, Venice turpentine
of each 4 oz. Boil them on a gentle fire
and stir them; then strain them all in-
to fair water. Draw them between
the hands and work them well; then
make them in rolls; and if the water
have it dried [?], then in place thereof
rosin put Burgundy pitch, and
when you need but 3 oz of the pitch and
the resin and all the other ingredients.
You may divide the salve in
two parts and put camphor in powder
1 dram to the one part, and then no man
can say but that it is Flos, for
that the perresin makes it firm.
This will keep 20 years and
good, and is not much inferior to the
other in operation, and is far lesser of
price, and therefore I used it still in
my practice and did [so]. Thanks be to God.
A sweet plaster:
Take frankincense,
oil, wax of each 1 oz;
melt them and stir them together
to a salve. If you will have it
draw, use most frankincense; if you
will have it incarnate [breed flesh], most wax.
This is a fine salve but will not
stick well.

[Right Column (Emplastrum de Janua, de Minio & Nigrum)]
Plasters   51.
Emplastrum de Janua:
Take juices of smallage, betony, plantain
of each 1 lb, new turpentine, black pitch of each 1 oz;
mix, let them be boiled in wine and always stirred
with a spatula, and when the third part is consumed
dropped in cold water, etc.
do not cease; take off and add turpentine
1 oz and stir very well; then put 2 lb of white
wine in a basin and knead them upon...
wine... then soften
between the hands and gather it; it is very
healing.
An easier making [which] I did
often use:
Take juices of plantain, smallage, and
betony of each 1 lb; black pitch,
resin, clean wax of each 4 oz.
Let them be boiled together over a slow fire
until the juices be consumed; then add
Venice turpentine 1 lb and let all be incorporated
together, nor let them be boiled afterwards.
It avails for all wounds, new and
old, and I often used it.
Emplastrum de Minio [Red Lead Plaster]:
Take oil 2 lb, powdered red lead 1/2 lb,
powdered white lead 1 lb, sifted or bolted;
mingle the powders well together,
then put them into the oil and stir them
until they be well mixed; then set them
upon the fire and boil them gently and
stir them well, and when it does
begin to rise, take it from the fire a
while, then set it on the fire again
and let it boil until it be a salve when
dropped upon a cold trencher, or until
it be black and shining. Look for this water 49. 3. for old sores.
This is good for sores.
Emplastrum nigrum [Black Plaster]
of John of Vigo:
Take common oil 1 lb, litharge in
fine powder, burnt lead in
fine powder of each 3 oz, of wax 2 oz.
Let your things boil there
severally and stir them still about, and in
the end add of turpentine 2 oz and
of the fat of woodbine 2 oz little
by little, and stir them well; then last
of all put in the lead in most fine
powder and stir them together by little
and little. This is an excellent and
fine plaster; I had it by the name of the
Lady Godwyn's Cautia [?]. I did use it
in all my sores, etc.

Gratia Dei, a 2nd making, etc.:

Donum Dei, best plaster:
Take turpentine 1/2 lb, clean wax 4 oz, pitch,
resin of each 1 lb, olibanum 1 oz, mastic 2 oz,
lettuce, herb walter, plantain,
agrimony of each 1 handful; let the herbs be pounded
well in a mortar, then put in one
flagon of white wine, and let all be boiled
together to the consumption of a third part;
then let them be strained, and to the strained liquor put
pine resin, mastic, wax, etc., and
ram's suet 3 oz; let all be boiled
well and stirred very well. Take off from
the fire and put in turpentine and very well
let them be firmed. It avails for wounds; it suffers not
dead flesh to grow in a wound;
it is also good for nerves, shins, the spleen;
it draws out iron, wood, and venom
from any member whatsoever.
To cure wounds:
Take resin, deer suet, barrow's [hog's] grease,
clean wax cut of each 1 lb; the juices
of plantain, bugle, avens, orpine,
woodbine, daisies, betony, and pimpernel
of each 1 lb. Boil these...
then add perresin 1 lb, frankincense
1/2 lb, mastic 2 oz, olibanum 1/2 oz, myrrh
2 oz, all in powder. Boil them all to-
gether and stir them well in the
boiling; and being taken from the
fire and somewhat cooled, add to it of
turpentine 3 oz and stir them
until it be cold. This is very good.
A good sparadrap [medicated cloth plaster]:
Take wax, perresin of each 3 oz, pitch 3 oz;
melt them gently together and strain
them. Then take clean goat's tallow
12 oz and melt and strain; then let
it cool a little, then add powdered ceruse [white lead],
powdered calamine stone of each 4 oz, frankincense
1 oz, balsam 1 dram. Boil all gently and
stir it, and when it begins
to thicken add camphor in powder 1 dram;
stir it continually upon a soft fire;
then take it off and mix it with a rod
until it be cold; then anoint
your hands with oil and make it in rolls.
Make tents and plasters of this
salve, and cast them not away, but
wipe them and dry them and use
them again, by keeping them clean
wiped in a clean cloth, and a few
tents and plasters will heal a sore.

Triapharmacon.
Take litharge ½ quarter, common oil
2 lb, sharpest vinegar 1 lb; mix the finely powdered litharge
with vinegar and oil over a slow fire
20 hours always stirring; and with such
care, and when it comes away like wax without melting,
it suffices; for wounds, bruises, pain of the
limbs, etc.; it makes flesh grow and heals
them, etc.
The golden plaster.
Take litharge of gold 1 lb in fine powder, salad
oil a quart; put the litharge into the oil
and stir it with an oaken stick very well
in a new earthen pot newly annealed;
before, and boil it, and as it rises take
it from the fire and stir it, then set
it on the fire again, and when it rises
take it off again, and this do until
that it, being dropped upon a trencher,
it will come off clean without sticking;
then pour it into cold water and take it
off and save, then work it with your hand
in three several waters, etc. This is
good for any sores, bruisings, boils,
old sores, etc.
Emplastrum Catma.
Take litharge of gold in powder 4 oz,
wax 3 oz, ceruse [white lead] 1 oz, oil 1 lb;
the wax and oil together, then the other
being in powder put them in and stir
them a little while, then put in your
cloths and make cerecloths, and
when they are near cold smooth
them with your thumb and knead them
with a slick-stone upon a cool table.
Lay this upon the top of the other
plaster, etc.
Emplastrum Nerbon.
Take ceruse, litharge of gold, white
lead, red lead, of each ½ lb in most fine
powder, oil of roses 2 lb, wax
of each 1 lb; set the oil and wax over the
fire, and when they are molten, put in
the powder by little and little, still stirring
them; then take it from the fire, and when
it is almost cold put in the vinegar
by little and little and make it into
rolls. This is good for hot sores inflamed
with great torment.
Entractum Trinitatis.
Take red lead in fine powder ½ lb,
oil 1 lb, wax cut [small] 4 oz; boil them
until it be black and shining.

[Right Column (Emplastrum Saponis, 1614 Note, Stipticum Paracelsi at large)]
Plasters
Soap Plaster
Take red lead 1/2 lb, white lead, Castile soap,
of each 4 oz; olive oil 1/2 lb, oil of bays 2 drams.
Powder the lead and sift; then let them be macerated
very well in an earthen vessel well glazed,
and incorporated so that the soap floats on top;
then put on a gentle fire for half
an hour, always stirring with an iron spatula;
then increase the fire until the red colour
tends to a greyish/glaucous colour, continually
stirring with the spatula until it obtains a
dark brown colour; and put a drop upon
a table, and if it does not stick to the fingers it is
boiled enough, otherwise [boil] more; make rolls.
This draws out swelling
without breaking the skin and is a
sovereign (?) salve unto any member and has
many strange virtues, yet in 1614 to
me unknown.
Styptic Plaster of Paracelsus at large
Take galbanum, opoponax, of each 1 dram; ammoniac, bdellium,
of each 2 drams; let all be ground very finely, placed in a
glazed earthen pot, and also with strong wine vinegar
poured over, let them be macerated for a natural day;
afterwards let them be cooked on a gentle charcoal fire
so that the gums gradually melt, which done, poured into
a bag let them be strained, pressed out, and
separated from the dregs cast away; let the strained liquor
boil again until the evaporation
of the vinegar, stirring always lest perchance the gums burn;
keep meanwhile. Afterwards take oil
of olives 2 lb, new wax 1/2 lb, which placed in a pot
let gradually melt; then let be cast in
litharge most finely ground 1/2 lb, and let all be stirred
together so that they mix, and [of a grey]
(grey) colour become. Next take the gums
previously cooked, to the quantity of a nut each
time let them be put in until mixed they melt
by fire, namely all; meanwhile taking care
lest they grow hotter than right and boil over, for
by their own proper nature the gums are hot.
Lastly then add birthwort of both kinds,
calamine, myrrh, frankincense, of each 1 dram; all these
being ground and mixed, let there be poured on
oil of bays, pure turpentine, of each 3 drams;
let them be cooked with stirring with the utmost diligence;
with a stick dipped in, let drops be dropped into water
from time to time; if the matter sticks to the fingers
softly, let them be cooked further until they harden;
then at last taken off the fire into a great
basin full of water let it be poured, and with hands
anointed with oil of camomile or rose let them be mixed
or kneaded for 3 hours, 4 nights or
longer for use; afterwards in the 4th year it is
cleansed and compounded.
The use of this plaster follows.

Use of the Styptic Plaster of Paracelsus
It is for old ulcers as well as recent ones;
it heals, cleanses, produces good flesh,
consolidates and heals; in one week
more than another in a whole month: it does not
suffer good [flesh] to putrefy or corrupt, nor
bad flesh to grow out; for nerves either
severed or bruised it is a most excellent remedy;
iron, wood, lead, and other things also
it draws out from wounds when laid upon them,
by itself alone; it cures bites of venomous
animals, ulcers; it causes apostumes
and swellings to ripen when laid upon them;
against cancer, fistula, St Anthony's fire
(erysipelas) it is most excellent; it mitigates all
pains, etc. [With heat this piercing plaster.]
To draw out water, which is good
Let [me] use of Chittingfielde

of each 1/2 lb; deer suet 3 drams, mastic 2 drams, young
nettles and culrage (arsmart), of each 3 handfuls; powder
what is to be powdered, chop your

on leather. — Chittingfielde.

Mr Baskervile his salve

and lay on this salve. Nothing worth.

A Black Plaster
Take clear resin, stone pitch, wax,

A plaster: see p. 67, oil of linseed
Take clear and pure turpentine 4 oz, resin 4 oz,
3 oz, Greek pitch i.e. colophony 3 oz, pure mastic
3 oz, new or clean wax 3 oz, oil of linseed
purified 1/2 oz. Take a new earthen pot
well glazed and washed, in which place over a gentle
charcoal fire the turpentine, so that it dissolves,
stirring with a wooden spatula; and when it is well
dissolved, gradually mix in resin 4 oz
broken into small pieces and stir with the spatula; then
put in the pitch, and afterwards mastic powder;
stir with the spatula so they mix very well, but a
small fire is needed; afterwards add the linseed oil, and let it
remain on the fire until it simmers with boiling for
a quarter of an hour or a little longer.
Whether it is boiled enough or not
If it spreads itself upon cold water it is not
boiled enough; or [if] a drop of the plaster between the fingers
moistened with cold water, being pressed so that
it draws into diverse parts and stretches and
breaks of its own accord, it is boiled enough. Then pour
it very hot into a sleeve/bag of canvas (cloth
moistened with hot water) and let it be strained into cold
water, pressing the bag with sticks so that
without delay all may be strained through; and when now
it cools slightly let it be kneaded with hands moistened
with prepared linseed oil until it holds no more
water, and make rolls; afterwards keep in cold water,
which change daily, and so it will be
preserved for ten [years]. I understand not the working
of this plaster as yet.

A drink for wounds
Take comfrey, betony, pellitory, pimpernel,
and avens: these lead to the wound.
Madder, oculus Christi [clary], bugle, sanicle, red
cole [cabbage], and orpine: these two draw to the wound.
Herb Robert, bugle, sanicle, savin,
moldyne(?) and crowfoot: these be for fistulas
and aches.
And note that any man that hath
an open sore hath no hot fester.
There be two manner of festers:
the one hot: that [has] a fair colour, the hot hath
a long hole, the cold a narrow hole,
and then it is a fistula.
To heal him that festers
Take of herbs' leaves that lead to the wound, and
of herbs 3 herbs that draw to the wound,
of each 1 handful, but of betony 2 handfuls; stamp your
herbs well in a clean mortar and
make them in balls, and let them lie in
a clean pot close covered 9 days, then
put them in a fair pan and put to them
sweet butter and boil them together;
then put to white resin and boil it well.
Then strain it with a clean canvas and
stir it well with a clean slice while
it begin to cool; then have clean
wax ready molten and some gum
and stir them well.
Take hereof so much as a bean
or drink it with warm ale, and lay a
bramble leaf on the sore.
The like may be made for
festers and all open sores, and this may
be both eaten and drunk.
Bugle is not good for wounds in the
head.
Most approved empirical potion
Take senecio, i.e. groundsel, primula veris
i.e. tops of bugloss, dove's-foot, of each 4 pinches,
tops of rosemary, i.e. bramble tops, as well
as sage, as much of all, all
very well, and boil in good wine and honey 1 lb.
to the third part; strain strongly and let it be kept for use.
Let the patient drink morning and evening to the accustomed measure,
at noon and evening a good draught.
After nine days and ...

Groundsel purges the wound and leads to putrefaction;
it is found ... strained wound

[Left Column (Six Wound Principles & Styptics)]
Bleeding of green wounds to stop:
When one hath received a wound,
the first thing a surgeon hath to
do is to stop the blood, and then
to digest it or heal in the state as before.
I seldom or never used digestion if
that I came first to the hurt.
1. But I first stopped blood,
2. Dry stitched it or closed and drew
the wound,
3. conglutinated it if none had
meddled with it before,
4. without tenting, probing,
or any other great pain,
5. if a cut(?), then in incarnating
or filling it with flesh,
6. cicatrizing or skinning.
And this I intend to follow if God
please, in order as here lie the
devised [rules].
To stop blood
I very seldom used any other thing
but this:
Take hot burning coals out of the
fire glowing hot, and with all diligence
grind them betwixt 2 trenchers,
and with all quick speed throw
this hot dust in or upon the wound.
This presently stoppeth the bleeding
and hindereth not the healing, and
when the sinew(?) is there it doth
not fail, and is easy to be had
what to do next. Look in Sanguis
Veneris and here and desire God.
To stop blood of a wound
Take bole Armeniac and with the white
of an egg mix it, add thereto flax
and apply it. This sticketh too fast
and care must be had in taking it off.
For the same
In the eaves [trees?] there do grow a
long brown thing like corn
but far bigger: make them into
fine meal [powder] and apply it.
For the same
Take great spider cobwebs and
dip them in Sanguis Veneris and
so hot as may be suffered put them
into the wound.
For the same
Take the fine down of a heron and
put into the wound: or with Sanguis
Veneris hot. I never saw it fail.
Let it cut yellow silk and greatest in
the hole of the breast and under the tongue.

To prepare oil of linseeds
Take clean yellow oil of linseed, sufficient quantity; put
it in a glass like a gourd and a little hole in the
end: put to it as much fair rain water;
shake; let it stand that the oil may lie upon
the water: then let out the water at the hole;
then put in more water, shake it so until that
the water be fair and clear, and then it is
ready: any glass may do it, stop the hole
with a hole in the top and the bottom upward
for the oil will be outermost.

Harelips [hare-shares] in the lip

The cutting the skin: I will make it

much sooner and better.
If inflammation in the sore, put
it away with rosewater.
If a line single be well placed
upon both sides, it will help to hold
the better.
The patient would be purged and dieted before
this be undertaken, for fear of flux of
humour to the wound.
The stitches must be deep to hold fast
until it be well.
An especial note
One thrust through the arm with a knife,

make a tent of Flos Unguentorum and anointed
the tent therewith and put it in, and it stopped
bleeding, and in eight days was healed.

[Left Column (Dry Stitching of Wounds & Plaster Recipe)]
68 [Original Page Number]
Dry stitching of wounds.
When there do happen great cuts in
flesh, that is, as in the calf of the leg
or such like, the mouths and edges of
the wound will be very wide, so that it
will be very long time to fill them with
flesh: then dry stitching is exceeding
good and great ease to the party, and
furthereth the healing exceedingly.
For in stitching the flesh in such
a great wound, the skin will not
hold to draw the wound together,
and if it do, yet it will not hold
long enough to the healing.
In dry stitching I have often
observed it that the clout laid
on for plaster should be three-square,
and that shape will hold the better.
To make the plaster.
Take two pieces of strong linen cloth,
double them and cut them after the
fashion of three-square, and let them
be long and big enough for
the place; then:
Take good carpenter's glue, heat it so
good and strong as you can get it,
and melt it and put it upon
one side of the plaster (but not near
the doubling) afterwards all over;
then put the pieces together and with
a slick-stone rub it gently and
smooth it. But put no glue upon
the one side: then put glue upon
the undermost side which is plenty
full, and place them one above and
the other under the cut. Then you
must bind them fast on with a roller
and let them dry. Then the next
morning stir [draw] the cloths with a
double strong thread and draw
it gently together, and between
the threads dress the wound with
the twayt(?) or turpentine: the very
edges must have
no glue because
the needle will
not be thrust
through, it will
be so hard.

[Right Column (Alternative Dry-Stitching Pastes, Pin Sutures & Leg Diagrams)]
This kind of stitching will hold

When you will take it off:
Put some warm oil under one place,
and so remove it a little and little.

[Left Column (The Excellent Oil of Aparicio)]
The Excellent Oil of
Aparicio:
Take sweet and old salad oil 2 lb.,
clear turpentine 1 lb.,
frankincense, white and clear, 1/2 lb.,
wheat, sweet and clean, 2 oz.,
buds and flowers of St John's wort (Hypericum) 1/2 lb.,
valerian 3 oz.,
carduus benedictus (blessed thistle) 3 oz.,
sack, good and old, a quart.
Cut your herbs small and put
them and your wheat into a porcelain
pot with the narrowest mouth as you
can get: and thereto put your wine and
so let them stand 12 hours at least;
then put in your oil, and stop the pot
very close that no air go forth,
and set the pot on a gentle fire
without flame or smoke; and so
let them boil very softly. Yet you
must sometimes stir it with a wooden
slice [spatula], and stop the pot again, and
so let them boil until the wine be
consumed (which you may know by the
dropping a drop upon the fire: if
the wine be consumed it will burn,
if it be not consumed it will hiss.)
The wine being consumed,
take the pot from the fire, and then
strain the liquor through a thick
canvas, and make the pot clean, and
put in your liquor again, and set
it on the fire, and put in your turpentine
and frankincense in fine powder; and
let it boil less than the quarter
of an hour; then take it off, strain
it with a clean strainer and
put it in a glass or tin and stop
it close.

Oleum Balsami [Oil of Balsam]
Take galbanum, ammoniacum, mastic, white frankincense, storax
calamita, tragacanth, sagapenum, of each 2 drams;
myrrh, gum elemi, of each 2 drams; euphorbium
1 dram; saffron 1 dram; turpentine 4 oz.; oil 2 lb.
Powder the gums and in strong vinegar 1/2 lb. in a cauldron
of glazed earthenware, let them be dissolved over a slow fire,
and afterwards, when they have been somewhat dissolved
with the vinegar, let them be put into a new pot
glazed, and let the oil and turpentine be added; let the
pot be placed at a circular fire, so
that the pot stands bare upon the ground, so that the whole
matter boils slowly in the fire, always
stirring with a little stick (beware lest the gums
be burnt), and so let them boil slowly 4 hours,
always stirring; and at the end of the decoction let
the hardened gum be added and the oil
becomes clearer, and begins [to settle] what is turbid in it
will be marked: then it is perfect. Then
take it from the fire, strain through a linen cloth,
and let it be kept for use.
It can be divided into 3 parts, and in
one part put white vitriol and
verdigris 1 dram and boil partially, and it receives
a green colour, and will avail for old
ulcers to be healed.
Another part avails in fresh wounds,
to be applied with a strip of lard; and [good] for
burnt limbs, pain of the chest,
spleen, kidneys, stomach from a cold
cause, and of the liver, and for cold gout.
'cacabo terreo' is a pot of earth.
If this Balm be coloured with
Sanguis Veneris [see p. 71] it will heal far
better, yet not hinder the white.
Balsam for wounds.
Take turpentine 2 lb., olibanum 1/2 oz., lignum
aloes, mastic of each 1 dram; rhubarb, ga-
langale of each 3 drams; olive oil 6 oz.; let them be infused
and distil with a slow fire. It avails for wounds
and deep old ulcers, cold
poisons, toads [bites], for fistulas, noli-
me-tangere [cancerous ulcer], for palsy and for venomous
ulcers.
A green Balm.

powdered and put them into the oil on all

negar), then with waxes cast the turpentine, stir
them until they be melted, then strain them.

[Left Column (Sanguis Veneris Receipt & Glyster-Pipe Method)]
Sanguis Veneris.
Take oil of roses 1 lb., of the root of the
herb alkanet in gross or fine powder
which ye will; boil them until it be
very red, and so will the wound oil
very red—the redder the better; then
strain it and keep it. Alkanet 1 oz.
Put this warm into any
wound and wet lint therein and lay
upon the top of the wound, and upon
all a plaster. Dress the wound at the
first once in 24 hours, after twice in
a day: this doth so conglutinate that
one dressing will heal wounds.
Oil of roses healeth best because
of the temper; but salad oil will heal
very well, and so will the wound oil
before made with Hypericum or any of the
balms being coloured with alkanet very
red—the redder the better.
For wounds in the head, the
oil of turpentine is best, by reason
of the drying quality it hath in it.
For lack of oil, take May
butter, capon's grease, goose grease,
goose or hen grease, badger's grease,
or such liquid thing fresh without any
salt, and put to 2 oz. of such grease of
alkanet 3 drams in powder, and boil and stir
them until it be very red.
All these must be put into the sore
or wound very hot, and very hot
so that it scald not [or dried linarum(?) p. 350 & 36].
This healeth a cut, to my own
knowledge, in very short space, and in
thrusts deep and narrow I used it
as followeth:
I had a pipe like a glyster
pipe, but far lesser, which pipe I did
put into the thrust, and so far in as I
could: then did I put the warm
oil into the pipe at the bigger end,
and turning the pipe out gently, the
wound being raised, gently the hot
oil went hot to the bottom: so that a
friend of mine, Younge(?), would dress a wound
of 9 or 10 inches deep with the point
of a rapier, pike, a poniard, or tuck,
or any sharp thing; and he would not
wind in the pipe above one inch or
2 at the most; for with gentle cooling
the narrow wound doth presently
glue together without any more a-
do. As I have often proved, Deo gratias.
I now see and can use it better, but
myself, for I found the syringe too hot.
The pipe will stop in thrusting it in,
therefore put in a tuss [tent] or thread
until to unstop it. p. 36 in fine.

[Right Column (Syringe Critique, Praise of Alkanet & Dressing Rules)]
71 [Original Page Number]
The cause wherefore I got a new pipe was
for that an instrument of metal
would burn the sore and offend
the party and hinder the healing of
the sore, as I proved very often.
Many surgeons use this same
wound salve at first from me, yet
they think it in which a syringe (and
I refuse that) and keep it not hot,
saving the balm and keep it long
in digestion, because none of them
knew the true use of it.
In a cut stitched together,
put in the oil warm and gently
raise the wound that it go to
the bottom.
This will incarnate also if
you put in the oil not too hot; but if
too hot it will hinder the healing
of the flesh exceedingly.
I am persuaded God never did
give a greater blessing unto
anything for man's relief in
wounds than he hath done to the
alkanet: let us suffice and thank
God for it.
If the wound be not stitched,
but be at a reasonable big [opening], you may
go in then [into] the hole with a guard
tent, as in fistulas p. 26, and pluck
forth the tent again, and fill the wound
with the oil warm by dropping, and
raise up the wound that the oil
may go to the bottom and be filled
full of the oil; then wet lint in
the same oil warm, lay it upon the
top, and on all a plaster.
In cuts and slits that be not
stitched together, fill it with lint that
is wet in the oil warm and
lay thereon a plaster, etc., and no more.
And you may wet the cut with
the oil and put in some incarnative
in the wound with lint, and prevent
the young flesh.
All wounds healed in this manner
do heal statu quo prius: they are as
quick at the skinning as the first time
they were dressed, as hereafter I will
show, if it please God.
The knife [or tent] must be in when hot at the
bottom, and put around the stopping,
but a probe is better. See p. 26 in fine.

alkanet is good for old fistulas.

[Left Column (Balme artificiall)]
Artificial Balm:
Take whitest frankincense, cloves, mastic,
lignum aloes, galingale, cinnamon,
nutmeg, zedoary, cubebs, of each
1 dram; myrrh, hepatic aloes, labdanum,
sarcocolla, storax calamita, castoreum, of each
½ dram; figs, round birthwort, dittany, rosemary [?],
of each ½ dram, bayberries 3 drams, gum elemi
6 drams, clearest turpentine 1 lb, to the measure [?]
Incorporate all the premises
like a stiff paste, then distil them
in a retort of glass closely luted,
with a gentle fire for eight hours,
then augment the fire by degrees.
1. First comes clear water;
2. yellow, and swims on the first
like clear oil;
3. like honey, reddish.
1. is called Balm water,
2. Oil of Balm,
3. Artificial Balm, and has
all [the] virtues of Balm.
It keeps flesh from putrefying
and takes away that [which] is putrefied; it
heals the canker, fistula, pox, noli
me tangere, king's evil, and all rough
in the flesh, all swelling of eyes,
all bruises being anointed therewith;
it dries up haemorrhoids, the fundament [longeum],
palsy and ague. It does penetrate
for a drop put into the hand warm
is straightway seen on the other side; it
cures the rheum, comforts the
brain, clears the sight, if you do
the face and nostrils therewith twice
a day, and the hinder part of the head
washed therewith, it comforts memory;
it causes good appetite, consumes
phlegm in the mouth of the stomach
taking it with wine, and stinking
breath, scabs; dropped in the ears
helps hearing, bleared eyes, the
tooth; and it also represses and has
many other virtues.
Lute the retort with ashes.

[Right Column (Aqua Mirabilis)]
73 [original page number]
Aqua Mirabilis [Wonderful Water]
Take turpentine 1 lb, honey ½ lb, aqua ardens [spirits]
3 drams, lignum aloes well ground, sandalwood,
mastic, nutmeg, of each 3 drams, gum
arabic 1 dram, nutmeg, galingale, cu-
bebs, cinnamon, mastic, cloves,
spikenard, saffron, ginger, fine
musk, oriental ambergris, of each 1 scruple; thoroughly
let them be ground and mixed together
and placed in a glass alembic, closed
at the joints, and distil with a gentle fire.
1. The first water is limpid like
spring water.
2. And note: the 2nd water will be strongest
of fire [fiery].
3. And note: the 3rd water comes which is
black and thick like honey, str-
ongest, whence it ought alone to have the name
of Liquor.
1 is called Mother of Balsam,
2 Oil of Balsam,
3 Artificial Balsam.
1. Note: one for drink.
2 & 3 for anointing.
The first water, tepid in wine, is drinkable;
it consumes phlegm in the mouth of the stomach, restores
appetite [for digestion], purges the stomach from
every evil humour, does not permit an aposteme
to come to the heart, nor to the cordial parts;
dip a cloth in this water and put it in
the nostrils; with one finger [anointing] it cures
rheum; a bath as aforesaid cures evil
breath, from whatsoever cause; it prolongs
youth in him, takes away pain, and sight
it strengthens, cures wounds, and fistulas
if they are washed in it, and a cloth
moistened in it be laid upon them; it avails against
quartan ague if you rub the spine of the back with it
for several days; it avails against scabs
and haemorrhoids, a cloth moistened in it
laid upon them; against deafness, against
redness, palsy, and against
all infirmities from a cold cause.
2 & 3 avail for fomenting and anointing
infirmities that come from [the] disease
noli me tangere, king's evil, canker, and
scrofula, fistulas, malum mortuum, paralysis,
and all infirmities from phlegm or
putrefied blood.

Sanguis Martis [Blood of Mars]
Take red petroleum, coloured very red with
alkanet, in the sun in a glass, or set
upon the fire and boiled as Sanguis Veneris.
This assuages humours, mitigates
pain in the sinews, heals deep small
punctures. [He] expounds more thereof in Gesta:
I call it Sanguis Martis, differing from Veneris,
and of the same, yet greater quality.
... [properties of Sanguis petroleum]:
It heats, dries, of most subtle essence, penetrates deeply,
digests; therefore every
excrementitious matter it consumes; on account of this, epilepsy,
palsy, vertigo, forgetfulness, and [diseases] of the spleen, kidneys,
bladder, womb, sinews, of all joints,
and of remaining nervous parts, in cold pains,
wonderfully helps.
You may colour it green with verdigris, yet
yellow is safer.
Balsamum Sulphuris
or Dia Sulphuris.
Take oil of sulphur 3 drams, wax ½ dram, colo-
phony 3 drams, mixed to the weight of all
wax, colophony, and oil melted
together and well mixed; let it be thickened,
with myrrh most finely ground, little by little,
and boiled with a gentle fire, with a spatula al-
ways stirring, until it shall be well
mixed; afterwards indeed after a quarter of an hour's
space let them be taken from the fire, gradually
let them cool. It heals wounds and
ulcers, old and new.
Oleum Lumbricorum [Oil of Earthworms]
Take great earthworms in May 1 lb,
put them into a clean basin, put
to them white wine ½ lb, and stir them
together until the worms be dead;
then slit the worms and wash them
clean with clean white wine; then put [them]
into a glass and keep [them] in worm oil
white wine 3 drams, salad oil 1 lb; boil
them until the wine be wasted, stirring
them well; then strain them and keep it.
Sanguis Martis
In cold causes it is admirable, as I have
often proved by outward anointing;

[Right Column (24-Hour Balm 1619, Oleum Lumbricorum, Balsamum Dr. Johannis)]
No. 44. A most rare and precious Balm
to heal wounds in 24 hours.
Take virgin wax, Venice turpentine,
of each 1 lb; liquid storax 3 drams; pure
salad oil 3 lb; oil of balsam 2 drams;
oil of Hypericum, red plantain
water, rye water, of each ½ lb; red
sanders 2 drams; of the herb plantain,
marigold, sage, thyme, of each a small handful.
Make it thus:
At twelve o'clock in the morning
wash your turpentine therewith, and oil,
and let them stand until five o'clock
at night; then melt your wax first
at a gentle fire; then put in the salad
oil, then your Hypericum, then your
storax, and let them boil a little;
then let all stand so all night.
In the morning take it out of the water
and melt it again, and put thereto
your oil of balsam and Hypericum, and your
waters and your sanders in powder; then
boil it a quarter of an hour, then strain
it and keep it in pots, and the straining
cloth for a serecloth.
A Frenchman had given this
for tried, and a pistole before King
James, and healed it on the morrow by
that time of the sun, perfectly whole.
The wound may be dressed warm
or cold, but very warm is best.
This balm has many excellent virtues
in print by the King's grant.
I had the receipt in May 1619 of a friend
who saw it made and had it of the
Frenchman.
Chop the herbs and put them in
with the wounds; it is good in bruises, strains.
In the place of sanders, frankincense
put in alkanet, if it please God.

Incarnatives

[Left Column (Theory of Incarnatives, Unguentum Dulce, Unguentum de Sanis)]
Because that in the flesh must be filled
again with flesh and made even
with the rest of the flesh, nature
does not err, aided [by art], and therefore to
follow with incarnatives, [i.e.] breeders
of young flesh.
Moderate incarnative or regenerative
which make flesh to grow or increase,
be of a cleansing and drying quality
that they may wipe away the gross
superfluities and ... the subtle
be of the hard digestion and of ne-
cessity are engendered in a hollow
wound yet in due sort.
In a wound in a fat man, a dropsy
man, a woman, a child, or a gelded
man (which are moist), it is needful
to use medicines a little drying,
as frankincense, mastic, myrrh,
aloes, bean flour, etc.
In a dry body, use
Aristolochia, iris, flour of bitter vetch, and
of lupines, etc., and a wound that has
more quittor [pus] needs the more
drying.
Incarnative: Take washed turpentine, of
earthworms, comfrey, and round
birthwort, mix and prove.

[Right Column (White Lead, Alabaster & Chalk Ball; Box & Mortar Instructions)]
79 [Original Page Number]
Sanatives [Running Header]
Sanative
Take white lead and burnt alabaster, of each
in most fine powder 3 drams, chalk in as fine powder 2 drams,
fine fresh hog's grease 1 oz or q.s.
Make it thus:
Bolt [sift] the lead and chalk through
a linen cloth; then put
it into a mortar of wood, and with
an iron pestle heated in the fire
more than warm, labour the
lead and chalk with the grease
until they hang all together in a
mass or lump; then make all into
a round ball, and it will be as hard
as a stone. Use it thus:
If it be old and dry, shave it
with a knife into a saucer, and
put more fresh [?] grease unto
it, as much as a bean, and warm
it and temper it with your fingers
like unto a cake, thicker in the
middle and thin upon the sides,
and being broader than the sore,
bind it or sew it fast on; and on
it lay a plaster of de minio, or of
the yellow plaster, or such like dossel.
And when it does run, and
you take it off and temper it
again as before: but take heed
you make it not too soft by putting
to it too much grease, for the drier
it is, the better it is; and one of
these will heal 20 sore legs,
be they never so bad. See p. 275.
To cleanse the lead, have
a great box with a cover to put on,
and put a linen cloth betwixt the
cover, and therein put your lead and chalk
and shake the box, and the bulk [of] the
powder [sifts] through; and when it will
not [go] through, beat it again; or you
may have a fine little sieve for the
nonce; and the mortar must be wood,
very round in the bottom in the hole,
and a thick bottom, 4 or 6 inches thick,
to abide beating; the pestle a round,
long iron pestle such as men
use, and let it not be too hot, but very
warm: this is true. See p. 22.

White Ointment of Rhazes
Take white lead in powder and sifted ceruse
in fine powder, of each 1 lb; put them together
and mix them well; then put them into a
pan and put thereto oil of roses a pint,
and stir them well until they begin to
wax hot; then take it from the fire and
stir it still; then put in camphor in
fine powder 1/2 dram, and stir it until it
be cold. This dries, cools, and
abates swelling.
White Ointment
Take oil of roses 4 oz, white wax 1 oz;
melt them together, then pour them
into a mortar and add ceruse in powder
2 oz, camphor 2 drams; work them well,
then add the white of an egg and mix
them very well. It heals [and] cools.
White Ointment

2 drams, whites of 2 eggs; let an ointment be made for inflammation.
White Ointment
Take ceruse 2 drams, litharge of silver 1 dram,
olibanum 2 drams; let them be very finely powdered and
temper the ceruse with a little oil; then
let the litharge be added, then the olibanum, and with

let them be well stirred, putting in a little
oil [and] a little vinegar, and let it be made neither too
liquid nor [too] thick.
And when this ointment is more [needed],
take of it as much as you will and add bole and
dragon's blood powdered, oil of violets
and rose water in which gum arabic and
[?] are slightly dissolved, adding now a little
oil, now a little water, and always
stirring with a spatula until it is
of due thickness; then it is called
ointment of [?]; it is good for [?ulcer] and
in the anus and every excoriated place.

=== Canvas 124 (86) ===
[Left Column (Pin-Paper Litmus Notes, Sanative, A Plastor to Drye & Heale)]
86
Since I wrote the last medicine upon
the other side of the pin paper, I have tried
using the paper, found as follows:
1. How the paper is painted
The painters have a blue colour which they
call litmus, and that ground in water
and tempered with a weak size is laid on the
paper, and shows bluish-blue when
it is dry; so they do it and know the
colour and have so done almost these
threescore years. But what litmus
is made of I have not yet learned.
2. The true manner of dressing
the broken shin with it
Let the patient wet the paper with his
own fasting spittle very wet, and
lay it on bigger than the sore, and
be sure let it stick (for it will not
lightly fall off), and take it not off;
but as the sore fills with matter and
a bunch arises under the paper, you
must thrust out the matter gently
with your finger upon one side and let
the paper still stick; and a bit heals,
the edges will rise where the skin and flesh
by the edges must be cut off; but if
the paper break upon the sore, then
put on a new paper wet as at the first
with fasting spittle; so that commonly
2 or 3 papers heal the leg. And
when it is whole there is a little of
the paper will stick on still; let it alone,
and this I never knew to prove [other than]
be true. Thanks be to God.
And further, if there be a hole of a place
lower than the rest, with your finger you
must thrust down the paper as it
does stick on.
A sanative for all wounds
Take the leaves of daisies, woodbine, orpine,
plantain, cinquefoil, herb Walter, herb
Robert, periwinkle, groundsel, comfrey,
[?oxtongue] and pimpernel, or most of them,
of each 1 handful; stamp them with May butter, make
them into balls; let it lie [and] rest 20 days, then
put to [it] gum arabic and boil it well and
strain it; let it cool and keep it.
To heal a sore
Take plantain, ribwort, smallage, herb [?cub],
herb Walter, betony, pimpernel and sage,
of each 1 handful, of woodbine leaves 2 handfuls; stamp them
and let them lie as the other next before;
then boil all, strain all into a basin of
fair water, and when it is cold and skimmed
it off, dress a sore with this upon lint
in the middle, and in the edges apply this
ointment: Take honey 1 lb, powder orient 1/2 oz,
boil them until it be red; lay on this
in the edges.
A plaster to dry and heal
Salad oil 3 oz, yellow wax that is clean,
ceruse, litharge of gold and silver, round tur-
pentine, of each 2 drams; melt the oil and wax; then
stir in the powders by little and little and boil till
to a plaster according to art; then put in the turpentine,
pour on a cold stone and make it into a roll.
See [p.] 63, col. 1, [item] 2.
To dry a broken shin
[In] due time strew into the wound the fine
powder of flowers of sulphur or of common
brimstone.

sometimes; then applied the white plaster,

Inflammation [Running Header]
Mr. John Arderne the expert surgeon
in whose book are many excellent things
writes: that a woman in Newark had
her body, face, neck, and legs inflamed
and did lie as though she were dead,
and he gave her this medicine:
Take roots of asphodel, and very well
and most minutely let them be beaten, and with
pure water in which part of [?] powder was
first infused, so that it receives the tincture: and
quickly it is restored to health.
For the erysipelas and inflammation
Take the leaves of arsesmart [or orach], bruise them and
apply to all inflammations. See p. 345.
For heat, whether it [be] pimples or
scabs, or for St. Matthew [?]
Take strawberry leaves 3 handfuls, yarrow/ironwort leaves
that grows on the ground 1 handful; stamp
them in a mortar fine, then add thereto
suet and stamp all well; then boil it
gently, then strain it hard; melt
some of it, wet a linen cloth therein
and apply it; at night turn the other
side of the cloth and apply it. If
the skin be broken, wear the plaster
with wax [?] at each dressing.
For swollen, inflamed feet

linden tree) 2 handfuls, put in river

Oil of stramonia for scabs
Take leaves of stramonia 2 handfuls, olive oil
1 lb; chop the herbs very small and put it
into the oil with lees of the juice of the
stramonia; then boil all together till the consumption
of the juice: or you may make it with hog's
lard [axungia] accordingly. Mr. Bart[let].
Of imposthumes [abscesses]
It is to be known that all external imposthumes
which swell or are inflamed,
whether great or small, whether great [or small]
are arising from the four humours
peccant [corrupted]): whence an imposthume from
blood is called phlegmon, from phlegm
is called axima [oedema], from choler
red [bile] erysipelas, and [from] melancholy
scirrhus: and with these more mortiferous [deadly]
is made a cancer. And from these not well
cured is born a fistula. And note that
cancer, noli me tangere, old fistula,
herpes, lupus, St. Anthony's fire
are the same in genus and species: but divers
names are assigned according to diversity of mem-
ber: and if they are old, they yield to no
medicines (which I do not believe).
And if they are without corrosion, they are [turned]
into scirrhus, i.e. hardness, and improperly are
called Malum Mortuum.

=== Canvas 132 (94) ===
[Left Column (Diagnosis of canker vs. carbuncle, woodbind salve, Latin washes, lip & nose canker)]
Note of canker, how to know the same
and remove [it]
The canker comes of melancholy and does
puff or swell with hardness, or slits
with pain and heat and an evil savour, and
has most commonly fleshy brims turned
backwards, lifted up, knotty, of a wan
or blackish colour. The cause is putrefied
melancholy humour which runs into some
member, or else of some boil or sore
lying ill healed.
To know a canker from a
carbuncle
In the beginning a carbuncle is hard and
very red, burning, and great heat
in the veins, and in time will come
unto a head. The canker is not so full
of pain, but is harder, and does not so
soon grow to a head, but frets marvellously
in the flesh.
For a canker, whereofsoever it be
Take the leaves of woodbind, wash them
not, but pound them and sprinkle them with
good white wine, then strain out the juice
(for it is so thick it will not strain with-
out the wine); take of that juice and of
clarified honey, of each [equal]; boil them until
the juice be consumed, then ... [?]
it is good for many things in surgery,
and especially in fretting filthy sores
as in ... place and hand rotten.
Item, for ears, look in Sore Ears.
For a canker, cured
Take sal gemmae and powder of roasted eggshells,
and put upon the canker ...
A water for the same
Take vinegar and let it be heated so that it boils, and
let plume alum be melted in another vessel, and
and it will be like water; then ... in boiling
vinegar: and it is done and proved.
For the canker
Take rosemary, alum glass, hartshorn,
and common salt, burn them and ... seed
severally, then make them in powder and
mix them equally; then take woodbind water,
plantain water, and a little good vinegar,
and therein put your powder, and with this
water wash the canker often.
For the canker and fistula
Take the ... flower of salt barren, burn it,
make it into powder, then wash the canker
with white wine and strew on the powder,
and so for the fistula.
For a canker in the lip
Take the distilled water of woodbind and
dissolve therein saltpetre, as much as suffices; wash
the canker therewith; once or twice is
enough to cure it.
Canker in the nose
Boil stale ale and skim it clean; then
put therein ... honey and alum and
wash therewith.
Black plaster cures canker, and oil of camphor.

Bubo in the arse-gut
Bubo is an imposthume in the arse-gut or
longanon, with great hardness and little ache
at the first, which is without pulsation
and indeed is a very canker: it is not to
be seen at the first, but lies hidden in
the gut as a bubo does in [?]; and in time
swells and eats his way out and all
the [?] of the arse-gut, so that he
[who] endures runs [?], continually unhealed,
and this is incurable.
How to know it
Let the surgeon put his finger into the
longanon, and he shall feel a hard thing
like a stone and [?stinks] upon both sides
so that the patient may not go to the privy.
Sometimes here is another token:
that a man cannot stay from the
privy 2 or 3 [times] in an hour, and eftsoons
and then runs watery blood
stinking exceedingly.

The accidents are: the patient can

may not abstain from the privy.
In hot weather they are worse: sometimes they
desire to drink wine and such like water.

Bubo in
Bubo arises in the flank and
has many causes, [some] of them from
heat, cold, or corrupt [i.e., infected/venereal] women.
I heal them as follows:
First, if they were new, then
I used maturatives [ripening agents], and then
I lanced them; then cleansed [mundified]
the same and so healed them.
Therefore when you cut
them, cut the wound wide
enough, for then you shall put
in a large tent [wound-plug] and heal [with] less [trouble]
with far more ease and sooner.
Note: I knew one who had
one of them and caught cold in it,
and it was held up against the [abdominal] wall
so long that the roots of bryony
roasted and applied for 7 or 8 weeks
—the medicine wrought a hole
into the gut; and the excrement
ran forth and wrought a hole in the
hip, and so he lived in that state
some years—how long I know
not, but I saw him in Beldengua [?]
green at a ... where.
When you have lanced them,
use long tents of salve and
dip them in the oil, or [see p. 14].
Take oil of chamomile 1 oz, fresh
butter 2 oz, linseed and fenugreek
in fine powder of each 1 oz, [bread / yolks]
of egg; mix them and heat them
with barley meal and use it.

of matter expelled from the principal members
with supervening heat; and it is retained
more stubbornly because it is not bound by flesh,
nay rather wrapped as it were like a cancer,
and because it arises in the armpits and
groins. Cure:

phlebotomy from the basilica vein and
purgation; [these] are:

but heat and throbbing are increased, and
then pus gathers; therefore administer
