Sore Breast
Take a sheep's head, set it well on to boil
in fair water a good quantity three or
four hours; then let the clear water
run through a clean cloth, and into that
clean water put in of clean-dressed [wheat/oatmeal?] so
much as will thicken it into the thickness
of a thick poultice; and when it is thick
enough, take it from the fire and stir
in the yolks of 2 eggs, being first beaten
well with a spoonful of oil of
chamomile, and mix them well all to-
gether. Then apply this poultice very
warm, but not too hot, all over the sore,
being spread on a thick cloth with a hole
cut in the cloth for the nipple; change
this plaster three times in 24 hours
so that it may run off wet and moist,
not dry in any wise. See p. 184.
And when the breast is broken, then you
must have goat's dung dried of
a gelded goat, and made into fine powder,
and sifted [cersed], and mix of that powder
with pure honey, but not made too thick;
if the honey be hard, then melt it
before you put [in] the powder, so that it
may be like a syrup and beyond, and
make a plaster of the honey and the
powder (with a hole for the nipple),
and so dress it morning and evening,
that is, twice in 24 hours.
But you must not tent [plug] the holes in
any wise. See p. 102 at the end.
If it so happen that in healing of the
breast it grows hard or does then
puff or swell, then you must apply
the poultice again; and when it is first
broken you must apply the poultice two
or four days after before you lay
on your plaster of honey and goat's
dung.
This healed the Lady Fitzgerald's [or Fitzwater's]
breast when the Sergeant Surgeon
failed in their skill and the breast would
have been cut off; and she that
healed it had a hundred pounds
for her cures. See p. 184.
For a Sore Breast and rotten ulcers
Take fresh new-made goat's dung, put
it in a mortar, work/mix it with pure
honey, then boil them until it is very
thick like a plaster, and apply it
warm; this seems as good as with powder.
After 30 or 40 years' practice, I found
that the often changing of the plaster
hindered the cure, and then I changed it
once in every fourth day; and when it
did a greater cure, [after] 2 or 3 such days
and it cured it better in my mind, and
with 3 or 4 plasters finished the cure.

[Right Column (Red Lead Plaster, Sheepskin Application, Notes)]
Sore Breast
Take red lead in fine powder 1 lb and
sift it [to] 1 lb. So that look
how much lead you have, you
must have double as much oil;
then put your oil in [the vessel] that you intend
to boil it in; then put in your lead
by little and little until it is all
in; then stir it all together the
space of almost half an hour,
and let both be in, and to stir it with
is a green oaken stick as big as
a man's thumb, the bark being
upon the stick; then set it on the
fire, and when it begins to
rise, take it off the fire and stir,
and it will change into many
colours. But when it turns
black, it will ready stand; and
drop some of it upon a cold saucer
and let it cool to see if it is hard
enough or not; and when it is
well boiled, wet a clean table or
a stone, and cast it out and make it into
rolls; or if you keep it for your own
use, pour it into a stone pot and
take it out as you need it; but if
you carry it, make it into rolls.
Cut a piece of sheepskin leather
big enough to cover all the breast,
and spread on this plaster, and leave
a hole in the middle for the
nipple.

with the oil of mallows warm,

warm it and lay it on.

or 4 [without] doubt, that it may work, and
then change it; and at every change
anoint with the oil of mallows (p. 29).
And when it is ripe, let the

Of the [French] disease
The Pox with diverse names,
and here are diverse kinds of them.
Whether it be [the pox] or not:
Take unsalted butter, wax, sulphur, of each
half an ounce, fat of a serpent or snake/
eel 2 drams, Roman vitriol 1 scruple; let
a plaster be made and apply it.
If it be of white color, it is [the pox]; otherwise not.
Whether it be the pox or not; certain.
The way to cure them
1. First purge the patient
2. Let blood if need require
3. Anoint the sore
4. Sweat him by ointment
5. Diet him
6. Wash him
For the pox
Take lignum vitae [guaiacum] rasped or grated
small 1 pound, put in 12 pounds
of spring water; and let it lie and
infuse 12 hours at least; then in
an earthen or iron pot or a brass
pan close covered, let it boil
till 4 parts [?] boil away until the
half be wasted.
Drink of this every morning
and evening warm, and all day
before [meals] as often as you will.
Then fill the pot again with water and
boil it in all points as you did before,
and drink this with your meat and all
day at your pleasure the second [time] the
better. And you may boil the wood the
third time with half so much water.
Every third or 4th day give him
an easy purgation.
Save the scum of the water when it
boils, to anoint the sores withal.
The first day you may give him
this purgation:
Take Electuarium de succo rosarum, rhu-
barb chosen, of each half a dram; mix, and with
sorrel water let a potion be made.
Keep him close [indoors] 30 days at least.
If he be weak, give him this:
Take cassia fistula half a dram, rhubarb half a dram, senna
1 dram; let a potion be made with sorrel water.

and fat earthworms, of each half a pound at least;
wash the worms in warm wine 4 times;
chop the herbs and roots small; dress your
rat clean as a lamb, pluck your
swallows clean, then chop the rat and
swallows small; then put all the things
together on the fire in pewter; then take
it from the fire and set it up close
covered three days; then boil it until
the rat's flesh flies from the bones; then
strain it, and set it on the fire
again, and clarify it clean; then put it
in bladders and hang it in the roof.
Note that the fat of the rat and
the swallows is of great effect, therefore
get as many as you can conveniently get.
This oil is praised for ...
blasting, taking (if any such be) ...
where I wrote it out it was written for
the King's; purging of sinews, and sinew shrunk
as I never did see a better.
An excellent oil for aches

1 handful; mince the herbs small and bruise your

the swallows have been in the oil 9 days,
put all into a brass pot and let it
boil well as before said, and use it as
the other ...
First give the swallows, then for
10 days after the herbs, rat, etc.
This was Mr. Gilbert Tuffold's oil,
and it wrought great things with them.

An ointment for ache
Take great worms stamped clean from
their dirt, a pottle or more of good
old wine; boil them together until the
oil and the worms be crumpling
and the oil looks clear and brown, and
keep them well from burning too. Then
strain it and put to the oil: wax,
rosin or deer suet, turpentine, of each 1 pound,
frankincense 2 drams in fine powder, and set
it on the fire; put therein of plantain
1 handful, of althaea 1 handful, woodbine, celandine,
smallage, of each 1 handful, elecampane root
3 drams, and stamp them all very small with
a pottle of good white wine; and so let
them stand 24 hours; then strain
them hard and put it into the ointment
upon the fire (and beware it take not
fire) and let all boil softly together;
then let it cool till 23 hours;
then cut it into pieces and pare
off the dross and keep it in an earthen
pot. Apply very well and it will keep
40 years.
It is good for old sores, bruises, for
woman's breast, the colic, hollow
wounds, etc.
For ache and stiff joints
Take rue, sage, wormwood, betony,
feverfew, bay leaves, and plantain,
of each 1 handful; stamp them small, then put to
them oil of neat's foot, and put them into
an earthen pot and stop them close, and
so let them stand 3 or 4 months, and
then put to more oil and see the herbs be
well strewed; then set the pot into a
vessel of seething water and there let
it simmer under an hour, stirring it
very often. Then strain it and put it
into some pot.
It is good for shrinking of sinews, and
pain in the back, stopping of the liver
and spleen, bruises, knots, swellings.
before ... and apostemes; make it in
May and September.
For aches, bruises, spraining of sinews, etc.
Take neat's-foot oil 1 pound, of ox gall 1 pound,
aqua vitae half a pound, of rosewater 1 dram, bay
leaves, rosemary stripped from the
stalk, strawberry leaves, root and string,
lavender cotton, of each 1 handful; bruise them
small and put them into the oils, and let
them stand a time; then boil all in
a pan of a gallon on a soft fire
without flame, and look to it at the first,
and so in the boil let it be almost
cold; then strain it, but not too hard,
and keep it close stopped.
Anoint therewith before a good fire, etc.
* In the first part ... on this column take
the oil from the fire and drop in of the
wine and strain forth a little at once
until the oil leaves tumbling, then
put in more till all be in.

until the wine be half consumed; then
put in the pitch well cleansed, still
stirring it until it be molten; then

Sciatica
Sciatica is a certain species of gout, and
takes its name from the member where completely
it enters the hip [ischium], and in the beginning is a heavy
pain.
The cure follows
First let a sharp clyster be used, etc.,
let there be ... then gentle, so that the pain may yield; and
let them be bathed in sea water, or salt [water] with
salt and such an ointment:
Take liquid pitch, oil of colocynth, of each 1 oz.,
opopanax 1 dr., wax sufficient quantity; make an ointment.
And let them be purged with common pills;
these pills follow:
Take ammoniacum, sagapenum, bdellium, opopanax,
aloes, centaury, asafoetida, seed of rue, ..., celery,
anise of each 1 oz., colocynth, turbith of each 2 oz.,
cinnamon, acorus of each 2 dr.; make a mass
sufficient quantity; make pills. Give 1 dr. or 2 dr. or 3 dr.
They have the same virtue; wonderfully
they avail for arthritis, pains from humours
cold, viscous, and sciatica, podagra [gout], and
windiness of the nerves.
See page 122, col. 1, medicine 3, with
which ointment I have helped very many, and
cured it unto none [failed in none]. Thanks be to God.
For the sciatica, a practice
Upon the outside of the leg in the garter
place, there is a little pit between the bones:
there make an issue with the rod; so do this:
Take lapis infernalis, or for want
of them sublimate, in fine powder. First
lay on the place a plaster of Calus [?] in
which plaster cut a hole the bigness of a penny
or ... or as little or big as you will. Upon
the bare skin there put populeon or any
such like thing, and in that ointment put
lay the fine powder of sublimate, and
upon the top thereof a plaster of good salve
that will not flee away; let it lie
there 24 hours, and it will burn the
skin as broad as the hole is, and deep, and
better is in time, and taking out the eschar
will be a deep issue and a big [one].
Secondly, put in the same hole this
piece of an acorn stick [which] sundereth ...
but keep neither down which he shall
in the hole. And this is an excellent fine
way to keep open an issue.
Sometimes has been the use to
burn in the flesh with the powder of
cantharides, in that place being put
upon a plaster as broad as a groat,
the issue holds better [?].
The issue made, put a little piece
of yarrow cut round, and thereupon lay
ivy leaves, and part one of these, etc., such
of holes as a ...: let lie 12 hours
to heels and lie overmost. Let keep lie
12 days. Then put in another peg
bigger than the first, and let it lie 12
days with leaves such as afore; this
do until you see foul matter, then anoint
it with this ointment.

Against sciatica ...

prick it as a pudding. And take the
scum that floateth upon the water and
put it into a pewter vessel until
it be cold. Then press that in the

[Left Column (Podagra: Humoral Causes, Horse-Marrow Ointment, Choleric Gout)]
Podagra [Gout]
The cause of gout is twofold, namely
hot and cold.
If it be hot, with redness and swelling:
let phlebotomy be done from the basilic vein of the arm
of the same side, and let him be purged with pills
in common; and let them always drink such hydromel [mulsa]:
Take sage 4 handfuls, honey half a lb,
spring water as much as suffices; let hydromel be made to 2 lb.
But if the matter is cold and the pain
is strong:
let a little bag be made of pounded salt,
and toasted, and let it be applied; and upon its renewal
apply wool dipped in oil of chamo-
mile. If the pain recedes, foment with
sea water, and afterwards let it be anointed with
oil of bay [laurel].
If the humour be with sclerosis [hardening]
Take the crumb of white bread, boil in wine,
and let it be applied to the said place and frequently
renewed.
In every arthritis [joint-pain], oil of fox
and its fat avails.
Badger [taxus barbatus] boiled in wine and fre-
quently applied as a cataplasm, avails excellently.
And finest flour of beans,
and of lentils, mixed with egg-white and
warmed, and placed upon the gout at the joints,
helps much.
But if blood be the cause (nothing else
preventing), let phlebotomy be done; and let them beware of
foods that generate very much blood,
and let phlebotomy be done in the beginning of spring
and autumn; and let them beware of wine, and let them use
exercise before food; and let them be purged
with common pills, and afterwards apply
this plaster:
Take roses 2 drams, lentils 2 drams, flour
of barley 3 drams; let the roses and lentils [?]
be boiled, and pounded much with ...
..., and mixed with barley flour,
and let a plaster be made without ointment, and apply
a little oil and a little vinegar...
An excellent ointment for gout
Take the marrow of horses' bones in great
quantity, and make it boil in oil of roses
for a long time; afterwards pound in a mortar with seed
of juniper, cleansed and powdered; and again
make it boil in the aforesaid oil to the consumption of 2
parts, and afterwards strain, and add wax as much as suffices;
and with this ointment anoint the place, and you will see
a wonderful effect.
Podagra [Gout] from Choler
When it comes from choler, there does not
appear a swelling tumour in the joints, but
it troubles with heat and burning with redness.

Podagra [Gout]
A noble medicine for the gout
Take elderberries when they are ripe,
and the berries of wallwort [danewort] when they be ripe,
of each [equal parts]. Put in the bottom of an earthen pot of
salt 1 handful; then a handful of berries, then
salt, 2 or 3 layers. And so let them stand
2 or 4 days, and they will turn unto
water. Then put all into a vessel of lead
or pewter, and set it in the ground or
in a cold place. Anoint the place where
the fire [burning] and the pain will cease; then
anoint it with the marrow of horses'
bones and be whole.
For the gout and aching of
joints

and let it stand 24 days at the least;

Oil of butter for the gout
Take butter out of the churn, only made

over a warm fire one night or

out. And there will run first an
oil yellowish or dusky, and after that
there will run a more yellow, or clear
oil; and lastly there will run a black
thick substance, and then cease your work.

away by heat of the fire.

Incombustible Oil, or [Oil] of Soap

Oleum Lucatelli [Lucatellus's Balsam]
Take salad oil 4 pounds, turpentine
a pound, clear yellow wax half a pound,
pure red sanders in powder 2 ounces, of
choice sack half a pound, of damask rose
water a sufficient quantity to wash the turpentine;
wash the oil first, cut the
wax small, put the wax, turpen-
tine and oil together in a kettle
big enough, and on a small fire, and
let it boil half an hour or a
little more; then take your kettle off
the fire, let it cool a little; then
stir in the sanders by little and little;
stir it continually until such time as it comes
to the bottom or skin [end]; then set
your kettle upon the fire again and
stir it continually very fast, and so let it
boil until it boils off all the froth
and when it will boil no more and
is red, take it off the fire, let it cool
a little, then strain it and put it into
gallipots: your kettle must be twice as big
again as your receipt, and your
fire must be very little, without
flame, for it will quickly catch
fire and endanger all, and will not be put
out again without the bellows and sack.
To [ap]ply, see [page] 347.
Unto all wounds and ulcers apply

and then use to lay on only a paper
over the balm; give it inwardly
with warm sack for a surfeit. It
does help the gout and many
other things. Memorandum: so made.
Lady Nuniston gave [this] for the torn rupture:
wash the oil with the sack, [and] the
turpentine with the rose water.
Lucatello was an Italian and
sold this oil for 10 shillings.
After it is made, set your gallipot close bound
with a double cloth with a dish in the ground
3 or 4 feet deep, and let it stand so
3 months; it is then perfect.

A wonderful [remedy] for a swollen shin/leg
A certain man had his shin suddenly
swollen from the knee even to the ankle with
redness and burning, etc. Take juice of
Calendula, i.e., marigold, and mixed with
vinegar; anointing lukewarm, [he applied it to] the shin,
and with a linen cloth soaked in the same
juice, he placed it lukewarm around the
shin, and within 3 hours, when he had removed
the medicated cloth afterwards, he applied a new [cloth]
of the juice, and it was quickly cured. Best usage.

Malum Mortuum
To heal marmolds [chronic leg ulcers]
Take a clean linen cloth and wipe the
leg therein close and tight; then
pour upon the leg hot water,
as hot as may be suffered; then wrap
the leg in its bed one night and
a day; let it take no cold nor
air. The second day, take away
the cloth, and put into each sore lint,
or a linen cloth wet in cold water.
Then spread this ointment following
round about the edges of the sores,
laid upon cloth; but touch not the
sore in any wise. Then cover the
leg with a linen cloth wet in hot
water very hot; and do this each
day twice, until such time as the sores
with a cloth dipped in cold water, the
little sores may be healed with the
unguentum senade [p. 38, recipe 2].
Black ointment for gangrenous
ulcers and hard [sores], ointment of
Dimlin
Take copperas, saltpetre, ashes of
broom, ashes of black tortoise/snail shell, and
atramentum [vitriol] of each ½ dram, quicksilver
2 drams, verdigris 1 dram, goose grease
31 drams; pound the ashes doubly in a mortar at
the fire; afterwards add the remaining powders,
and put all well mixed in a box,
and it will be a black ointment.
For malum mortuum, a plaster
Take wax, resin, tallow, oil, of each [equal parts],
make a plaster. Anoint the pimples with
unguentum album, and do it not away
until it peel off; and always your
plaster must be made smaller and smaller.
An especial plaster for
malum mortuum / marmold
Take litharge of gold in fine powder
1 lb, oil a quart, white wine and
old stale urine clarified over the
fire of each 1 lb, vinegar 1 lb; boil them
all on a soft fire; then by little and
little put in your litharge, and
stir it well; then add wax cut
small 2 oz, of olibanum and myrrh
in fine powder of each 3 drams or ½ oz, and
make it up; it heals all sores;
it is for lords.

Scrophules [Scrofula]
There are three kinds of scrofula, and in three
ways they are to be cured, namely:
1. By dissolving,
2. By putrefying, 3. By cutting.
In healing scrofula, let the patient
bleed or purge tough, gross, and viscous
phlegm, namely:
Take choice turbith 3 drams, ginger 1 dram, sugar
3 drams; make it in fine powder and
incorporate it well, 1 dram for a dose
in warm drink or with wine to the powder;
neither heats nor excoriates...
at the end of phlebotomy made and repeated,
and provokes urine, vomiting, bath, and water...
where another...
Let him abstain from repletion, whence...
gross foods. Let him abstain from venery
and superfluous speaking, laughter, and the like,
since they draw matter to the place.
And let him beware lest his head ache,
be heavy, strife, anger, etc.
And let him not sleep under rain or flat
under his head.
From the application of cupping glasses altogether
let him beware, because it not only draws matter
to the place, but thickens it.

Dropsy
To know whether the dropsy be of heat or cold
Inquire where the swelling did first begin: above or beneath; if it
began first above, then the dropsy is cold; if in the feet, then hot. And
in the dropsy the more you drink, the more you may [desire].
In every kind of dropsy
Without doubt it restores anyone merely with the giving of 1 dram of choice rhubarb,
powdered and ground, given at dawn with 2 drams of compound oxymel mixed,
with water of a decoction of garden lettuce and roots of fennel and smallage; I have cured many.
And I did not give this remedy except every third or fourth day according to the patient's strength.
Likewise to the weak we did not give 1 dram of rhubarb; to others for whom rhubarb sufficed not, I gave rose and first oxymel of squills or compound with decoction water of lettuce and fennel roots, especially when the sick man was without fever.
When indeed there was fever, I gave with the same water compound syrup or laxative honey of roses; and for flux of the belly I gave syrup of quinces with the same water, or syrup of verjuice and rhubarb once or twice a week according to strength, with comforting and binding foods; and the quantity of rhubarb was not above 1 dram without harm.
For the dropsy
Take a new-laid egg, put away the white, and to the yolk put as much
of the juice of flower-de-luce [iris] as will fill the shell; set it in the
embers until it be hot, and sup it off fasting; do this every morning and
void much water.
Royal Medicine
Take raw juice of iris root as much as an eggshell can hold, fasting...
And juice of soft iris root... cures every dropsy.

[Left Column (Latin treatise on Paralysis: definition, Cura, Nota, Causa, ointments)]
Palsy
Paralysis differs much
from the greater apoplexy, yet
resembles the lesser; and frequently
the lesser apoplexy terminates in palsy.
Sometimes palsy is without sensation, and
sometimes it perishes with sensation. And in this
it differs from spasm, because in palsy
the limbs are extended and are weak
[and] soft, but in spasm they are hard and
are curved.
Cure
Give in the morning diuretic oxymel; afterwards
let him enter a dry bath, and there remain
2 hours, and let him be very well rubbed; and in
clean water let him be very well washed. A bath
may be prepared with sage. Then put him in bed
and let him rest quietly 3 hours.
Then let him rise. And for eight days in the morning
let him drink a spoonful of sage water with 1 dram
of powder of castoreum. And if his ability
allows, foment the limbs with this water.
Take ardent water [aqua vitae] where castoreum
... 1/2 dram, nutmeg, lignum aloes, cinnamon,
... 1 dram, zedoary, stoechas, anise,
... of sage, hyssop, nutmeg
of each 1 1/2 drams. Let a powder be made and mixed
and distilled through an alembic.
Note
Those who tremble are more easily
curable because they are not truly
paralytic, but disposed to this.
The cause of palsy are humors,
liquid phlegm etc. ... obstructing
nerves and arteries, from which obstruction
follows deprivation of the spiritual senses
destruction of motion.
In every case oil of laurel
and of juniper avails.
Ointment for palsy
Take castoreum, euphorbium, calamint,
origanum, dittany, greater comfrey,
of each 1 handful, sage 2 handfuls, cowslip,
peony of each 1 1/2 handfuls; let them be powdered and
put in fat of fox and goose;
melt, add wax as much as suffices, and let an ointment be made.
For palsy of the tongue
Take juice of sage, juice of cowslip,
meadow water [or aqua vitae] of each 1/2 oz, egg whites
2; let a plaster be made and applied
to the nape of the neck, and the tongue will be loosed.
A very good ointment for palsy
Take juice of sage 1 lb, castoreum 2 drams,
hog's lard as much as suffices; let an ointment be made.
It is good sometimes to provoke
vomiting in palsy.

Cramp
Spasm is a contraction of the nerves
towards their origin: and by
consequence the muscles are contracted.
And spasm may be called
extension, because the nerves are stretched
in breadth.
Cure
Take unwashed wool, and dipped in
warm oil of mastic, and applied to the stomach
and praecordia; let the head be fo-
mented with oil of spikenard or of laurel
applied on the head.
If [with] a sharp clyster, and it be made
in a warm place in which its use may be.
If the vertebrae are dislocated [dislocantur],
old oil [of ...] avails, and
upon a plaster of mastic-tree leaves with
wine and beaten honey, and anoint with
oil of philosophers.
Oil of philosophers is thus made
Take of labdanum as much as you will,
storax root, aloeswood, amber,
musk, myrrh, frankincense, spikenard,
cloves, marjoram, aromatic balsam,
red storax, of each, gum [of pine?] or
colophony, as much as suffices. Distil thence an oil,
and it is called oil of philosophers, or divine [oil],
or [oil] of perfect mastery.
It helps epilepsy, vertigo, palsy,
spasm, and diseases of the nerves,
cold joints, gout, and sciatica, and
pains of the back and knees, splenetic persons,
[diseases] of the kidneys, bladder, and womb, etc.

half a drachm; turbith 1 drachm; honey as much as suffices; make an electuary,
of which let him take a little for 7 days, to the quantity

=== Canvas 197 (159) ===
[Upper Full-Width Section (De Panaritio)]
159 [Page number]
Concerning Panaritium [Whitlow / Felon]
Panaritium is a hot aposteme happening at the side of the nail, of vehement
pain, and sometimes it ulcerates and leads to corrosion; and sometimes runs
sanies [ichor] from a subtle and fetid ulceration, and then there is fear [danger] of the finger.
Cure
In the beginning let it be steeped in hot vinegar mixed with barley meal; afterwards put
this plaster: Take burnt tragacanth, frankincense of each 1 dram, verdigris half a dram; let them be brought together
with honey and apply upon it. If the humour was corrosive, then administer calcadion [?]
p. 42. When it ulcerates, apply aloes with arsenic in the manner of a plaster or in
powder, and let it be covered with a cloth dipped in wine. And when it begins to run
sanies from the ulcerated panaritium, then cauterize and cleanse so that the
malice [spread] not into the whole finger; then cure until it be healed. ... let it not be applied with oil etc.
If the nail corrodes ... Take ceruse and mix with powder
of orpiment and, a plaster being made in this manner, apply upon the nail. Master John Arderne to the same.
He writes that a woman having a stroke upon the thumb with a mallet, and it did
rot, could not heal it with Sanguobolus p. 78, neither with unguentum viride, nor with pulvis
rubeus; but was treated with a hot iron so far [to cauterize] it, and then healed it.
This disease Panaritium is called a whitlow, and it is a dangerous evil,
and hot impostume; and will eat the bone in the finger's end quite away in
a short time as I have often seen, and out of the one joint to harm [?] the rest of
the hand when others have been long about it and could not do it.
I healed them as follows and failed not if they came in time. Thanks be to God.

[Bottom Left Column (Pricked Sinews, Fistula Tents)]
Sinews pricked or hurt
I have [known] many that took on them great
skill when a sinew has been pricked or else
partially cut [?] some sinew; that after 12 days
or more with dressings have not been healed;
and the reason, as I conceived, was for
that they could not stop a certain kind
of watery blood that issued forth from
the sinew hurt or cut; which may
be done by digestives to turn the blood
into quittour [pus], i.e., thick white-yellow
matter, and so heal it up. See [p.] 139.
If the sinew putrefy, or of white
sugar be put [to] the sinew pricked to it,
will make the humour issue and cause the
wetting [weeping] of the sinew to cease, and it will
heal well after by digestion. See [p.] 349.
But in a desperate cause you
may do thus:
Take rosewater or sinew water 1 oz, sublimate
in fine powder 1 dram; mix them and let them seethe.
Dissolve them [and] put in this water.
But my second way of healing
fistula p. 23, with the tent, is most
certain as well in deep and narrow
thrust new and green wounds, as in
fistulas and old sores; but because it
is painful, seldom to be used but in case
where other drinks [?] will not serve.
Often used it, and never saw it fail. Thanks be to God.
In stubborn and long sore arm the hand

with basilicon and it did ... present
See p. 41, r. 2, & 67, r. 2: you may roll

anoint it with basilicon or such like.

[Left Column (Latin Treatise on Hernia & Cauterization)]
Rupture
Hernia is a pain that happens either
from relaxation of the siphac [peritoneum], or from
incision [rupture] of the same.
From relaxation it quickly descends
little by little in a long time, and not
suddenly as far as the bottom of the purse [scrotum].
From incision [rupture] it suddenly descen-
ds to the bottom of the purse.
And these species are called
hernia intestinalis.
Moreover, there are other species that happen
in the purse of the testicles, which are three:
namely, aquosa [watery], ventosa [windy], carnosa [fleshy].
Aquosa is nothing else than a gath-
ering of humidity, and the cause is
weakness of the testicles; because superfluous
matter thus flows to them. And some-
times indeed it happens from a blow
or [hurt of] the testicle, and its sign is
shining and heaviness in touching; humidity
yields to touch. 2
Ventosa is known by disten-
sion without weight, and lightness
to touch. 3
Carnosa: the signs are heaviness close
by, and hardness with ...
of pain, and the cause is offence of matter
to the testicles or a blow; and
all these species can be cured
by cauterization.
Potential cauterization of rupture
In the place upon the share-bone [os pubis] ... in-
cised [?] or other like signs, and
there apply caustic [combustible] matter;
being burnt indeed, quickly in medicine
apply a sharp medicament which
so long is to be repeated until through the bottom
it may be seen; to the midst the burnt flesh
which is called eschar remove; and
heal the member with generating
quickly to incarnate [grow flesh] by caring, and a little
lying supine, and it delays 40 days continually
until the powder [wound] has been very well consoli-
dated; and after he has risen, let him hold [wear]
a truss [bracalia] artificially made for
another 40 days, so that perfectly
he shall be healed.
Concerning actual cauterization
with iron: This is so painful
that no man will endure it,
as I think; therefore I did
forbear to write it.
Os pectinis is the share-bone [pubic bone].
161 [Roman numeral signature]

Cutting ruptures
Take fine hackled [?] flax and make
thereof a broad pledget, then spread
thereon the white of an egg well
beaten; thereon strew the fine
powder of bole until it be
thoroughly wet and red; then in the
midst of the pledget cut a hole
to thrust the yard [penis] through.
Make also a tent of the
almost as big as a man's little
finger, with a long thread at
the end, and dress it like to
the pledget with bole etc., the long
thread does serve to pluck out the
tent forth of the cod [scrotum].
Then take up the cod betwixt
the finger and the thumb and
hold it fast with the left hand
and let another hold the other
side fast and strain it hard
abroad; then with the knife cut
a good round slit in the skin of
the cod; then let the cod
be laid abroad flat.
Then open the hole and gather up
the siphac [peritoneum] with your fingers and
hold it fast in your hand.
To hold where the gut came out
being taken up, gather it all
towards the neck of the yard
where it is fastened and where
with your thumb nail break it
off with the vein of the garter [?] that
grows there; take the greatest
pain to endure.
Then be sure you hold fast the
siphac.
Then have your ligature ready that
is fastened, take 2 pins and for a
double thread of good linen (well
waxed with yellow wax) and
hold it fast at one end with your
right hand, and let another ...
hold the other end and cast it
about the siphac with your hold
in the left hand as near the
bottom as you can, and pluck it as
hard as may be, and cast it a
bout twice or thrice and knit it fast;
then cut the threads long off and
let it lie in the cod or purse.

Hernia
Then put in your tent into the cod and
let the little thread hang out, and

To know whether a man be curable or not ☾ ☾
In a cold phlegmatic man, fat and..., it hardly cures; but a pale or fair-complexioned and sanguine man may be helped, and this is certain. ☾ ☾

[Right Column]
☾ ☾ How I got in the bowels when they were hard and very painful ☾ ☾
Spread some of this fore-remembered plaster upon a linen table napkin, and then warm it a little and wrap the scrotum therein. Then let one with a soft hand take the scrotum and gently work the gut into the body in a very gentle manner. ☾ ☾
But if the patient be fat and the gut be out so that there is no room for it, or if by hanging in the scrotum it be hot and swelling the gut so that it will not stay in by any means:
but if the gut be out and through wind or cold air become hard and full of pain or heat or burning, this plaster will take the pain away. ☾ ☾
Or if you have not the plaster ready, then bray rosemary and smallage first cropped small with the grease aforesaid and apply it as aforesaid, and it will do it, as I have often proved. ☾ ☾
And sometimes by reason of the costiveness of the patient the gut will be hard and painful; then he must be made soluble [laxative] as in page 5, 22... for this purges him within an hour, and afterwards medicines may go down at any time without dread.
Another way to get up the gut
Take a live hen, a live cat, or a live whelp; slit it through the middle and apply it all hot, and when it is cold put it into hot water and apply it again, and do this until it go up. I always used that before.

[Left Column (Flos Unguentorum, To Grounde, To Lyve & To Myke)]
Take rosin half a pound, turpentine, clean wax,

3 drams, camphor 2 drams, mastic half a dram; make it
as on p. 50 with white wine, and it will be

To Grounde-making [Green Ointment]
Take the greenest olive oil you can get
with the common green trochisk [?] that is sold
at the apothecary's 2 pounds; vervain, smallage [apium],
woodbine, mouse-ear, daisy leaves, vale-
-rian, mallows, plantain, ribwort,
sanicle, alexanders [smyrnium], yarrow, of each 1 handful.
Shred your herbs small, pound them, and
put them and the said oil together
and boil them on a gentle fire until
it be very green; then put in rosin
in powder little by little until it be
very green and well melted; then put
1 dram wax cut in
small pieces, 3 drams, and let it boil and
skim it clean; then put in oil of
frankincense and mastic in powder
of each 2 drams, myrrh and sarcocolla both in
fine powder of each half a dram, of turpentine 3 drams;
let it boil a little and stir it well, then
strain it and keep it: it healeth all
wounds and sores, old or new. Proved.
To Lyve-making [Ointment]
Take rosin, white wax, deer suet,
boar's grease purified, of each 1 pound; herbs
of bugle, avens, thyme, daisy,
woodbine, pimpernel, of each a quantity,
white wine a pint; mastic and myrrh,
red myrrh 2 drams; powder all that will be
made into powder, and boil them all
together and stir it with a hazel stick,
and when it is well boiled take it off
the fire until it be almost cold, and
then put in turpentine 3 drams; stir it
well, then strain it into a clean
vessel and there let it cool, and then
melt it again and put it in boxes,
being well stirred and mixed. This hath
many good virtues as the other.
To Myke-making [Ointment]
Take rosin, frankincense, of each half a pound, clean
wax or virgin wax, stag suet, and
turpentine, of each 3 drams, mastic, olibanum,
of each 1 dram, camphor 3 ounces [?], white wine
a quart; powder that will be powdered
and boil all in the wine until the wine
be wasted (except the turpentine), which
must be stirred in when it is cooled a
little; strain it into fair water and
draw it and work it; divide it into
2 or 3 parts, melt half at once 2 drams, and
it is an ointment.

boil them to a plaster so perfect

when they are mixed together,
and the black of itself is good in
cleansed ulcers that be hot, and
the yellow/red one in cold ulcers; and you
should have it taken off and often wiped
and laid on again. See p. 350.
To heal an old sore
Take wax and rosin of each 2 pounds, deer suet
3 drams, cloves and mace of each 1.5 drams, saffron,
myrrh, olibanum 1 pound, red wine 2 pounds; let boil
upon the fire, continually stirring 2 or 3 hours
until the wine be consumed; take it from
the fire and stir it until it be cold, and
then make it into rolls.
Make a hose of linen cloth and spread it
with this salve and wear it until after
the sore is healed; or lay on a plaster
and let it lie a quarter of a year.
Mr Thornborough's Balm
for the pox, and hot and bodily diseases
Take of the spirits of wine a sufficient quantity, and
unto one quart thereof take of the
gum of guaiacum 3 drams, and as followeth:
First take sarsaparilla, cut it in the
length 2 inches or somewhat more,
cut one piece in 4 parts lengthwise,
and put into the glass to the spirit so
much as will fill up the glass full
with the spirits, and there let them lie
until the wine be yellow as gold; then
unto every quart of the wine put of
the gum of guaiacum 3 drams to steep,
and stir the glass until the gum be
all dissolved; then if you will you may
put in of pure Indian Balm one good
spoonful; but the more Balm the better
the medicine is, and the more gum you
put in, the colder it is.
Applied cold it healeth
green wounds, bruises, or
sprains.
Taken inwardly it cureth the pox, the
jaundice, tympanies, quartan agues, and
it openeth all obstructions, purgeth gouts,
and may be taken at all times in a pint
of small beer burnt, one or 2 spoonfuls,
without diet or danger; but you must eat
no venison, eggs, nor salt meats, neither
drink any wine, nor [know] women a month
after.
Keep it closely stopped or it will turn to balm, and
it hath many other virtues.
Aonob [catchword/note]

Take white lead in fine powder sifted

=== Canvas 215 (177) ===
[Left Column (Discenteria: 4 manners of fluxes, 3 manners of dysentery, Cura Dissenterie)]
Dysentery
There be 4 manners of fluxes:
1. Dysentery is when one
voids blood mingled with, as it were,
the scrapings of guts.
2. Diarrhoea: the bloody
flux is when blood passes from
a man without mingling with any
thing like scraping.
3. Lientery is when the
meat [food] runs from a man all
whole and undigested.
4. Simple flux is when
one is loose of that which
it has eaten, etc., and as it is
digested and thin.
There be three manners
of dysenteries:
1. In the upper gut
2. In the middlemost gut
3. In the nethermost gut.
In one it is like the washing of
flesh, and is soon healed.
In another, like scraping of gut
or parchment.
In the third it runs like to
whole gobbets [lumps], and is often times
incurable.
Cure of Dysentery
Take decoction of quinces, ...
and elder [flowers], a drink.
Or wine of pomegranates,
or acacia with gum arabic,
or tragacanth with
syrup of myrtles let them take,
and use binding foods.
Otherwise
Take juices of ribwort plantain, plantain,
comfrey major and minor, of each
equal parts, and give to drink.
Otherwise
Take tormentil, boil in water
and give the strained liquor, and temper tormentil
in milk, etc.
Otherwise
Take syrup of quinces and of myrtles,
and after cessation of the flux, give ...
hyssop ... wine is much good.

Of goat dung, as I find written:
If the fistula have many holes that are
narrow and crooked, so that medicines

honey, warm it and lay it on; and the

it taketh away the pain, the swelling,
and draweth out all filth and rottenness, and
purgeth the sinews that are corrupted.

For a canker
Take goat's dung 4 parts, the gall of a bull if

So that it seems to me, that goat

=== Canvas 226 (188) ===
[Left Column (Of the Salvatory Box & Mr. Woodall surgical extracts)]
Of the Salvatory Box.
Put into the six several places of the box these
six unguents, namely: Basilicon, Apostolorum,
Linimentum Arcaei, Aureum, Diapompholigos,
and Dialthea, or rather Unguentum
Populeon; and Unguentum Album for the 2 last
namely Diapompholigos and Dialthea.
Mr. Woodall, p. 31, title 'Boras Box'
In new wounds let the flesh gather as proceed as
it will, the ground being clean (and no rotten
or putrefied bone in the wound); and when you
will cicatrize it, lay on a little burnt alum
or wet lint in copperas water and let it lie
and dry again, and lay on that dry lint.
Look in p. 139, rule 1, at the end.
Melilot plaster simplex, good in green wounds;
it draws and heals well, and he praises it
for chilblains [kibes] in heels.
He also praises [Emplastrum] de minio, a good discusser
of hot humors, an assuager of pains, mollifier,
repels [humors?] and is very commodious for
for wounds and ulcers, and he refers all to Mr.
Gale's note in his Dispensatory.
In page 68:
Note here for a general rule in opening of
tumors that be full, [it] is great ease to the
patient; but never press out the matter
too forcibly, nor seek to run out at once,
because it contains natural heat and fine
spirits, and sudden evacuation is not good;
therefore leave it to nature to work upon.
And for the furthering of the fall of the eschar,
it is mere folly; for he says the longer it
lies on, the better he likes it, for he says
you cannot keep on the eschar by art if that
nature will cast it off.
He also says that upon an aposteme [abscess],
a caustic medicine is better and safer
than a knife, if the aposteme be ripe; for
the caustic can pierce no further than
it reaches unto, because the matter will
choke the caustic; then may be used
attractive medicines, as gum elemi or
galbanum spread upon leather, or maturatives
as Diachylon cum gummis, or a mild poultice
of the decoction of althaea roots, or linseed,
if the cause be cold, add fenugreek a
little; or apply the poultice, p. 35, rule 1, at
the end: Take watercresses etc., and these warm,
not hot, or some other poultice. And [when] it is open,
he applies Basilicon warm; and now
and then dry lint, and cleanse [with] abstersive
medicines; and powder of vitriol with a
little lint wet therein to touch the ulcer
once or twice and no more.
An aposteme opened by caustic followed
within 4 days: put in no tent, but dress it
with Basilicon warm; put a little within
the hollowness until 2 dressings, and lay
on your warm poultice; after, Basilicon alone
warm applied, well spread, and keep it dry;
bolster it well, and it will heal of itself,
for nature intends the healing of itself.

196  ... of vitriol / oil of vitriol
Pure and not diluted, neither ought nor
can it be taken within the body: for besides its
acrimony, intensifying like fire, and what-
ever it touches it burns: indeed it corrodes all things
except glass, except stone and fatty things,
such as wax, tallow, oil, and of liquors
even of oils it changes the colour, especially ...
..., to which if it be mixed, it renders a bloody
colour, if even in ... it be contained
although cold, and suddenly ... to itself
..., so much it grows hot of its own accord, that with hands
one can scarcely hold it. Poured upon the earth
it boils, just as pure ...:
wherefore also ... by the chemi-
sts it is called. Just as therefore pure
..., so also this oil the stomach
comforts, and excites to appetite for food
and stimulates, warms a cold stomach,
consumes phlegm, thick and ... hu-
mours it cuts, helps colic and dysentery,
thirst and heat of ... in
fevers it extinguishes: and where loathing
it averts, it immediately stops hiccup
and drives away nausea and loathing,
but it must be tempered with certain other [things].
For heat and thirst in fevers
Rx. Syrup of juice or infusion of violets 1 ounce,
cinnamon water 1 dram, barley [water] 3 or 4 ounces,
oil of vitriol 3 or 4 drops, mix, let it be given.
Of [vitriol] his oil
I saw it applied onto a sore nose with the point
and it caused a great eschar which was
wet with oil and long ere it dried; this did
... at length.
For heat in hot agues
Rx. Fair water 4 ounces, oil of vitriol five
or 6 drops, sugar a little, rosewater
3 drops, wine vinegar as much, mix them
and drink it.
Otherwise
Rx. Of the oil 4 drops in plantain, sorrel, or in
any other cooling water.

[Left Column (The Virtues of Oil of Vitriol — Wodgate)]
The virtues of Oil of Vitriol
[vitriol] Wodgate
It helpeth the infirmities of the lights [lungs],
with fennel or fumitory water. It doth
put away the melancholy humours from
the stomach, with balm water. And doth
comfort the stomach after a wonderful
manner, and doth defend the whole
body from inward apostumes and infla-
mmations. And therefore is used in the pleurisy
and in wound drinks and proved good,
for it attenuates the blood wonderfully,
and defends the ills from corruption
and putrefaction.
It conglutinates ruptures of bones and
veins: and comforteth and strengtheneth
all parts of the body exceedingly and is a
principal cordial.
It prevents the scurvy taken inward
with wine or beer and is good in the spasm, and
if it must be daily used 2 or 3 drops.
In that calenture it appeaseth all other
medicines taken in plantain, sorrel or
any other cooling water or in the midway
that they being loose-bodied phlebotomy used.
In rotten and putrefied gums, touch
the gums gently with the oil: But
touch not the whole flesh.
In angina and ulcerations in the throat
and mouth, that will not obey other medicines,
touch it once with this oil warily and then
it will heal with any medicine that [follows].
It is good for inflammations in the throat
as squinancy or angina, a few drops
in a little gargarism or lotion. To make
... honey savour: put a few drops. And
the body to the salivate [?].
In ulcers and fistulas to enlarge an orifice,
remove a callous, to prepare it unto
healing: ... touch it with lint wet
in the oil upon a probe end.
It is good in all purgative medicines
and diuretic workings.
It is good for a weak stomach oppressed with
phlegm or slime, and in conserve of
roses a few drops to turn the colour;
it is excellent in that case.
In pestilential fevers it is excellent as Mr.
Callender ... appeareth and on
the other side.
The little dose is so much as will make it
taste somewhat sour. In pestilential
fevers and calentures you may give more,
but remember to shake it well before
you give it, for it will sink to the bottom.
And hath other virtues
The [vitriol] mark for oil of vitriol.

[Left Column (Pine-Kernel Restorative, Complexion Balls, Cock Restoratives)]
198 [Page number]
Restoratives
A praised restorative
Take the kernels of the pine-apple [pine nuts], and
take off their skins, then pound them
small; then strain them with strong
wine (such as Rumney), and let the wine
cover them three fingers at least,
and eat thereof.
To restore the complexion
lost by sickness or women
Take fennel seeds, carrot seeds,
linseed, of each 3 ounces; grind them well;
temper them with new cow's milk,
make them into balls as big as beans,
and eat 3 first and 3 last.
To make a restorative of a cock
Take an old cock, dress him clean, wash
him not; put him in a new earthen pot
without any liquor; put to him galingale,
ginger, and nettle seeds, all in powder; stop
the pot close, and set it in a kettle of
seething water, and boil it there 48 hours;
then eat the liquor that comes of the
cock.
To distil a cock
Take a cock, pluck him alive and let him
remain so one hour; then kill him, clean
him, take out his bowels, wipe the blood
as clean as you can with a clean cloth (but
wash him not); then chop the flesh and
bones together as small as you can, and
put all into a good water glass with a
narrow mouth; stop it close. Put thereto
12 spoonfuls of pure red rose water,
12 good dates minced finely, 12 cakes
of Manus Christi, or as much fine sugar
— but Manus Christi is better — of old gold
at pleasure. Stop the glass close and leave
a little hole for air for [fear of] breaking
the glass; wrap the glass in hay, and
let it stand in a pot of hot water
24 hours; then strain all hard, and
let it cool, and it will be a jelly; keep
it clean. And you may add cinnamon
and nutmeg in powder if you will; 3
spoonfuls with other broth at one time
is enough.
To stew a cock (best)
Take a cock, dress him clean, put him
whole into an earthen pot; put to him
clean water and no salt, parsley roots,
fennel root, succory [chicory] roots, clean
scraped [and] washed (their piths cast away)
and shred; borage leaves, orache leaves,
bugloss leaves, a little thyme, a few
raisins of the sun, and a few prunes.
Boil [catchword]

[Right Column (Pig Restoratives, Egg-Yolk Water, Pigeons & Chickens)]
Restoratives
Boil all until the bones fall from the flesh,
keeping the pot close stopped; strain all
hard and keep it, and drink it warm.
Before you drink it, let it settle and
skim off the fat with a spoon.
It were better to give it in other broth,
3 or 4 spoonfuls as before.
To make a restorative of a pig
Dress a pig clean, cut him in four
quarters, and boil him in two quarts
of running water; skim it clean, and
add sage chopped small; then boil all to
a pottle [2 quarts]; strain it through an hippocras
bag or a fair cloth, and drink it at
your pleasure warm.
To distil a pig
Take a young sucking pig that is not too
fat; dress him clean and quarter him,
head and feet and all; put him into an
earthen pot with a cover; then put in dates,
prunes, currants, of each 4 ounces; cinnamon,
cloves, mace, of each half an ounce; white sugar candy
2 ounces; chicory 1 handful; maidenhair, liverwort,
bloodwort, hart's-tongue, violet leaves,
strawberry leaves, of each half a handful; fennel roots
the piths [taken] out 2 or 3; sweet marjoram,
langue de boeuf [bugloss], of each 1 pugil; fine spring
water a quart; put all together, mix
them well, shut the pot close, set it in a
kettle or pot of boiling water, and let
let it boil 24 hours, and as the water
in the kettle consumes, put in more hot
water; strain it as before, keep it close
stopped; put 3 or 4 spoonfuls of this in
broth or a caudle, and eat it.
Methinks these might be put into a glass
still with head and receiver, and distilled in
water as aforesaid.
Excellent restorative
Take 30 yolks of new-laid eggs and
lay them in a platter of fair water
one hour; then take them forth and put
away the string [chalaza], and put them into a
quart of milk hot from the cow, with
a pint of rose water and the crumbs
of a new manchet [fine white loaf]; beat them all
together, then put them in a glass body [cucurbit]
and set on the head, and set it in balneo [Marie]
with a receiver close fastened, and distil
thereof 2 pounds of water; drink the water
fasting. I have found great proof of
this water. It may be distilled in an
other stillatory well set with sand and
ashes.
Restorative
Take young pigeons and chickens, of each [equal parts]; cut them
in pieces, then boil them in 3 pounds of wine
until the flesh fall from the bones; add
nutmeg, cloves, and cinnamon in powder,
and drink thereof often.
An excellent restorative
Take capped dates 3 or 4 ounces [continued on p. 199].

Restoratives
Take capped dates 4 ounces, wash them clean
and take out their stones and piths,
then cut them small; pound them in
a brazen mortar until they be
very tough like wax; then put
them into 4½ ounces of clarified honey
[Marginal note:] Set it on the fire
and stir them well until the dates
be dissolved; then put thereinto of
long pepper, cloves, mace, and
nutmeg, all in fine powder, of each
1 dram. Set all on the fire again, and
let them seethe softly, and stir them
well, and put in the powders by little
and little until all be well stirred
in; then let it boil until it be
somewhat thick; then put in 1½ drams of
fine ginger in powder, and stir
it as before. Eat thereof first and
last; this was my great-grandfather's,
William D[ineley], and is excellent.
To restore a man
Take the bruised/seethed roots of satyrion [orchis], and
with the powder of black pepper and
honey, as much as suffices, make an electuary.
For an old man
Take capped dates 1 pound, take out their
stones and piths, pound them in a mortar,
then boil them in a quart of good
muscadell [muscatel wine] until it be somewhat
wasted [reduced]; keep it in a glass close
stopped; take thereof in broth or in other
thing, 2 or 3 spoonfuls at once.
For the same
Take fennel seeds, parsley seeds, ca-
raway seeds, cardamom, of each half a dram;
rhubarb, alum, of each 2 drams; mastic 1 dram,
all in fine powder; then melt sugar
as much as suffices, and stir in the powders with a horn
slice [spatula] until it be thick, and then
knead [?]; then put it in boxes and
eat thereof fasting; this is good
for a surfeit.
A good restorative
Take the bulbs [tubers] of satyrion that will
sink, dry them in the sun and
make them into powder. Take of that
powder half a pound; borax in powder half an ounce;

little; then stir in the satyrion, and stir
them well, and when it is left
standing it is enough; eat it last
at night. And grind sperma-
ceti and borax together, and drink
it with ale or muscadell.

hectic [fever] or consumption.
The powder of the great gilly-
flowers taken with new goat's or
ass's milk cures hectic [fever] in 40 days.
A good restorative
Take a well-fleshed capon, roast him
well; then take the brawns [breast-meat] and
the hard flesh of the wings, the
merrythought [wishbone]; put away the
skin and the fat and sinews; then
take blanched almonds, dates (the
white piths taken away), of each
by weight; mince the flesh, the
almonds, and dates small by
themselves; and beat them all
severally in a mortar very
small; then beat them all well
together; then have sugar a good
quantity, of red rose water a less
quantity; boil them and take off the
froth; then put in the flesh, the
almonds, and dates; let all boil and
stir them well for [fear of] burning,
until it be like marmalade;
then have ready cinnamon in fine
powder and [corianders/spices?] as much as the
dates, and stir it in by little and little;
then let all boil a little and put it
in a close box or pot; and eat
thereof divers times in the day as
much as a nutmeg at a time.
It is a high restorative for
old folk: the Lady Alice of [?].

[Right Column (Aqua Caponis / Capon Water, later hand)]
Restoratives
201 [Page number]
Aqua Caponis, or Capon Water.
Take a capon, the guts being pulled out, cut it
in pieces, the fat being taken away, boil
it in water, as much as suffices, in a close vessel; take of
this broth 3 pounds, borage and violet water, of each half a pound,
white wine 1 pound, red rose leaves 2½ drams, the
flowers of borage, violets, and bugloss, of each 1 dram,
pieces of bread hot out of the oven half a pound,
cinnamon bruised half an ounce; distil it in a glass
still according to art. This water is cordial and
greatly nourishing, and strengthening for such
as are in consumptions, and restores strength
lost either by fevers or other sickness; it is
a sovereign remedy for hectic fevers,
and marasmus. London Dispensatory, Culpeper.

Waters

[Left Column (Waters for Fistulas & Ulcers)]
To eradicate the callous of
a fistula, polypus, scab, scurf,
and manginess of the face, pock-
ulcers, etc.
Take rose water and plantain water, of each 1 lb.; of
honeysuckle [water] 1 lb.; rock alum and sublimate,
of each 4 drams; mix, gently strain, and digest it in a glass
or near the fire; or boil it to the con-
sumption of a fourth part.
To make Lac Virginis that
will skin ulcers and kill tetters.
Take strongest white wine vinegar 1 lb.; litharge
of gold, most finely ground, 1 lb.; let them macerate
together 3 days; stir them twice or
thrice every day; then settle one whole
day; pour off the clearest and keep it
in a glass close stopped. Then take rain
water 1 lb.; common salt 2 drams; rock
salt [sal gemmae] ... Boil these to the
dissolution of the salt, let it settle one
day or more. Then take of the clearest
in a glass 2 parts of the first water,
2 parts and more, by 2 drams of the one and
2 drams [to] 2 drams of the other; put them both
in a glass and it will [turn] like milk,
much commended for the killing of
tetters, etc.
Against fistulas and old ulcers:
Take waters of danewort, ... , and southernwood,
of each 2 drams; powdered sublimate 2 drams; mix them with-
out fire. Or take sublimate 6 drams, fountain
water 2 lb.; boil them together in a
double vessel at a gentle fire one hour.
Against fistulas and old ulcers:
The first water may be applied simply
of itself. But the latter water
ought to be mixed with the like pro-
portion of salad oil and applied with lint.
Against fistulas [and] corroding ulcers:
Take waters of plantain and roses, of each 1/2 lb.;
chalybeate water 2 lb.; alum 2 drams; white
sugar 1 dram. Boil them together unto the
perfect dissolving of the powders of the
alum and sugar.
Against fistulas, ulcers, tetters, etc.:
Take sulphur and white lead in powder, of each 1 dram; rain
water 3 lb.; boil them gently one
quarter of an hour; then skim it, and
put the liquor over the fire again, and
when it begins to simmer, put in mercury
sublimate 1/2 dram in fine powder; stir them
together the space of 2 or 3 minutes,
take it off the fire, let it cool, keep it
in glasses against fistulas, ulcers, scabs, etc.
Against fistulas, noli [me tangere], etc.:
Take greenest vitriol 3 drams; burn it in a
crucible until it return to its natural
greenness; let it cool; powder it; cast of that
powder into 3 quarts of boiling water;
let them steep, and then will arise a
black scum; take it off with a feather; so
long as any does arise; then keep the
water against fistulas and noli me tangere.
Against ulcers of the privities:
Take rock alum 1 dram, powder of verdigris
1 dram, rose water q.s. Boil them to the
space of an hour, strain it and keep it.
Out of 'The Surgeon's Closet'.

Take fresh butter, capon's grease, and
goose grease, of each 1 1/2 oz.; live sulphur,

For the same:
Take hog's lard and live sulphur, of each
1 dram; waters of purslane and roses, of each
q.s., with saffron 1 dram; mix and ...
Against inveterate redness of
the face or any other parts:
Take white nitre 1/2 lb., rock alum 1 lb. 2 drams.
Armenian bole 2 drams, rain water q.s.; put them
all into a pot and boil them to the wasting
of the water, and take of the dry mass
1 dram and dissolve it in rain water q.s.
and use it.
To produce a curative:
Take mercury sublimate 1/2 dram, plantain water
2 oz.; stamp them together in a stone mortar
with a wooden pestle until it wax
white; then put it into a little linen
bag; then take juice of lemons 2 oz., rose
water of red roses 2 oz., mix them and infuse the
sponge/bag in [it] until it has imbibed all the liquor;
then make a light expression thereof
and keep the liquor in glass; apply it
with a feather.
For swellings, fretting ulcers:
Take plantain water 2 oz., sublimate 1 dram,
sal ammoniac 1 1/2 drams, common salt
1 dram; boil them in a double vessel until
a fourth part be wasted, and keep it.
For the same (344):
Take water of plantain and red roses,
of each 1/2 lb.; alum 2 drams; sugar 1 dram; boil
them together unto the melting of
the sugar and alum.
Keep it. Plantain water 1 lb. and rose water 2 lb. is against
it.
To heal an old sore and take
out heat:
Take ashes of ash-tree 2 parts, with fountain
water q.s.; make lye thereof, let it stand
2 or 3 days and then well clear and strain
it; [it] must be taken off with a feather; pour the
clearest into a basin, add thereto sal ammo-
niac q.s., stir it to dissolution and keep it in glass.
Fomentation for a red face:
Take mercury sublimate in powder 1/2 dram, infused in juice
of lemons 5 or 6 hours; bitter almonds
blanched and bruised 3 drams; thrice-camphorated water;
mix, let a fomentation be made, with which let the face be fomented morning and
evening, but with caution from the eyes. Dr. Sadler.

Ague Cake
For the ague cake in the left
side called the rose cake:
Take new butter forth of the churn,
wring out the whey and wash it
not in any wise; then have black
wool small carded in broad flakes,
and lay one of them in a frying [pan],
add to butter, and so turn the wool
often in the butter until the wool
be black. Anoint the side with some
of that butter warm and stroke
it downwards something hard,
and put the fingers under the ribs
to loose the cake; then lay on the
wool as hot as may be suffered; do
this morning and evening nine days
together, or until he be well.
One ball of wool will serve 4 times.
For the same
Take good vinegar a quart, of the leaves
of hollyhock that has white flowers,
of linseed, of each 1 handful, the grated crumbs
of leavened bread 1 handful; chop the leaves
small and bruise the seeds, and boil
all together until it be thick, but
not too thick; then plaster-wise
lay some of it upon the cake as hot
as may be suffered; dress it morning
and evening, and warm no more
than will serve for a plaster, and change
it at every dressing.
For the cake in the belly
Take cottonweed, fry it in fresh
butter; bind it hot to the place
and let it lie 24 hours; do
three or four days together.
For the same
Take the leaves and roots of daisies, of
smyrnium [alexanders], orpine, of each 1 part; chop and
bruise the herbs well, then fry them
in fresh butter, suet, or grease;
do this and lay this on the grief all
hot twice a day.
Many think this disease is
the hardness of the spleen.
For the ague cake
Take hart's-tongue 3 handfuls, boil it in a
gallon of fine wort to a pottle [2 quarts];
strain it through a clean cloth,
keep it in a glass close stopped, and
drink thereof first and last.
For the same
Take the root of gladden [iris], make it into powder,
give half a spoonful thereof in
white wine; and let him take half
a spoonful of the powder in pottage.

Stone
For the stone, a proved medicine [CC]
Take of the juice of ribwort, garden tansy,
feverfew, of each 3 oz, of houseleek 2 oz;
put them into a pint pot, thereto oil
of honey 1 quarter [?], or 2 oz; boil them upon a
gentle fire, and in the boiling stir
therein the fine meal of beans, as much as suffices to
make it thick for a plaster.
Spread of this alone reasonably thick
upon a linen cloth fit for the nether [lower]
belly; but spread not the salve so near to
the edges of the cloth, and that the cloth be
double, it is the better.
This plaster must be so long spread as
will reach from one hip bone unto the
other, and the cloth bare without salve
long enough to fasten upon the navel.
The salve must also upon the small of the back
be laid upon two long holes [?] or width thereof, that
you must be sure to cover those holes with
the salve, for there the stone does breed.
Lay this plaster on in the morning and so
wear it until the next morning, and
then make the plaster new; and this do
three days together, during which time
let him drink of:
spring water blood-warm (but
not hot in any wise), or the distilled water
of elder flowers, or of the water of
linaria or toadflax, or of bean
leaves distilled, or any or all of them,
6 or 8 spoonfuls morning and evening
blood-warm, the cold out and no more.
If this be used in the beginning
when a man or woman has not been
long troubled or often sick of the stone,
thrice in a year it will free him of
the stone in the kidneys for ever.
But if he have often had it
and the stone inveterate and hard, needless
it will help him and give ease for
a time, using the course and water
as follows; or take my tide pills ex
nocte insumge [at night?].
A powder for the stone [CC]
Take cinnamon, anise, fennel, cumin, of each
2 drams, liquorice 2.5 drams, galingale 3 drams, spikenard 1 dram,
gromwell [milium solis] 3 drams, ben [?] 3 drams, powder of black roots [?]
dose 1.5 drams or 2 drams to a strong body.
Put the powder, 1 dram or 1.5 drams, into a good
draught of white or Rhenish wine; let
it stand and soak well, then drink it
fasting, and fast 2 hours after it at the
least; take this 2 mornings together. The
first morn the better: it first loosens the
matter; the second removes and carries [?] phlegm,
the third all the stone in waist and bladder, the
stone. Do this after the plaster is wrought
and the water drunk. I have seen
great good of these, sometimes severally
in men and women. [CC] Thanks be to God.

[Right Column (Colic, Tobacco Clyster & Umbilicus)]
221 [Page number]
An experiment for the colic and iliaca
Take a bladder, put it [on] a clyster pipe stopped
close with a peg as you would give a clyster;
blow the bladder full of the smoke
of tobacco, knit [tie] the bladder close that the
smoke go not out; put the pipe into
the fundament, pluck out the peg
and thrust in the smoke, emptying [it];
in time it eases, as I was told by an
honest friend; but I can see no reason to
keep the smoke from passing forth. See ...
A servant of King Henry's lay very
sick, to whom the King did send 2
of his own physicians and bade them
preserve his life, but by the grace ...
he was sick unto death. So the
King went from his sick man and
thought never to see him again. When
all the company were gone, his gentle-
man took a pipe full of tobacco and
put it up his fundament and blew in
the smoke, and then put in another
pipe and blew that in also; he presently
felt a stirring and recovered and
was whole before King Henry knew [of his] death;
this was Erson whose person was going
into Scotland.

years they have enjoyed.

For the same

Strangury
The signs of the strangury are
the urine dropping, and burning with
great desire to piss and can do but
a little at once.
The cause
ulcer in the bladder, or imposthume
in the reins or liver, which causes
the urine to be sharp and biting.
To loose the strangury
Boil the root of asphodel in water, then
take them and boil them in wine and
oil, and thereof make a plaster and
apply unto the groin.
For the strangury and heat
Take the seeds of gourds, cucumbers,
and citruls of each half a dram, of melons 2 drams, of
white poppy, purslane, and endive of each
1 dram, kernels of cherry stones half a dram, of
saxifrage 3 drams; make a fine powder and use it
with stale ale.
For the same. Mr. E. Comfort
Take the hooves of the feet of swine
and burn them to ashes, and beat
them to fine powder, and drink the
quantity of a hazelnut with stale ale.
For the same. Broom
Take watercresses, boil them in fair
water, and with that water drink the
powder of broom berries.
Against burning of urine and
ulceration of the bladder
Take oil of roses, mix with goat's milk
and let it be injected with a syringe.
To restore the yard of
him that has the strangury
Take rosemary, woodbine leaves, sage
of each half a handful, alum 3 drams, honey 3
[spoonfuls], spring water 3 pounds; boil all unto
a quart; let it cool and use it with
a syringe.
Purgation for the same
Take powder diasenna half a dram, syrup of
horehound 1 dram, mix, divide into
2 parts, and according to heat let it be drunk with white
wine every third day on an empty stomach,
and fast 4 hours after; it is a strong purgation.
For the strangury
Take rosemary leaves or flowers and
boil them in white wine 2 pounds to half;
that is, put it in a close cup and add sugar
1 dram; drink it cold and apply the herb
hot unto the groin, and let him lie on
a bed 3 or 4 hours after. And
this wine is good to give with other
medicine withal.
For the strangury
Boil ivy berries in white wine and
use to drink it fasting. Excellent;
then put the berries in the ... wine.

Strangury is when
urine is distilled drop by drop.
Dysuria is when urine is retained
for many hours and afterwards follows
expulsion, and it is caused by ..., or
stone, or thick humour.
Suria [ischuria] is when for a month
it remains [retained] and brings danger.
Cure
Let phlebotomy be done from the vein which is between
the foot, and let him be purged with Benedicta, and

and give him 1 spoonful of white wine and of this electuary half a dram:
Take yarrow, ..., ...
prepared of each 2 drams, goat's/stag's blood half a dram,

of nettle and ... of each 2 drams, sugar 3 pounds;

In strangury, if he does not urinate, ... that

Of Ulceration of the Bladder
Oil of roses for ulcerated [bladder], etc.
Take as many roses as you wish, and grind in a mortar
and then put them into as much oil as pleases you,
and let it be as good as possible; some say then boil over a
gentle fire, and add more roses, thus very often,
and close the mouth of the vessel; afterwards stir with a spatula,
and in a leaden vessel with the opening closed
let it be buried in damp earth and stand there 40
days, etc. See Platearius, etc., unto the end.
If you do not have roses
Take white roses with tender shoots of branches as much as suffices, and in
a mortar grind very finely, and add oil as much as suffices so that
before, etc., and let them be boiled until the oil is parched/reduced.
Very good in all things as before.
For ulcers of the bladder
Take of the aforesaid oil of roses and mix with goat's milk
and let it be taken by mouth, and let it be injected through
a syringe into the bladder.
And with the aforesaid medicine let there be mixed
some consolidating liquors, such as juice of
plantain, comfrey [greater and lesser],
and add dragon's blood, bole [armenian], or ceruse [white lead],
most finely ground.
My opinion is that
Take sweet salad oil to alkanet, etc., as
in page 71; Sanguis Veneris I repute to be best
and pleasing to take at all times, etc.
In the bladder scabies [roughness] is generated from
burnt and salt matter: and then in the urine there appears
superfluities like bran and scales,
and a foul odour is perceived.
Let him drink every morning on an empty stomach 3 oz of water
of a decoction of barley and liquorice, and after
an hour, water of a decoction of violets, mallows,
marshmallows, and the like.
And inject with a syringe oil of roses with
milk of a woman, goat, or ass.
If he urinates pus
Take calves' bladders in wine and dry [them], but
do not burn them, and thereof make powder, and give of this
powder in broth, and he may use it in his
dishes: for a woman, the bladder of a female calf;
for a male, the bladder of a male calf.
The Signs [of bladder disease]
When one is diseased in the bladder, he has
no appetite to eat; his meat belches up
again; sometimes it is hot, sometimes
cold; he cannot sleep quietly, and he
is as [though] he were dissolved/loosed.
Item, the same here
Take fennel seeds, parsley seeds, radish
lovage, carrot root; boil all in [running]
water very well: then strain it with
a linen cloth; put to it white wine and
sodden pepper, and boil them still, and
eat together again, and drink it 7
days together fasting, and he shall be healed.

Plethora of the Stomach
To the stomach sometimes happens corruption
of food with some swelling which they call plethora,
and then there is elevation with extension of the upper
and lower [parts] with faintness: and sometimes it hap-
pens from corrupted wine; or what is very
corrupted [and] cold.
Let it be purged with common pills and afterwards com-
forted with diagalanga.
or thus
Take pomegranate flowers, boil in harsh wine and give
morning and evening one spoonful for three days, and
this avails for dysentery and lientery.
Of Phlegmon [Inflammation] of the Stomach
Sometimes there is made in the stomach an aposteme which is called
phlegmon, and then appears swelling, tossing
of the body and restlessness and wakefulness, but ex-
tremities [cold] and when it is toward the bottom it is
hard to digest and the hairs of the person stand on end with
pale pain.
Take flour of linseed, fenugreek, of each, let them be boiled
in wine and make a cataplasm, and let them take foods
light. And phlebotomy is not suitable,
namely phlebotomy; other remedies namely mentioned in Apatia.
A Vomit
Brew so much of the powder of asarabacca
as will lie upon a groat in wine or
posset drink warm fasting, etc.
Take gamboge 1 scruple, cream of tartar half a dram, barberry 1 dram,
oil of anise 4 drops, mix; let him take in the morning with faithful care.
Of Itching of the Stomach
Itching happens sometimes in the stomach and to consumption
goes. Sometimes it happens from excessive coitus.
Take myrrh, ammoniacum, frankincense, of each
let them be incorporated with juice of cabbages and make a plaster;
put upon soft leather and let it be applied until by
itself it falls off.
Of Loss of Appetite from a Full Stomach
Consider the cause and remove it; if however
you are ignorant [of it], namely serve a vomit.
To make one vomit [moon marks]
Take prepared stibium [antimony] 2 or 3 grains in fine
powder, put it into 3 or 4 spoonfuls of
white wine infused 10 or 12 hours
in hot embers or hot water and strain
it and drink the drink: sack is better.
Or give 3 grains to a strong
body in fine powder in conserve of roses
or bread and butter. But to them that is weak
2 or 2 grains at the most.
I did commonly make them eat hard bread
and then gave it. Audt. [Approved].
Be sure the sign be not at the heart.

[Left Column (Epileptia: Causes, Types & Signs)]
Epilepsy
The epilepsy or falling sickness
comes of a moist humor that
fills those places of the head that
should be void [empty], and stops the
hinder part of the head, which
is the beginning of the sickness
and fills the sinews [nerves]; and therefore
when this accident [fit] of the sickness
does come to a man, it makes him
for a time to lose his feeling
and his moving.
Otherwise, this sickness
comes of a humor in the head,
and then it is called Epilentia.
Sometimes it comes of
fumes that fly into the head
out of a feeble and sick stomach,
and then it is called Analeptia.
If it come of infirmity of
other members, then it is called
Cataleptia.
There are 2 sorts of Epileptia:
the greater, and
the lesser.
In the greater, the principal
places of the brain are stopped,
wherefore in their access [fits] they
feel nothing and foam at the
mouth, and all the body quakes,
and they are hard to help.
In the lesser, the principal places
are not altogether stopped, and there-
fore in their access they feel some-
thing and all the body quakes not,
but the hinder part of the head.
The trembling of the body is an evil
sign in the epilepsy; and if they do
fall often and arise quickly, the sign
is the better for their help.
If a woman have this sickness and
was not healed before she have her
sickness and natural courses [menses], she
will never be healed—this is, if it
come to her in her childhood.
If the sickness come of humors
in the head, these are the tokens:
heaviness of the head, the
confusion of his wit, slothfulness,
dimness of his eyes, biting of the
tongue; their water [urine], nature [semen], and siege [stool]
pass involuntarily, and in the great
epilepsy they fall and feel nothing.
249 [Page number]

[Right Column (Falling Sickness: Analeptia & Cataleptia)]
Falling Sickness   249
If this sickness come of phlegm, it is known
it is known by the softness, whiteness,
sloth, and much sleep.
If of melancholy, by blackness,
leanness, and such like.
If it come of both, then the signs are
mixed of both.
Analeptia comes of fume or
smoke in the stomach, or else of
melancholy; the tokens are:
abominations to meat and drink,
the trembling of the heart, pricking
of the stomach.
Phlegmatic meats and meat
that breeds melancholy do them much
hurt.
Sometimes they fall not, but are
feeble and weak about the time of their
access [fits].
This sickness may be of phlegm,
choler, and melancholy; and you
may know of which by their signs.
Cataleptia comes of smoke that
flies fast off into the head and there
it is cold; and this smoke comes of
a blood which makes a man hot and
burning without fury, and to have
a swift pulse; and oftentimes it
makes him swoon, and sometimes
they have a fever with it, and answer
not when they are spoken unto, and
it is evil [hard] for them to speak; their
eyes water, they sigh much, and
sometimes their breath stinks.
In any of these three sicknesses, if the
patient foam much and white, and strain
their teeth hard when they are fallen,
then the disease is of phlegm.
If he close his eyes as though he did sleep
and foam not, and arise quickly, it is of
choler.
If he wax black and turn his mouth aside
and strain his hands together, and lie
still as though he were dead, and
foam a little, then it is of melancholy.
They which have the Epilepsia or Ana-
lepsia should be dieted with meat
temperately hot.   [catchword: thus]

Morphea [Scurf / Leprous skin eruption]
Morphea is an inequality of colour
of the skin without inequality of the flesh.
Let the matter be digested with Oxymel
of Squills; or with Syrup of
Fumitory; and afterwards let it be purged
with Electuary of the Juice of Roses,
and afterwards anoint with this ointment:
Take a serpent and burn it
in a new earthen pot well covered.
Take of the ashes of the aforesaid cocks [?],
old shoe-soles burnt, black feathers
of hens burnt, of each 2 oz; quicklime,
quicksilver, arsenic, of each 2 drachms;
fern root burnt and ground 2 drachms.
Powder all and temper with strong
vinegar in the manner of an ointment:
anoint twice or thrice or more as it
shall seem [good] to you with this ointment.
Lastly put him in a bath, and anoint
him with a depilatory ointment, and
let him sweat in the bath and be washed with water,
and he shall be healed.
If anything remains, take powder
of serpent with cumin, pepper, and
salt ground, and give a little on an empty stomach,
and this twice or thrice as you shall see
expedient: and if it is necessary, again to
the bath as before.
A depilatory ointment is thus made:
Take arsenic 1 oz, quicklime 3 oz by weight
in a little pan and mix well, and let them boil
in good vinegar and dissolve a little, and
draw a hen's feather through the middle, and if
the feather is stripped [of plumes] it is boiled enough;
if not, [it is] not.
Note: the aforesaid powder with this
ointment avails much in the curing of
leprosy.

and it excoriates [peels] and anoints [?].

Scirrhus
Scirrhus is a hard tumour like a stone,
and a certain glutinous, thick, and cold
humour: and the harder it is, so much
the worse to heal: and in pure scirrhus
there is neither sensation nor pain.
Let black choler be purged, and let him abstain
from foods generating black choler.
Let ammoniacum be dissolved in
oil of bricks with sagapenum and laid
upon, it destroys scirrhus and all hard
apostemes and all hardnesses in
a short space of time: a plaster made thereof
strengthens, and laid upon, it is wonderful.
Corns in the toes
Take a piece of parchment that is thin and
cut a little hole therein as big as the
corn; lay thereupon a plaster [plate] of the
gum galbanum spread upon leather,
and that will ripen it that you will
turn [it] out, then heal it with salve.
But sublimate will eat
out by the root and heal it as the
title Fistula you may see.
Or
Make strong mercury [?] water, and
cut the corn to the quick and pick
out the core, fill the hole with this
water 3 or 4 mornings together,
and this will kill it.
Or
Spread a plaster of salve,
cut a hole in the plaster as big
as the corn (almost), lay on lapis
infernalis [silver nitrate], and thereon put another
plaster, and so kill it and heal it.
Or pare it to the quick
and lay thereon the leaf of wall-[rue / houseleek?]
and that will soak it, pick it
out, and heal it as the black plaster
written page 62.
Some warts are hard, others
soft: those which are hard are from black
choler; soft ones truly from phlegm.
In the beginning let the offending humour
be purged; then:
Take powder of euphorbium: temper with oil of myrtle
and therewith touch the warts;
or wash with caustic water, or bind
with a silk thread until it fall off.
I had many in my hands, and
I healed them ... for ...
and they were rid of them ...
in short time.
