[Right Column (Napthe)]
Naphtha | 259
Naphtha is a great fleshy aposteme,
and very soft like a fungus
and in it there is neither heat nor
pain, nor pulsation: and sometimes
they are of a dark colour, and of little sensation,
and then it is a cancerous aposteme: and
then it is in no wise to be cut off.
When its root is slender and very
pendulous like a testicle, then it is not
necessary to extirpate it, but tie it with
a silk thread like wool, tightening it so
long until it be wholly cut off.
The counsel of surgeons is that with
an iron instrument it should be cut off;
nevertheless in incisions I never
meddle with any pustule
of that kind [if] it can [be avoided]; yet to many it well
happens, but this is rarely, as
physicians say.

[Left Column (Formica / Noli me tangere)]
Formica, or
It is called 'noli me tangere' [touch me not] because
if it is touched, the more humours flow
to the place and the disease is augmented.
Cure
First let it be digested with oxysaccharum
and let the patient be purged and cleansed,
because the humours are prepared from blood
and choler.
On the third day let stupes be made of cold herbs,
cold [?] and equalled [?] and flux.
Give tincture with apple and water of cherries
limacio [?].
On the following day make phlebotomy of the saphena [vein],
because the hot humours are from the liver.
However, better of the cephalic [vein].
Then let the crust be removed with a razor
or other instrument, and let powder
made of oak galls, the smaller ones,
vinegar of old ..., quicklime,
atramentum [vitriol], and tartar, of each, be tempered
with lye of [?] ashes
of lead, moderately thick: and let it be
laid upon all night: and let an anointing be made
with unguentum populeon round about.
On the morrow however let it be removed, and if
they be foul, with some instrument
let it be scraped. Then:
Take powder of oak galls with juice
of plantain be tempered, and made
moderately thick, apply.
And upon it let be laid leaves of plantain
bruised, softly with the juice pressed out.
And lastly let the place be washed
with the aforesaid lye, and let it be dried
with a cloth ... and upon
put leaves of plantain and ...
thus do for nine days: If
however the aposteme be mortified, flesh
red will appear, and now apply
snails beaten with all the juice, because
it makes preservation and curation.
On the following day let it be washed with the aforesaid
lye and apply powder of red roses,
frankincense, and mastic.
At the end of 10 days they will be dried from
the mortified skin; being done, apply a plaster
of oak galls and temper with juice
of plantain tempered until it be healed,
which is done in the space of 6 weeks.
Let the patient beware of ... and
of all melancholic meats, which
are sharp and salt, inflaming
the blood.

To kill a ringworm [CC]
Take a piece of fine gold and cross

Say this 3 times; then say 'In the name
of the Father, etc.', still crossing it, and
lastly say Pater noster, etc.
Cure: another
Hold a penny between the finger
and the thumb of the right hand

say Pater noster, etc.
Rubbing the ringworm with gold with-

For the cough

Ringworm: a secret

White juice of liquorice
Take green liquorice, scrape and cleanse from the external
rind, and slice it longways very small and dry it in
an oven; when it is well dried, beat it in a mortar
very fine, but not searce [sieve] it; put to it hyssop water
as much as suffices to make it the consistence of a poultice; let it
stand in infusion in a gallipot three days, stirring it
twice every day; then press it through a linen cloth
with the hands very well; to the remainder that will
not pass through, put hyssop water as before, and strain
it, and do this so long till the residue will not pass
through the strainer; to this expression put white
sugar candy 8 or 12 oz in fine powder; mix them in a
pewter dish; set it on a chafing dish of coals, with
a gentle fire and boil it so long till in stirring it
you find it part and clean from the dish; then take
it from the fire, and suddenly work it in what
form you please; you put the rest on the fire
again and when it is hot work it again; do
so till you have put it into what form
you please. Before when it is done you be quiet [?]
enough, otherwise it will grow [to] lose the colour.
This white juice of liquorice is rarer than any
other in staying running rheums, coughs, and
is very rare. Dr. Nants [?].

Take three or four new-laid eggs; put a

274 | Sleep
For to make sleep
Take opium 1 dram, place in a fine linen cloth
and put in the nostrils; 1 grain of opium suffices.
Take diascordium 1 dram; taken, sleep is
caused.
For thickening catarrhs and
inducing sleep
Take liquid storax, white [olibanum], olibanum, myrrh,
juice of liquorice, opium, of each 2 drams; let them be tempered
½ oz, 6 grains, let a mass be made. Dose from 4 grains to 6 grains
at the hour of sleep.
Sleep-inducing ointment
Take juice of henbane, mandrake, hemlock,
lettuce, white and black poppy, and seeds
of all the aforesaid herbs if they can be had,
of each 1 dram, Theban opium and our opium of each ½ dram, hog's lard
fresh, as much as suffices; pound all these together strongly
and afterwards make it boil well; and if it is not
thick enough add a little white wax and let it be made
an ointment. And when you wish, anoint the fore-
head, pulses, armpits, and palms of the hands and
feet. And immediately he will sleep so that he does not feel
an incision. And if anyone for another
cause cannot sleep, whence that
ointment helps or lingers a little.
And when you wish to revive [him]
apply to the nose behind a thick cloth
well toasted and moistened in strong vinegar
or other strong-smelling dungs, and immediately he will
wake up.
For the same
Take juice of greater nightshade, henbane,
lettuce, and poppy; take a sponge
and put it in that juice and dry [it]
in the sun; and when you have need,
warm the sponge in hot water
and hold it long to the nostrils.
Plaster which makes one sleep well
Take populeon, juice of white poppy,
henbane, of each ½ oz; let it be tempered with
juice of houseleek, purslane, milk
of a woman, oil of violets, white of an egg, and a little
opium; mix, let a plaster be made, and put [on] the temples and
forehead, and he will sleep willy-nilly.
For provoking sleep
Chamomile made with oil of violets,
saffron, and a little wax.
For the same
Take seed of white poppy, melon,
gourd, of each ½ dram, seed of lettuce
1 dram; pound all with endive water and
let a drink be made with sugar added, and drink
in the evening.
Powder of nutmeg taken internally avails;
and 2 grains of opium put in a cloth and put in
the nostrils.

Ears
Some say that strong vinegar lukewarm
instilled drop by drop into the orifice of the ear more
than other medicines strengthens the hearing,
because it strengthens the instruments of hearing and
prevents rheum from descending to it from
the brain.
If however in those narrow
passages there be, and the house of the ear gross
stopping them up, whereby hearing is impaired,
it burdens and in the ears diverse ailments
generates.
Item, oil of bitter almonds
and of peach kernels, lukewarm in the ears
instilled, opens and strengthens the passages.
And physicians say that he
who preserves hearing [?]
should observe to fumigate the ear
over the steam of hot water: and if in
that water wormwood or penny-
royal be boiled, it will be better.
One must beware with the utmost care
of all tumult, and of all noise
of a mill or water falling from on high,
and not to bathe in muddy and

Ears
Impostume [abscess] in the Ear
Boil the roots of elecampane in
fair water until it be very
tender; then spread it upon a
linen cloth; make a tent [pledget] of it
and roll the salve inwards,
and put in new, and then oil of
sweet almonds: this is excellent
for swelling and running ears.
And roast an onion tender,
take out the core, fill the place with
oil of bitter almonds, and let it
settle a while; then press the
onion and drop thereof into the
ear, and stop the ear with black
wool, wet all with a moist rag
and sleep [?] upon it: this helped Mr.
N. when he despaired of help.
A certain ear medicine
Take young mallows, two handfuls;
put them into a new earthen pot that
was never used; put into them
half a new brick, hot. Cover the
pot mouth with a linen cloth and
tie it fast with a string so that the
fume goes not out; have a little
pipe like a clyster-pipe thrust
through the cloth before it be
tied upon the pot, and take the fume
into your ear through the pipe;
or make a little hole with
a bodkin and let the fume go into
the ear, put on a moist rag and
wrap your head warm and sleep
upon it. The pipe may be fitted like
a clyster-pipe: look in the same words [?].
for a pipe, p. 71, made of box[wood] not
much bigger than this picture, and
1 inch long,
or 2 or 3 inches; or a quill with a little
hole cut in the top.

Eyes
Into the eyes fall many diseases;
if the disease come of phlegm, purge the
head with pilulae cocciae, aureae, of each 1/2 dram, and
diagrydium [scammony] 3 or 4 grains; mix and into five
pills divide. Take them late in the night
and drink after them, then sleep upon
them.
To purge the head's humours
Take iris root, long pepper, mustard,
cress, nigella, stavesacre, leaves
of hellebore, pellitory, ginger, cinna-
mon, of each 1 dram; let it be a coarse powder: tie
of this powder in a linen cloth and chew
or a berry [?]; hold it in the mouth
and spit out the gross phlegm, and
wash the mouth before and after eating.
Such another
Take mastic, pellitory, mustard, nigella,
cress, stavesacre, hellebore [...],
ginger, cinnamon, of each 1 dram; make a coarse powder;
wash the mouth well before and after,
and swallow not the phlegm lest [harm] do
draw out; if you often use [it, it will] all help.
For pearl [cataract/film] in the eye
Take the tops of hemlocks 3, pound
them with bay salt and bind them unto
the wrist of the contrary arm, as
if the pearl be in the right eye, then
bind the medicine to the left [arm].
This must be when the eye begins
first to be sore. See p. 293.
For the pearl
Take herb Christopher in May, pound it
small like green sauce, 1 handful; then pound

and green; then put it into a glass; set it

Concerning tacamahaca
It is proved by experiment [that] what-
ever defluxions it represses;
taken up on linen, and applied to the ear
or tooth to which the defluxion happens,
applied to the temples
in the manner of a cerate, [checks] defluxion into the eyes,
and other parts of the face. The pain
of teeth it allays, [applied to] teeth, even eroded
ones; and if a corrupted tooth
be cauterised, it prevents the corruption
from creeping further. To the breast and shoulders
applied as a plaster, their pains
it ends: Carolus Clusius, Monardes.
Concerning caranna: ibid., p. 9.
Defluxions into the eyes and other
parts it represses, to the ears and
temples applied.

Spots of the eyes and redness of the eyes
Take quicklime 3 drams, rainwater ½ lb; let them be mixed
and stand three days in a stoppered vessel; afterwards shake,
having been shaken let it rest for 24 hours in a stoppered vessel;
then let the matter be strained through linen and add of sal
ammoniac whitest 10 drams powdered, mix very well, afterwards
let the water be distilled through a filter. Instil into the eyes
daily 3 drops. Some leave the water in a vessel
of brass [so] that it may acquire a sky-blue colour
which is called sapphire water; [good] for
fluxes and defects of the eyes. It avails also for fistulas, cancers,
etc. A. Bolg: Ch. Lime and Sapphire as below.
To prepare the calamine stone
Take calamine stone as much as you will, make it in powder,
then burn it and cast it into a pot of strong
vinegar and suddenly cover the pot; let
it stand a while, then drain out the vinegar;
then burn the powder again and quench it in
the same vinegar as before: then drain out
the vinegar and burn the powder again
and let it cool: and tutty may be burnt
in the same manner, but it must be quenched
in fennel or celandine water.
Concerning the gallstone of oxen
The stone in the gall-bladder of oxen, bruised, and
put into the nostrils sharpens the sight, and fluxes
lest they flow into the eyes prevents: and avails
for ... and is called Alcheron.

Antonius Betus on the qualities of Sapphire [water]
Take quicklime, quench in common water, which
when the lime has settled, decanting they collect pure
and in it a little sal ammoniac they dissolve. That when it
has been completely dissolved, in the aforesaid lime water,
they cast it into a brass basin, where when through the night
it has stood in the basin it acquires the colour of sapphire, and
placed in glass, is transparent; and for almost all
defects of the eyes, nay for any ulcers to be cleansed
most useful, cancer, burns,
and many other defects also this water
is reported to heal; to the eyes only a few drops
are applied, as if much salt
it has or much from the brass it has drawn. 52.

Diet of lepers
Let him avoid coitus altogether, and all hot
things: such as onions, leeks, pepper, and
strong wine, legumes, and melancholic
things, and all hardened salted foods, milk, fish,
pork; let him avoid anger,
solitude, labour, cold, and excessive
heat; let him flee filthy places and
all fruits, fried things, [and] things roasted in
baked pastry.

Of Polypus [Nasal Polyp]

[Left Column]
A superfluity of flesh rising up in the nose is
sometimes a polypus, and sometimes is not
a polypus, though it seems to be; for in the wider
part of the nose it grows, and sometimes exits the nose, and
rests upon our lip; the cure of which is
such: with a spatula through a certain depth
let it be raised, and with a lancet
let it be cut, and it ought to be done between the membranes [?]. And if
anything remain within the nostrils, a tent of
Unguentum Ruptorium, which is made of
quicklime and [Sarracenic/spatarontic] soap and
soot, should be introduced. Then with egg yolk
mixed with common oil let the tent be dipped,
and inserted. Afterward, when the heat has
ceased, let it be cured as ulcers [with] powder and
green ointment, etc.
But if the whole flesh be between the nostrils, and
causes great obstruction: according to the size
of the opening, first let a tent be introduced
with juice of malum terrae, once, twice, or thrice if
necessary; afterward let it be cured with a hot iron
or Unguentum Ruptorium as aforesaid.
Polypus is a certain evil flesh
growing within the nostrils, of which there are several
species. There is a certain polypus as if [reddish]
in body, and so called from distension
[?]: which is very tenacious although it is
of soft substance; such mucus moves in the
cavity of the nostril, gradually separates
everywhere from the nostrils, does not adhere, yet since
by its small quantity it cannot come out,
remaining there it blocks the nostrils and passage,
advancing little by little; and thus it is incurable.
There is another species of polypus altogether
adhering to heat, and it is soft; and that
sits in the cavity of the nostril, which by inserted
forceps [?] can be seized.
Incurable polypus: these are the
signs: the place black, the whole nose hard,
large, and livid; and the superfluity of flesh
does not descend into the opening nor is moved,
but grows much there upwards.
Polypus which is not likened to moss/mucus:
Thus it is cured
Let the nose be compressed upwards toward the forehead,
and let the patient sit in some higher place,
and let the physician subtly and skilfully
grasp [it], and thus cautiously with diligence draw [it]
whereby it happens that the polypus [leaves] the palate opening
by expulsive force; if this happens,
the cure is that it be cut; afterward let there be put in
the nose a tent of wax, and good skin growing
grows and amends the polypus.
Powder of polypody put often into the nose does
cure polypus.
Powder of hermodactyls with some cephalic
comforting medicine, corrodes the polypus.
Take powder of antimony; make a tent and with lard
anoint it well; afterward dip the tent in powder
of antimony [and] place upon the polypus, etc.
Take the juice of roasted leeks, a little green
wax, a little powder of tartar, and put it
into the nose well mixed upon the polypus.

Fractures
Broken Bones
297 [Original Page Number]

[Left Column]
In p. 337 I wrote of fractures, but
since I see other practices, and because
I have written them out of order, I
thought fit to write them together.
First, take measure of the bigness of the
leg; then provide splints, cut them
and of convenient length to the place;
then arm the splints with flax without
shells/shives [lest they] prick the flesh; and
make things to compass the leg
round about; but one splint must
not touch another, but there must
be a little space between.
Then you must have some
bolsters as in p. 337.
You must also have a strong lye made
ready of fair water, which water you
must make boiling hot before you put
in your ashes, with some of these herbs
following, namely: fennel root, juniper [?],
wormwood, rosemary, sage, chamomile
flowers, or melilot flowers, or some
of these; then put in your ashes and so
make the lye slippery; then drain the
herbs and ashes from the lye, and put
in good store of salt when the lye
is clean, and not before.
Then take a good cloth, 3 or
4 folds, and wet [it] in the hot lye, and
wring the cloth hard; then let
the cloth be smooth, wrapped about
the broken leg very smooth without
seam or wrinkles, and hot.
Before the cloth be put on, make
sure the bone be placed right
where it should be, and that your
bolsters fit it well [?].
This four-folded cloth must
be so long that the ends of the
splint must lie upon it and
not upon the bare flesh.
The edges of the cloth must
meet together and wrap over
upon the top of the shin-bone with-
out seams, knots, or bunches.
Then take another double cloth
wet in water and vinegar (if there
be cause); wring it hard and lay
it smooth upon the other, and let it be as
long as the first or rather longer.
Now all these things being made
ready, put a good strong splint
under the leg, and bind it at the
upper end slack; then lay down the
side strings and the rest of the splints.
First put the end of one splint
under the band already slackly
tied, and so proceed until all the
splints be on; then tie the linen tape fast
at either end 2, and 2 in the middle.
Remember they touch not one the
other; if there be a wound, then
follow the order in p. 337, etc.

[Right Column]
And some of the waxen ointment of
the cerecloth following:
Take wax 3 drams, resin and sheep's suet of each 1 dram;
dip therein coarse cambric, make there-
of a cerecloth and apply it close up-
on the fracture very warm; and bind
it on fast as aforesaid, and let the cere-
cloth be longer than [the] splints as aforesaid.
For opening the fracture and bind-

And when you open the leg, see it
be straight, and bind it up as it

make a pair of junks of 2 handsome straight
sticks rolled in a towel or such like, and

and under the foot, and bind them above

If the patient be very costive, you

If we lack one thing or another in fol. 337,
then follow this course, etc.

Weak Limbs

For a feeble and weak limb
Take so many yolks of egg as shall suffice
to half sheer [measure] if it be in winter
that the member be cold; if it be hot
then put all the whites with the yolks,
or more whites than yolks; and if it be
very hot then use whites only without
any yolk at all; and put to those yolks
or whites [that] you take as much oil of olive
as the egg: beat them in a platter
with a knife until they be all as one
matter: then take flax and make there-
of pledget and plaster as broad as you
will, and make [it] now and encompass the limb;
apply those plasters warm as fast
as the weakness goes. Then take of
rose water and vinegar mingled together,
but mostly vinegar, warm them together
well: wet a linen cloth therein and
wring it well and wrap this cloth
about the plasters and limb; and
wet the roller [bandage] in the same and wring
it and roll it up. If there be seared [flesh]
put some of the medicine to the limb
or place in the sore for to dry and
This plaster does marvellously resolve
venomous matter and refortifies the
member and causes quick blood to
run and refresh the member, disposing
it to health. But if there be dead
flesh in the sores, let it away and
take it out. This is good against the
ache of the limb, decrepit, toward
blackness, or swelled, or weakness and rotting
or corrupt and scald; then lay on this
plaster first or the oil, and dress it
as aforesaid once in a day. Master Browne.
Oil of Mastic for the same
Take mastic, olibanum, of each 3 ounces in fine
powder, olive oil 2 pounds; boil them until
a third part be wasted: this is good for
weakness in limbs of cold cause, to wrap
and comforts the limbs of old men; and
is good for the hectic [fever].
Oil of Castoreum
Take castoreum 2 ounces, oil 2 pounds; boil them as the last
oil: it is good in all cold causes for the
iliac and colic passions, the falling
evil [epilepsy], etc.

[Right Column]
For a dried, withered,
and decayed limb
Take galls that men put into ink and
steep them in good wine and vinegar,
and let them soak well; then beat

gathered with the heat, rub the limb
well therewith a good while, then
wrap it up warm within the same
limb, and doing this many have been
recovered. Jarott.
For the uvula

as much frankincense as of the

For the same
Take album graecum that is ready wrought,
make it in powder and mix therewith a
little cinnamon in powder and blow it
up to the uvula.
For the uvula
Take daisies' leaves and root, wash them

For the same
Take feverfew, chop it very small, add to it

[Left Column]
Gangrene is said to be not simply
dead flesh, but still dying
retaining a little sensation with black
colour: the part indeed which still retains
sensation scarify frequently, and
let it be purged gently, now with many
and deep wounds, now with few and
light ones as the place requires; and when
the dead blood is extracted it is
cured.
Take meal of bitter vetch and with vinegar and honey
cook and let a cataplasm be made, and you may
add a little salt.
When the dead part has been removed, which is
while...
a cautery, and on the third day apply powder
of hermodactyls with honey and quickly
let the eschar fall.
A defensive in gangrene
Take oil of roses, oil of myrtle, of each 3 ounces,
juice of plantain, houseleek
2 ounces, whites of eggs 5 in number, bole, terra
sigillata finely powdered, of each 1 ounce,

Otherwise

Gangrene

[Left Column]
A defensive
Take Armenian bole, terra sigillata, of each 1 ounce, vinegar
a sufficient quantity; let them be mixed.
The rotten flesh must be cut
away at one dressing with some
sharp instrument or knife.
If these serve not, then use
caustic medicines, above set,
to cause an eschar.
If that will not serve, it must be cut
off, which is the last remedy, and in some
cases must not be deferred too long.
For the gangrene
Take salad oil 1 pound, clean wax, litharge
of gold, litharge of silver, ceruse
all in fine powder and sifted: of each 2 ounces,
turpentine of Venice 2 ounces: melt your
oil and wax and then stir in the
litharges, one after the other by little
and little, and boil and stir them till
they be black, then stir in the ceruse
by little and little and boil them until
it be very black: lastly put in the
turpentine, stir it and let it boil a little;
drop [it on] the platter in clean water before
the turpentine be in; if it be too hard
put in more oil, if too soft boil it
better, and being cooled, spread a skin
to a pail of clean water and stir it
well; then on a wet table make it in
rolls. This heals the gangrene
if it be not too far spent. See page 62.
For Persian fire and erysipelas
Take alum half a drachm, white of egg beaten, add
rose water and nightshade water of each 1 ounce, juice
of... 2 ounces, mix and apply; it does not
fail except in a desperate case.
For the cold fire, i.e., gangrene
Take fern root, scrape them small: boil
it in half hot milk and half hot water
[till] it be a little poultice: spread it and apply
it warm, a good breadth, and then keep
and when it is dry lay on new: and
in 3 or 4 plasters, etc., it does it.
For the cold fire
Take the brine of a man that...
moisten a cloth therein and apply thereto.
When a wound runs to gangrene
Apply the new made dung of a bull on
the place as hot as may be.
For the cold fire
Take new unsalted cheese made of goat's milk,
cut it in slices and apply: then boil red
cresses in water: wet cloths in the water
and lay on the cheese, and when the cheese is dry
lay on fresh, and new wet cloth.

Scald Head
For the white scald
First shave the head and wash it
with vinegar; then wash it with warm urine
every day to kill it. Then take fresh
swine's lard feet, and shave therein of
new wax out of the hive that did
never swarm; melt them together
and anoint the head therewith: this will
heal it very soon; but it will break
out again half a year after; and if
it do, wash it with new urine as you did,
and [so it shall] be perfectly killed.
To heal a scald head
Take the liver of a thornback [ray] and
boil it by itself; and seethe the root
of elecampane and then blend in
clean water with three handfuls of
smyrton [?] until the root be soft; then
stamp the liver and all together and
strain it hard, and therewith anoint
the head. If he have tow of burned
wool, and with that make one plaster and rub
the bald place, and hair will follow.
For the same
Take the green tops of broom, and
red dock root scraped clean, of each 2 handfuls;
stamp them small; then take fresh butter
and bear's suet or sheep's suet, of each 2 lb., and
boil them or skim them well; then let
them cool, and put into them of the fine
powder of brimstone 3 oz.; stir all together
until it be cold, and therewith anoint
the sores.
Unguentum Catesden for the same
Take gall of soot, oil, liquid pitch, of each
2 oz.: let all be ground and an ointment made, and the shaven
head anointed: which wonderfully avails in healing
and restoring baldness and hair,
but it smells very foully.
Unguentum Aristotile for the same
Take soot, bay salt, oil, and tar, of each 2 oz.;
stamp the salt and soot together; then
melt your oil, tar, and 1 oz. wax together,
then put to the salt and soot, and stir all
well; and being well boiled, strain it
and put it in a gallipot. Clip the hair
close, and anoint therewith, and upon the
ointment cast the powder of burnt lead.
And when you wash it, make
the grease/lye of hay that was made before
Midsummer Day; and to that lye add yolk
of egg and honey, and wash it twice a
day.
For the same
Take lamp oil 1 lb., fair water 1/2 lb.; set on fire and
boil them together; let them cool, add quick-
silver mortified; stir them and anoint
therewith the head.

In the year of the Lord 1625 in December
One K. in Wrexton being sick of the pleu-
risy, bled at the nose and spat blood,
his throat clammy and almost choked.
The physician appointed him to be phlebotomized
and to be let blood, which I did; but
before the physic was made or any
came to let him blood, I gave him
the first medicine made of the roast
apple; and after I gave him the distilled
water of his own [corn-rose] to drink,
and he amended. The water was made thus:
I put the leaves into the still,
distilled them dry; then I put in new
leaves into the still, and poured in the same
distilled water, and in the remainder I
also put of the leaves, and did distill it three
times until the water was red, as red
wine. And so it will be if it be but once
stilled so the [flowers] be tender, or leaves
put in the water and set in the sun, and
take out the leaves and put in new
three or four times: you need not cast
away the water; it is worth £20.
I made the medicine thus:
Cut out the core of the apple and put in
2 grains of olibanum, and roast it, and
make all kneaded, and put to a leaf, and
gave him the water one draught, and
he mended, thanks be to God.

Childbirth [Partus]
Juice of dittany or powder of its root

Speedy deliverance
Set strong ale upon the fire on the

warm, let a woman milk her
milk into the ale and so make a posset,
and let the woman drink the drink.

Aqua Vitae
Aqua composita, excellent
Take for every gallon of ale or liquor

Aqua Mirabilis [Wonderful Water]
Take turpentine 1 lb., honey 1/2 lb., aqua ardens

1st water is called Mother of Balsam;

1st: drink with wine;
2nd & 3rd: for anointing.
1st water is clear like water;

Anthony's Quintessence
Take claret wine, as much as suffices; put therein grains [of paradise],
cinnamon, mace, of each as much as suffices, in coarse powder;

then put in sugar to make it sweet, and

and drink thereof at all times as much as suffices.
Spirit & Water of Wormwood
Take of the leaves of dried wormwood 1 lb.,

Metheglin
Take mustard, mugwort, origany, pile-
root, pellitory of Spain, liverwort,
saxifrage, sage, zedoary, vervain,
woodbine flowers, chamomile, hart's-tongue,
marjoram, marigolds, endive, rose-
mary, wild sage, avens leaf and all,
borage, betony, bedwind mint, honey-
suckle [called] cocks' heads, eglantine, the
root of elecampane, fumitory, galingale
root, fennel root, hyssop, langue de
boeuf [bugloss], agrimony, scabious, thyme, tur-
mentil, wall cresses, of each 1 handful; mugwort,
bay leaves, of each 4 handfuls. Gather these about
Bartholomew-tide [24 Aug], wash them then clean
and pick the roots clean, and slice the
fennel root, and take out the pith.
Put to these 200 gallons of water if
your furnace be big enough, or
more; let them boil four hours
at the least; then cleanse your water
from the herbs through a sieve in-
to a vat. Then make clean the furnace,
and put in your liquor again; and for
every three gallons of water put in
one gallon of honey. Then let all
boil gently, and still skim off that which
arises, and especially a blackish scum
as long as any scum is to be seen on it
[little]. Then abate the fire and put your
liquor in coolers to cool, and let it stand
two days at the least.
Then put it into your yele-vat [fermenting vat] and put
to it of good barm a gallon at least
and stir all together, and so let them
stand a day or 2, then fleet [skim] off the
barm, and let it stand and stir it and
so let it stand another day.
Then put it into your casks, and dress
them with clay like cider vessels and
fill them to the board [brim], and then let

Bind
315

[Right Column (Metheglin Brewing & Fermentation Instructions)]
315
Metheglin
Bind your herbs in bundles, bruise the roots and
boil all in the water while they be very soft
and tender. Then let the liquor run through
a hair sieve into [a] vessel to cool until it is
blood-warm. In the mean time temper
the honey in some part of your warm liquor.
Then put all into the vat and so
work them together with a bowl a good
space. Then assay if a new-laid egg will
swim therein; if it will, it is then strong; if
not, put in more honey and labour it
together until it will bear an egg.
Then boil it again and skim it
as long as any froth will arise, then
let it cool and
Have ready a hogshead wherein a
little has been wine or beer, and one of
the heads must be out, which vessel must
be first seasoned with some of the first
liquor. Set this vessel upon its ends,
fill it with the liquor, and let it cool,
and then when it is cold cover it with
a clean cloth and on that boards. And there
let it work sixteen or twenty days
or until you see all the froth cast to the side
of the vessel; then take away that froth.
And put in of good barm a
pottle at least, and work them together
with a dish a good while.
Then cover it again and let it
work 4 or five days, until you may
smell it clear and see [if] the barm
looks black.
Then take that black barm away and
put in more and stir it as you did
before; and then let it stand again
until you may smell it clear and the
barm [looks black] as before.
Then taste it; if it be too sweet
of the honey, put in more barm and work
it in all things as before.
In this doing you may have the taste without
cloyingness, and when it pleases your palate,
the hogshead being [a] hand-breadth above the
bottom, draw forth your liquor and
put it where you will keep it.
It must have vent for a time after it is put
in the vessel and then stop it fast.
This may be kept five or six years.
By dividing this preparation you
may make a little at once.
The best time is between Bartholomew-
tide and Michaelmas.
This was my Aunt Windsor of
Addington her practice.

To Make Good Braggot
Take mace, cloves, spikenard, and zedoary,
of each 3 drams; pure galingale, long pepper, of each
3 drams; ginger, bay berries, nutmeg, and
grains [of paradise], of each 3 drams; cumin seeds, anise-

coarsely, and put half in a little linen
bag; hang the bag in 2 or 3 gallons
of ale [so] that it do not touch the bottom; first
put in the ale of pure clarified honey
1 lb., stir it well, let it stand a week or 10
days; drink it fasting, and before
supper. It comforts the stomach, breaks
wind, etc. If you will have it purging,
put in of turbith electuary ½ oz. or more in
coarse powder.

Powder Without Equal
Take of orpiment, verdigris [aes viride],
of each 1 oz, burnt vitriol 2 oz, alum
guttatin [rock alum] burnt 3 oz; let each by
itself be most finely ground upon a
grinding-stone: the parts being well ground upon
the grinding-stone, let them be rubbed together,
until they are well mixed, and in a
little leather bag let them be kept: and for use
reserved. For 7 and 2 [years]
it can be kept in great efficacy;
dead or superfluous flesh,
or putrid [flesh], it mortifies and burns away.
If the surgeon in a wound or
ulcer places it, having no dead
flesh, it does no harm;
but the wound without any other help
it will most excellently conglutinate, dry,
and heal: not however without biting/
smarting: because for certain, if this powder
were not biting, it would surpass all
other cures:
The use is such:
When this powder is put into an ulcer
or wound, immediately upon it let there be put
scraped lint, i.e. lint, or tow of flax with
scissors finely cut: and upon [it]
let a plaster be put: and let it be well bound;
and so leave it for 48 hours or more
without removing [it].
When however the plaster
you remove, and the lint or tow
on which the powder was put, if the powder
with the mortified flesh draws
out, the business is well dispatched.
Then you ought to put on equal [parts]
of swine's blood, or lint,
or tow of flax, until the hollow of the wound
shall again be filled with flesh.
But if at the first removal
the powder, the applied powder, with the
mortified flesh does not come out freely;
then apply equal [parts] of swine's
blood as aforesaid: and put upon [it]
a plaster, and so let it remain 24 hours
hours.
And note well that it is necessary
[that] in the powder, or wound,
or ulcer placed, it be not removed
until it comes out of its own accord: i.e.

There is also another rule in which almost all
modern practitioners: I do not say pru=

foully in error in too frequent
of wound and ulcer ... and such opera=

because the natural heat in the body, which
is the principal author of the cure, by

extinguished: and so the digestion of humours
coming to wounds or an ulcer is hindered,

wherefore the generation of pus [sanies] cannot take place, and by
which not the purging of wounds but superfluous humours
running to the wounds are retained and aggravated
more: hence the more swelling in the wound

is the occasion of the other, wherefore the wound or ulcer

pus which in the bottom nature ought to pour out,
it emits as it were a watery and virulent humour.
And so many times from a slight hurt,
incurable evils are perpetrated.
Hence Galen [says]: a wound does not recover that is often
moved/dressed. And Hippocrates says: rarely are
to be removed and more rarely washed [wounds] in which medicines
are frequently removed.
The common sort however allege a cause for this:
they think such busybodies to be diligent and careful
when rather they are more pernicious, as in a little
time those who labour would know.

or thrice in a day; because such an opinion [keeps] the generated pus
hinders, shuts in, wherefore pus or sanies
not only is rendered fetid or makes a stench,

increased humours purge, for accidental heat
[tends] to conversion into pus. For pus is
the greatest presumption of health.
For pus with the rest, blood with humours
corrupted, and natural heat is divided, therefore
when fair [and] good;

of a wound or ulcer: because they will not [keep] the air from them
changed especially, and consequently wounds

other things [?], etc.

nature works better about digestion, whatsoever

Take chicken broth 1 lb, yolks of eggs 1 oz, common oil

Of the tertian fever and ... / Second days
First purge choler: then do this 3 or 4 times

The Sweating Sickness
The Sweating is nothing so painful
as the burning fit is with rumour [tumult]
about 2 or 3 hours before the
sweat rises; and take heed to the
patient, for he shall in great
pain for 2 hours or thereabout,
and perhaps be ready to die before the
end of 2 hours: and when you shall see
the pain come towards his heart, then
give him a spoonful of good aqua
vitae mingled with some treacle, and so
give it him 2 or 3 times if need
be to cause him to sweat: if then
he belch upward or down or down=
=wards, it is a good sign of health;
then and always keep head and all the
rest of his body warm, and let none
part be bare but his face: and when
he has sweat well, abate the clothes
by little and little, but not suddenly,
and let him eat very little, or else
nothing at all is best.

of marsh sorrel, boil it and

Drink of that same wine morning and evening for three days.

[Right Column (Tertian, Quotidian & Quartan Fevers)]
Fevers
In a tertian fever
Take roses, boil in rose water, and in that
strained liquor add sugar as much as suffices; let be made
a syrup. Give it: it comforts the stomach,
provokes sleep, mitigates burning heat
and warmth, etc.
Against a tertian
Take knotgrass crushed and place upon
the pulse of the arms before the third fit;
it removes it: centinodium is knotgrass.
For a tertian marvellously departing
Take plantain, sempervive [houseleek], petty morel
rue of each 1 handful; pound them, straining, then
mix the juice with barley meal
and the white of an egg, and apply
it to the stomach.
For a continual quotidian fever
Take parsley seed, mint, let them be infused
in water all night; in the morning let it be strained,
add sugar, and let it be given to drink: it extinguishes
intolerable fever pain and
loosens the belly.
For the quartan ague
Take dragon's blood, Armenian bole
of each a sufficient quantity; boil them in water until
it be thick: put thereto lapis lazuli
1 dram; give every day 1 dram for 3 days together:
1. takes away the heat; 2. the fit; 3. it
heals him.

Take best rhubarb 1 dram powdered and put

For the tertian ague
Mix barley meal with the juice of

For the fits in the ague

[Right Column (Ague & Sweating Sickness)]

Fevers
For the ague
Take the greatest spider you can get, put it
alive in a walnut shell or such like,

with a thread: the next fit is curable and then

For the same
Take aqua fortis 1 lb, honey of roses 1 pound [?], [place] in
a vessel at an anthill up to the top
of the rim; the ants will enter
in great quantity. Then let them be distilled;
give 1 [spoonful] or more according to the strength of the patient;

For the Sweating Sickness
Take a good quantity of bean flour, of the
best treacle, of powder imperial of each the [same]
weight; the [walnut?] in powder the weight of
mace the weight of 1 dram part; seethe ...
10 leaves of sage sifted well and put on the
mace and shell: set in a quart of ale upon
the fire, boil it and clarify it clean;
then put in all the rest and boil them together;
give hereof to the sick when he sweats,
warm: this was Dr. Cardinall's medicine
for the sweating: the weight must be as
1 dram in the pound, and he in the wine does
make ... half pint at 2 grains the
halfpenny.
For the same
The cause of this disease is when a man
does burn and not sweat: or else does
sweat about the stomach only.
To help the fit of the pestilence [sweat]
Take fennel, marigold, sorrel, of each 1 handful;
make posset ale with new ale and a little milk,
and in 2 quarts of that posset ale boil the
herbs until half the ale be wasted; then
strain it and put 10 or 12 good spoonfuls
of this ale warm into the milk, give hereof
to a woman. | For the second:
Take warm ale and put therein a little butter
and cinnamon in powder, and drink it, and
beware of cold drink and taking cold
when he does sweat: drink no wine
nor hot spices, and keep him with reasonable
clothes: this receipt saved lives: this did help
my father Anno 1551 when many died thereof.
The medicine on p. 333 and the red tincture
... is good for the same disease.
For preventing all sweat
Take rosemary, distil it, and that water
makes the heart very light
and cheers in a manner the heart: or boil
rosemary in water, and it is strong and
does make sweat: and part of water,
one pound of rosemary and another of wine,
and distil it in an alembic, and the water
will make the heart glad therewith: keep that
water and keep the grounds and
strain upon the top for other purposes.
The water is also good to keep
the heart from failing. It also did help
my father Anno 1548, and prevented all
evil sweat.

Tyzanna [Ptisan]
The right making of ptisan
Unto every pint of good full hulled barley
or husked barley or French barley put
10 oz of spring water: boil them till
the water looks brown like beer, and
give 4 oz fasting or when the body is not too full;
it is good in hot humours and against
heat in hot agues.
For heat of the liver and heart
Take husked barley 2 spoonfuls, of spring
water a pottle: boil away a fourth
part or less; strain it, put into a clean
earthen pot and put liverwort, lungwort
of each 1 handful, hart's-tongue and [violet?] leaves;
then boil it unto less or less, strain and
drink hereof every morning.
Otherwise
Take the same proportion of water and barley,
and add violet leaves, strawberry leaves,
endive, succory of each 1 handful, parsley roots,
fennel roots of each 2 parts, scraped and
sliced and piths taken out: liquorice,
aniseeds, of each 1 or 2 oz, raisins 1 oz,
... and thin sliced roots; clean it and
boil it to a pint and a half: drink it
fasting: this will not last above 4
days good.
A ptisan of great value
Take best white wine, pure water of each 1 lb and
let them be mixed, and put in violet herbs, origanum,
and pennyroyal of each half a handful, hart's-tongue
leaves ..., elecampane root 1, white
sugar 1 oz: ... let them boil to half, strain, drink ...
cold, or warm in the morning.
To make husked barley
Take good clean barley, put it into a stone
mortar: sprinkle a little water on it
and beat it, and when it grows dry
sprinkle on more water; so do until
it be clean; rub it and wring [with] your
hands, let it dry, winnow away
the hulls: to every 1 oz of barley take 10 or 12 oz
of water and boil it to the half, and
drink it first and last.
A ptisan for the cough
Take spring water 2 gallons, clean husked
barley 3 handfuls, 24 figs, great raisins, currants
of each 3 oz, sugar candy, ginger, liquorice
of each 2 oz, aniseed, fennel seed, coriander seed,
cumin seed of each 1 dram [?]: boil all in a new
earthen pot, [add] the bark of parsley and fennel root and
liquorice of each half a handful: boil all to half, strain it and
drink hereof first and last warm.
For the ague [Bestell?]
Take green fresh [?] and centaury of each 1 dram, ...
half a dram; boil in strong beer q.s.; drink it in the
morning fasting, and one hour after take some
posset drink, and follow it 3 days, and at night
following take diascordium 1 dram, confectio alkermes 1 dram
dissolved in dragon water and borage water of each 2 oz.
Proved.

[Right Column (Sweating Sickness, Enemas, Fractures)]
Sweating [Sickness]
An order for them that have
the Sweating Sickness, out of Dr.
Hooker his Chronicle
If a man be taken in the daytime, let
him not put off his clothes, but lie down
in his clothes: and keep himself warm
moderately 24 hours: and as moderately
as may be.
If in the night when he is in his bed,
he must not arise, but sweat there
as moderately as he can 24 hours.
He must not eat nor drink in his
sweating, but if he thirst let that [drink]
be warmed on the fire and less warm,
no more than may well suffice to
quench/keep his thirst.
And above all things beware that he
thrust not out his hand nor feet forth
of his bed, for if he do it is death
presently.
You may set upon the mouth of [it?]
so heated air come into the chamber and that
no blast of wind come in.
Let as few people be about him;
many bedchambers may be [used].
Let him make his bed and lie down,
and lie in no hot [place?] nor give
hot food.

A note in binding up broken bones
Take splints made to the end and armed with

Fractures
See p. 297.
In the book
written by one

concerning gems and stones,

ostracola [osteocolla]: it is

ostracola, and

In broken bones there
must be one to hold the body, and one
to hold the member and strain [stretch] it
out in length that it may be placed
as it was before the breaking.
Then the setter with both his
thumbs must put down the ends
and place them right, and after
they are placed put this plaster close to
the leg, as smooth as the skin.
Take wax, rosin of each 4 oz; melt
them together, stir them well and
strain them: then make it a roll.
Spread this salve upon
a linen cloth very thin: then
have ready new bole [Armenian bole] in powder 1 oz
and make it in a heap upon the

in the bole, and therein pour
of oil of roses, and white of linseed [oil]
of each a sufficient quantity, to mix the bole
and oil with a knife or spatula
like to a poultice spread: then
cover the plaster all over with the
bole thick: cut the plaster in 2
notched plates upon the top and bottom
to lie smooth upon the limb,
and that it may meet even at
the edges (commonly in my skill
takes the leg straight): then you
must splint it round with
thin splints wrapped in flax, and
then bind it hard with 3 or
4 bands strong and good.
Nine days after, take off
the splints and plaster and see the leg
be straight, and bind it fast as you
did before, and measure the limb
just as long as his fellow limb.

Corns upon the toes
Sew a piece of pigeon [skin] or a piece of leather
about the toe with a hole in it upon the
top of the corn; lay upon that hole a plaster
of galbanum, and that will keep in heat and
the corn will come forth throughly with the
plaster ... 62, or first
cut the corns and pull them out, and
lay on the same plaster or leather.
To destroy all corns
Make strong mercury water, pare the
corn clean, pick out the hard [core], fill the hole
with the water two or three mornings together,
and it will kill it. Proved.
For the corn
Sew on a plaster with a hole as before, and
let not the hole be too wide, and lay on
mercury sublimate tempered with some flax,
and it will bring it out by the roots, and
then heal the hole.
Or lay on the plaster with a
little hole, and upon the corn apply
Lapis Infernalis [silver nitrate]; upon that a plaster of
Flos Unguentorum; this will burn and kill it.
(Bruise houseleek and lay on the corn and it will
kill them in 4 days.)
For broken bones, excellent
First set it right and bind it well that it
stir not, and let the patient keep himself quiet
in his bed; then use this ointment:
Take delicate flowers of Geranium reduced to powder
and scented; then with grease of a suckling pig

cloth imbued with fragrant dew let it be spread and to the broken
place bound.
Internal marrow of the stone Beinbruch [Osteocolla]:
Take half a dram in red bread macerated morning and

For the same
Take ossifrage, i.e., Beinbruch, 1 dram of powder, and in lesser [fractures]

1 dram or half, fasting in the morning for four or
five days. In this way it removes pains,
and severe symptoms, and fractures

With the same stone, skilled [physicians] are wont to prescribe it in the form
of a cataplasm, with Geranium
bruised, and olive oil or rose oil, with such
happy success, that without any pain and
inflammation of the part the bones are joined together.
This stone is called Osteocolla, and Beinbruch.
It grows in sandy places of the Palatinate
not far from Speyer.
Also near Heidelberg and Jena in Saxony,
also in Silesia in a most limpid spring of the village
of Ironwalda, and around Darmstadt, in the
Bergstrasse, as the Germans call that place.

[Left Column (Plague)]
Plague
For the plague
Take malmsey 3 lb., put therein rue, red
sage of each 1 handful, of yarrow [?] 2 drams; let this
boil well, then strain it; and to the
strained liquor over the fire, put
therein long pepper, ginger, nutmeg,
all in fine powder, of each 1/2 dram, good treacle
2 drams; let all boil a little, then take it
from the fire, put therein good aqua
vitae 4 oz., and stir all together.
For a preservative
Take 2 spoonfuls in the morning fasting
with one spoonful of ale warmed.
But if he be infected, give
six spoonfuls of the drink and 3 of the
ale warm (if the infected be able to
take it); if not, then give him less at
a time and give it often; if he be
strong, once in a day will serve; if he
be weak, a little at once and often; and
this is good for the smallpox, measles,
sweating sickness, poison, and surfeits,
and must be used until the patient be well;
one in London did get much [money/repute] with this.
For the plague
Take aloes 2 drams, myrrh 1 dram, saffron 1/2 dram,
castor 1/2 dram, mastic, white ginger [?] ...
sugar 3 drams, all in powder and well mixed.
For a preservative give as
much as a bean with wine, ale, or beer
fasting; if one be infected he will cast it
up, then give it until it tarry ...,
and they that have taken it report
that a seated pustule doth suddenly
vanish when the infection is gone.
Experiment for the same
Every morning eat a branch of herb
perdon and swallow the juice; but [it] is
better to drink the juice in wine, ale, or
broth, and this part shall not hurt it.
An excellent medicine proved
in the disease in harvest 1571
Take malmsey a quart, pomewater apples 3, the ...
bole armeniac in fine powder 1 dram, of
treacle 3 drams, water of mint or ...
mix them all together and let all boil till
it come unto a pint. Take spoonfuls
taken warm in a morning and after every
time for 24 hours; give him that is in
fear 2 spoonfuls warm, and also let
him take every minute of an hour one
spoonful until he have taken a pint.
If [you] cannot have pomewater, make it without.
None that took this did die. Thanks be to God.
Another excellent medicine
Take water of purslane and ...
roses and pennyroyal imperial, of each
1/2 oz. and ... powder ...
mix them well and put in a vessel ...
closed so that it may not breathe: take ... weight
... well mixed,
but if anyone thinks himself infected, [give] in greater
quantity: it is excellent, for it is approved,
it helpeth the headache presently.

[Right Column (Pestilens / Family Receipts)]
Pestilence
339 [Page Number]
For the same
Take of the best treacle, let one good part of
zedoary grated and root of tormentil in
fine powder; temper upon a trencher
with a knife; then put them in glass and
put to dragon water and pimpernel water
a sufficient quantity, and mix them well. Eat every morning
the quantity of a nutmeg upon a knife's
point: this must be prepared [as on] p. 333.
For the same
Take the stinking malson [mayweed?], ...
it with stale ale and seethe it to green, put to
good treacle a sufficient quantity; warm it, drink it fasting,
and sweat sometime after it; and every
other day in [the] morning for a preservative,
but he that is infected must take it often.
This hath been proved by my grandfather and
my father and myself in Tewksbury,
and not one died that did take it. Thanks
be to God.
For the same
Take terra sigillata, dragon's blood,
true bole, of each 1/2 oz., brimstone out of the rock
1 dram, all in as fine powder as may be; put
the powders in a mortar with good treacle,
beat all together one hour, then put it
in a close box or glass; give the quantity
of a nutmeg in the morning fasting and
drink after it ale or beer, and send it
often to him that is infected: this was
given unto the assizes in our year and none of
them died, as is said.
For him that is infected
Take garden tansy, yarrow, feverfew, of each
1 handful; pound them together, strain it [with] some
of the sick man's urine and ... put to
it, drink it warm. Elizabeth Nicolas my
grandmother gave it to marked [plague-spotted] and my own
and they escaped.
A sovereign medicine
Take a new-laid hen's egg, make a hole in the
end, take out the white clean, and
fill the shell with English saffron as full as it
can possibly [hold]; dry the yolk and saffron
together before the fire or in an oven after
the bread is out, that the shell be black and
burnt and the substance dry; then take the full

Bezoar Stone
The Bezoar stone, it is said, if bound to the arm of the left
side so that it touches the bare skin, is held
to resist poison and guard the heart lest by poison,
pestilent air, or contagion it be harmed.
It also opens pestilential carbuncles; if
sprinkled on, it overcomes and draws out all venom.
Taken internally, if the powder from 2 grains to 10 grains
be administered with some convenient liquor, it wonderfully
aids all affections of the heart.
For syncope in the very paroxysm or
a little before, with rose water if fever be present; if
absent, with water of carduus benedictus, balm, bugloss,
or clove gillyflower, 4 grains are given.
For palpitation of the heart, with balm water
daily in the morning on an empty stomach, 2 grains
offered can profit much.
For taming melancholic humours, whether [affecting] the
whole body or only a part of it,
namely occupying the head, it performs wonderful effects.
For leprosy, elephantiasis, evil
scabies, itchings, impetigo, erysipelas,
and other defects of the skin, as an immediate remedy
it heals.
Quartan fever also, even if it does not
cure it, yet it takes away its symptoms: for
sorrows of mind, anxieties, and oppression of the heart
which are common in these fevers, it soothes and removes.
For epilepsy and the sacred disease, whether
it oppresses adults or infants, it helps not a little.
To nursing infants it is given with milk; with wine
and to older ones with water of lily of the valley, linden,
or peony. To children 2 grains, to others triple or
quadruple, or even more according to the constitution of the
disease and the body, is offered.
For poison also and ... fevers,
with success this stone alone is administered with
grass water or carduus benedictus water.
Against poison and the plague
Take the roots of asphodel which men call
daffodil; bray them small, mix it with wine
and drink it; and to eat the root fasting
is a good preservative from poison.
Bray the root and apply it unto an anthrax [carbuncle],
and it will kill it.

out all saving the dregs, and apply it hot.
Draweth out in carbuncles, boils, and swellings.
Note: it is greatly commended to take 3 or 4
grains of the Bezoar stone in scabious

Scorbutum [Scurvy]
The scurvy is a chronic disease, not
simple, but compounded of many other
infirmities; and therefore begin the cure
by opening obstructions: therefore give
him a lenitive clyster [...]
Then let him blood a little; the next day,
if he be strong, give pilulae Rufi, and
feed him good spoon-meat, and in his
drink infuse dried wormwood.
And give him Diatrion Piperon
first and last.
Mithridate, London treacle, and pomis [apples?] are good to
eat fasting. Aqua vitae of rosemary and the
sun, and currants are good, and the won [one?]
ginger and [etc.]
And purge him with pills of
euphorbium 3 scruples or half a dram; these purge cold
watery humours both by stool and urine,
and by heat give warmth to the stom-
ach and entrails: if the stomach only
be oppressed, give him pilulae Rufi 1 dram.
Sweating is good, therefore you
may give him mithridate, or some good
treacle 1 dram, and sweat him not with
too many clothes.
But to keep him soluble:
Take the roots of althea [marshmallow] and linseed bruised,
fenugreek bruised, of each half an ounce; boil [them],
to the decoction 1 pound add species hiera
picra 2 drams, salt a little spoonful: but if
you will not purge much, leave out the
hiera picra.
Another clyster
Of beef broth 2 pounds, linseeds 2 drams, the
root of althea 2 drams, aniseed, fennel seed,
of each 2 drams; boil them well, then add oil and
honey, of each 1 ounce, and give a pint.
New milk, the yolk of
one egg, and coarse sugar is a good
gentle clyster.
Suppositories may be used
Take a long piece of alum and pare it smooth,
or the end of a candle, or a piece of
hard soap, as big and long as a
finger, and thrust it up, anointed
with oil or butter: or honey and salt
sodden until it be hard; put it in skin
and with fresh butter roll it up, etc.
Note: if the patient have the gut
to be clung [costive/constricted] and hard, put a
little piece of an oiled clout [cloth] upon
the nose of the clyster pipe, and thrust it
in home; then draw it a little back,
and deliver the clyster.
If the fundament be excoriated,
use no salt in any wise, nor
no salt broth in the clyster.
If the gums be swollen or stink, then
scarify them: and with water, honey, alum,
and herbs, boiled strong of the alum,
wash and rub the gums.
Lapis medicamentosus dissol-
ved in fair water does make
an excellent lotion for putrefied
gums.

The green salve for all sores

and when the wax and rosin be
melted and boiled well, pour
all in a pot or in a basin being

A green oil
Take olive oil a quart, and
put thereto white wine half a pound, and
take wormwood, southernwood,

tongue, of each 2 handfuls; cut them small

and contusions.

To make oil of herbs
Take the herbs, lay them in the shadow
to wither; put the withered herbs in
a strong glass or a tinned vessel
the same being full; put in oil and
set the glass and oil in a pot of
water, and there let it boil 3
hours; let it cool, take out those
herbs and put in more and boil it
again; and for to cool, linseed oil
is best: and white roses, wild poppy
and violet are good for inflammations
made with linseed oil, or as

Oils
To make oil of wheat
Take pure cleaned wheat: put it into a retort
well luted: and by degrees of fire draw
forth the oil: it will heal well and is good
for many things.
Oil of wheaten bread
Take the crumbs of wheat bread as it does
come hot out of the oven, wrap it in a linen
cloth very close, and upon that cloth put
a coarser cloth and bind it very close: set it
in hot horse-dung 41 days: then press out
the oil.
Oil of violets for the pleurisy
Take good oil 1 pound, of young violets stamped 4 ounces;
put them to the oil and set them in the sun,
and in the end of summer, boil them in a
double vessel 4 hours: strain it, and keep
it close stopped: this oil assuages heat
in hot inflammations, mollifies exulcerations,
hoarseness of the breast or lung, mitigates the
hot impostumes against the pleurisy.

Oil of mace, wheat, and other
Take mace 1 pound made very small, beat it

Lucatellus [balsam] by the Lady B.'s receipt
Take pure salad oil 3 pounds, Venice turpentine
1 pound, red sanders 6 ounces, clean wax cut 1 pound;

upon a very small fire of coals: then

basin: and let it cool and then put it

be put in: it must be put into wounds
very hot, and it cannot be too hot: and
it must be bound or rolled close, and lie 2

bruises anointed hot: and much colder.

[Right Column (Lucatello's Balsam)]
Lucatello's Balsam
Take wax cut small, and put in a pan
over a gentle fire to melt; to that the best
oil 3 lb. being well beaten with one lb.
of sack [and] of Venice turpentine 1 lb.
washed in red rose water 1/2 lb.: let this
boil well together stirring them conti-
nually with a wooden slice, then put
in red sanders [sandalwood] 2 oz. in fine powder: and
let all these boil with continual stir-
ring, till the wine and water be quite
consumed, and when you see no more
fume arise it is enough; take it from
the fire and strain it into gallipots, the
colour [the deeper] it is, the better.
It cures any bruise outward
by anointing the place very warm:
inward by drinking the quantity of
a walnut melted in a draught of sack
warmed, or broth, 3 or 4 mornings fasting.
It cures the biting of [a] mad dog
or any other venomous beast, drunk
in the like quantity and manner, and the
place stung or bitten anointed with it.
It cures the sciatica, stitch, or any
pain coming of cold, by anointing
the place by a fire, and then laying a bag
of warmed ashes on it as hot as you can suffer.
It is good against the plague drunk
in sack and anoint the nostrils with it before
you go abroad: and burn it as a fume:
It will stop blood by dipping
lint in it warmed and binding it reaso-
nably hard to the place.
It helps digestion after surfeits
being drunk in warm sack.
It cures burning and scalding
after the fire is taken out, by anointing
the place, or dip lint therein and lay on
it; it heals without a scar:
It cures any wound or cut
without scar, applied as a plaster and
pouring and anointing the place; if the
wound be deep you may put in a tent
of lint dipped in the balsam, and lay
a cloth dipped therein on it.

Beard to be taken away
Take orpiment in fine powder, unslaked
lime; grind them together, and temper
them with the white of an egg neither
too thick nor too thin: put this upon the
place where you would have the hair
away and there let it dry: then
wet a cloth in hot water and with
your finger take away the hair.
For the same
Take strong lye, of orpiment 1 oz.,
unslaked lime as much, [white?] of a swan's
egg; make them into fine powder,
put them in the lye and let them boil
until it wax clear: then take it off
and let it cool: and therewith anoint
the place where you would have the
hair away: and it will come away.
For removing hair (depilatory)
Psilotrum (depilatory ointment)
Take salt, quicklime, orpiment,
of each [equal parts], let them be powdered: boil diligently
in strong lye, stirring strongly
so that they may be well incorporated, for four
or five boilings: remove from the fire
so that the heat may subside. And meanwhile
the place to be depilated with hot water
fumigate, and foment, so that the pores of the skin
may be opened: afterwards the place to be depilated
in a place remote from cold air, with
a cloth smear it: afterwards with luke-
warm water the hairs thus moistened, you will be able
to pluck out: and beware lest the depilatory
tarry too long upon the place, but
soon after application let it be removed, lest with
the hairs also the skin be taken off.
For the same
Take quicklime and let it be placed in water,
and let it stand in the sun, until that water
by the heat of the sun is consumed, and so let it be done
every day for a month, always to which
it is to be put on. And at the end of the month
let the lime be taken, and let it be powdered,
and fat of sheep [?] be mixed in: it plucks out
hairs without pain.
For the same

[Left Column (Treatise on Hiccups / Singultus)]
352 [Page Number]
Hiccup (Singultus)
Singultus, [or] hiccuping, cometh diverse
ways: as of too much eating and drinking,
and this hiccuping cometh commonly after
the eating and drinking: this may
[be] helped by making the patient aghast, afraid,
or ashamed, disdained, or right glad, or
by thrusting his finger into his throat,
holding him toward a thing ...
And hiccuping may come of corrupt humours
in the stomach, that maketh the stomach
weak and feeble, and this hiccup cometh rather
before meat than after. And this may
be helped by vomiting or purging
the offending humour. And then after
give him good meats and drinks;
let him beware of surfeiting.
Sometimes it cometh of cold
in the upper part of the stomach
and maketh that part not able to
deliver the corrupt humours that
are in the stomach.
Sometimes of wind and feebleness
in the stomach, and that may be in two
manners: either of cold wicked humour
or of some sickness, as a flux or a fever,
and when it is of a fever it is dangerous.
And if it come of a long flux, you
give him comfortable meats as
broth made with hen's flesh, capon, etc.,
and then give him Diapenidion
or Diatragacantha: and syrup
of violets with the mucilage of psyllium
and camomile; and apply unto his stomach
linseed and fenugreek boiled
in oil, and anoint the stomach with
oil of violets and oil of roses, and
if the hiccup come of sharp meats the same
things are good.
If it come of emptiness give him sugar roset
and cold herbs as purslane or lettuce,
or give him Diacerasam plumbea [?] etc. in the like.
Boil herbs and violets in water
and wet a cloth in that water and apply
it warm from the mouth of the stomach
down to the members all over the belly.
If it come of hot humours give him
cold things and purge him.
If it be of cold, give him oxymel to vomit
first and after purge him: then feed
him with the herb of wormwood with sugar or honey,
or rue boiled in honey, and hot electuaries,
and anoint his stomach with hot oils as oils
of bays and spike oils.
If it come of blood purge him with
cassia fistula with warm water.
If the stomach be hard
Take dates, take out the stones, grind them
with fresh grease, and plaster-wise lay
it on the stomach: and it helps it:
and the hiccup.

[Right Column (Hiccup Receipts & Sadler Addition)]
For the hiccup
Make him sneeze, or
let him hold his breath.
For the hiccup
Take a good handful of sage, pound it and
strain out the herb, and with that
herb and ale make a posset and drink
the ale hot.
For the hiccup
Mix the fine powder of betony with honey
and eat thereof.
Boil sage in water and thrust hands
up about the wrist in the warm water.
Aniseeds dried and smelled unto doth
help the hiccup.
For the hiccup
Take oil of rice, mix with wine
and give.
For the same
Castoreum with juice of mint and 3 oz.
in a tepid drink well mixed. Let it be given
1 or 2 spoonfuls when the hiccup is urgent.
Of dill seed 2 drams, let it be boiled
gently in generous wine; and syrup of water 1 oz. ...
... or smell to the body.
Or apply a cupping glass to the
region of the stomach: [it] is excellent.

=== Canvas 381 (351) ===
[Running Header & Page Number]
Diseases of the mother
351

[Left Column]
The dropsy of the mother
This disease may come for want of her
natural purgation; and then she
must have her purgations or she will
not be healed.
And it may come of phlegmatic
humours, and of wind in the mother,
and she may swell as if she were
with child; and this swelling is easily
known from being with child.
For this swelling arises
suddenly, and the child swells by
degrees; and this swelling arises
and falls again: the other increases.
This swelling removes from place
to place; the other does not so; and
more, this moves uncertainly; the
other reckons both by day and night.
In the dropsy, the woman's
cheeks are soft and ill-coloured; in
breeding child, the flesh of the cheeks
are firm and well-coloured.
And here is great difference
betwixt the dropsy of the mother and
wind in the mother: for wind will
lightly be vanished away; the dropsy
will not. All the wind is upon one
side; the dropsy holds all the mother.
To heal this infirmity, look in the
precipitation of the mother.
A suppository to purge the
mother.
Take the meal of barley and mix it with
honey, thick like paste for bread, and
wrap it in a fine linen cloth, and
put it up into the matrix, and let it
lie there all night or longer if need
be. If it make the place sore by
long lying there, anoint the place
with oil of roses or oil of violets.
Flaying [excoriation] of the mother does
come of a choleric humour in the mother,
and the signs are burning, pricking,
and smarting within.
And the mother may have
pimples, scabs, and blains with much
itching within; then wash these pimples
with juice of woodbine and milk mixed
together, or put it in with a pessary.
I did heal a woman that
had little red pimples no bigger than the
heads of little pins, with much smarting
and burning: quarter-water [or rosewater?] with a little
camphor, and she being washed therewith
was healed, I think for ever, for I did
never hear her complain again.
And some heal the marvel [matrix?]
calf's foot to anoint it withal, and
some with fresh or May butter.
Flaying [excoriation] of the mother does
come of sharp choleric humour
in the mother; and the tokens are of
smarting, pricking, and burning in
the place.

[Right Column]
For the matrix
Take album graecum [white dog-dung], 1 scruple or 1 drachm; temper it with
lily water.
For precipitation [prolapse] of the uterus, of whatever kind:
Take bay leaves, myrtle berries, of each half an ounce; seed of garden
parsnip, 3 drachms; let them be chewed/bruised, afterwards
let them be boiled with generous wine: of this
decoction give to the woman 3 ounces; let this
drink be repeated, if there be need.
Suffocation of the matrix, Quercetanus:
Take fecula of bryony, as much as suffices; let a pill of 10
or 12 grains weight be formed, mixing in
a little castoreum or asafoetida:
it is a supreme and precious remedy
against all suffocations of the matrix, and
is a singular cleanser of the matrix.
Plaster for descent [prolapse] of the matrix
Take mastic, labdanum, of each 3 drachms; galbanum half an ounce; gum
storax 2 drachms; make a plaster, and let it be applied upon
the navel. Dr. Sadler.
Pills for suffocation of the uterus, Dr. S[adler]:
Take Venice treacle half an ounce, castoreum 2 drachms, oil
of amber 1 scruple, with syrup of stoechas [French lavender]; mix, make a mass of pills.

=== Canvas 384 ([352v]) ===
[Full Page (Upside-Down)]
The year of our Lord God 1564 was the coldest spring and the windiest that ever I did see; it was the gayest [most abundant] year of blossoms of
all manner of fruit trees, and great plenty of fruit, and the most part of apples did rot/rise in the winter following by reason of the frost; it
was so vehement; also the summer and the winter were very windy, and [the] end was fair/fen.
In the month of January: If thunder sounds, it signifies strong winds and abundance of crops to be at hand.
In the month of February: If thunder sounds, it announces that death by disease of many men, especially of the rich, is at hand.
In the month of March: If thunder [sounds], it signifies strong winds and plenty of crops, and strifes among the people.
In the month of April: If thunder sounds, it announces a pleasant and fruitful year in all things, but marks the death of wicked men.
In the month of May: If thunder sounds, it signifies that it brings scarcity and famine in that year.
In the month of June: If thunder sounds, rich and poor men and the trees of the woods shall be endangered.
In the month of July: If thunder sounds, there shall be a good harvest in that year.
In the month of August: If thunder sounds, it signifies abundance of crops and the slaying of mighty men.
In the month of September: If thunder sounds, it signifies abundance of crops and the slaying of mighty men, and first announces grief.
In the month of October: If thunder sounds, it announces strong winds and a good corn-harvest, and scarcity of hay.
In the month of November: If thunder sounds, it signifies abundance of crops and joyfulness and all prosperous things.
In the month of December: If thunder sounds, it signifies a good harvest, peace among nations, and that all things are prosperous.
If the wind was strong on the first night of the Nativity of the Lord, in that year kings, princes, and bishops, and other rich and mighty men throughout
the whole world shall perish. If on the 2nd night, men throughout the whole world shall fail. If on the 3rd night, in that year orphans and many women shall die.
If on the 4th night, in that year bread shall not abound. If on the 5th night, craftsmen shall perish. If on the 6th night, in that year many scandals
it signifies to be at hand. If on the 7th night, in that year kings and princes and bishops shall go to war and shall not perish, but shall return thence safe; afterwards
indeed prosperous things shall happen to them. If on the 8th night, in that year it signifies the burning of houses. If on the 9th night, in that year many
old men shall perish by dying. If on the 10th night, in that year many trees of the woods shall be broken by the strength of the winds. If on the 11th night,
in that year many cattle shall die. If on the 12th night, in that year kings shall go to war and fighting in war shall perish by dying.
If on the first day of the Nativity of the Lord the sun is seen to shine, in that year the servants of God shall rejoice. If on the 2nd day, in that year gold and silver
shall abound much. If on the 3rd day, the sons of men, calves, and lambs shall be good. If on the 4th day, in that year there shall be no war, [but] gladness, peace, and concord.
If on the 5th day, in that year there shall be much hay on the earth. If on the 6th day, trees shall bring forth a multitude of acorns. If on the 7th [day],
day, fertility of milk. If on the 8th day, there shall be abundance of fish. If on the 9th day, sheep and oxen shall
multiply. If on the 10th day, silver [and honey?] shall be on the earth. If on the 11th day, it signifies mortality of men. If on the 12th day, [if] the sun
is seen to shine, in that year there shall be many infirmities among nations.
In the year of the Lord 1592, all the bay trees in England died above ground, but revived
at the roots for the most part, whereof I had two in my garden.
Henry Dingley
In the year of the Lord 1598, no fruit, apples nor pears [...]
